knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A matching is a set \(M\subseteq E\) whose distinct edges have no common endpoint. It is a maximum bipartite matching when \[|M|=\nu(G):=\max\{|N|:N\subseteq E\text{ is a matching}\}.\] Thus maximality is measured by cardinality among all matchings, rather than merely by inclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A maximum bipartite matching is a set of pairwise vertex-disjoint edges having the largest possible cardinality among all matchings of the graph.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Combining Covered Vertices of Maximum Bipartite Matchings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shows that side-specific coverage attained by two maximum matchings can be attained simultaneously by one maximum matching.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $G=(V,E)$ be bipartite with colour classes $U$ and $W$. Let $M$ and $N$ be maximum-size matchings, let $U'$ be the vertices of $U$ covered by $M$, and let $W'$ be the vertices of $W$ covered by $N$. Then there exists a maximum-size matching covering $U'\cup W'$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Given two maximum bipartite matchings, a maximum matching exists that covers the U-side vertices covered by the first and the W-side vertices covered by the second.
assumptions_latex: G=(V,E)\text{ is bipartite with colour classes }U\text{ and }W.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\text{ a maximum-size matching }L\text{ such that }U'\cup W'\subseteq V(L).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Integrality and Cost-Nonincreasing Recovery for Complete Bipartite Matchings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integrality of the fractional complete-matching formulation and polynomial-time integral recovery under edge costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a bipartite graph $B=(V,W,F)$, every extreme point of
\[P=\left\{y\in\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}^{F}:\sum_{v:(v,w)\in F}y_{vw}\le1\ \forall w\in W,\ \sum_{w:(v,w)\in F}y_{vw}=1\ \forall v\in V\right\}\]
has integer coordinates. Moreover, for any edge costs $(c_{vw})_{(v,w)\in F}$ and any feasible fractional solution $y\in P$, one can find in polynomial time a feasible integral solution $\widehat y\in P$ such that
\[\sum_{(v,w)\in F}c_{vw}\widehat y_{vw}\le\sum_{(v,w)\in F}c_{vw}y_{vw}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every extreme point of the fractional complete-matching polyhedron of a bipartite graph is integral. Given any feasible fractional solution and edge costs, a feasible integral solution of no greater cost can be found in polynomial time.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{ext}(P)\subseteq\mathbb{Z}^{F},\qquad \exists\widehat y\in P\cap\mathbb{Z}^{F}:c^\top\widehat y\le c^\top y\text{, computable in polynomial time}

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \nu(G)=|A|-\operatorname{def}(G).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Augmenting-Path Algorithm for Bipartite Matching
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directed-reachability formulation of one augmentation step for a bipartite matching.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $G=(U\mathbin{\dot\cup}W,E)$ be bipartite and let $M$ be a matching. Form $D_M$ by orienting each edge $uw\in M$ from $w$ to $u$ and each edge $uw\notin M$ from $u$ to $w$. Let $U_M$ and $W_M$ be the vertices of $U$ and $W$, respectively, missed by $M$. An $M$-augmenting path can be found by finding a directed path in $D_M$ from $U_M$ to $W_M$; augmenting along such a path produces a matching $M'$ with $|M'|>|M|$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Orient matched edges from W to U and unmatched edges from U to W. Searching for a directed path from an unmatched U-vertex to an unmatched W-vertex finds an augmenting path, whose edges can be toggled to obtain a larger matching.
assumptions_latex: U_M=\{u\in U:u\text{ is missed by }M\},\quad W_M=\{w\in W:w\text{ is missed by }M\}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{A directed }U_M\text{-to-}W_M\text{ path yields an }M\text{-augmenting path and a matching }M'\text{ with }|M'|>|M|.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(L\dot\cup R,E)\) is a finite bipartite graph.

notation.meaning: vertices incident with edges of M

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Perfect matching in a finite, balanced bipartite graph.

source_refs.locator: Section 10.1. Bipartite Matching p. 246

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A matching \(M\subseteq E\) is perfect if every vertex of \(L\dot\cup R\) is incident with exactly one edge of \(M\). Equivalently, \[V(M)=L\dot\cup R.\] Consequently a perfect matching can exist only when \(|L|=|R|\), and then every perfect matching has cardinality \(|L|=|R|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A perfect bipartite matching covers every vertex exactly once; hence the two color classes must have equal size.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Integral weights of perfect bipartite matchings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes edge weights whose total is integral on every perfect matching.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a bipartite graph and let \(w\in\mathbb{R}^{E}\). Every perfect matching of \(G\) has integer weight if and only if there exists \(b\in\mathbb{R}^{V}\) such that \(\sum_{v\in V}b_v=0\) and \(w_{uv}-b_u-b_v\in\mathbb{Z}\) for every edge \(uv\in E\) contained in at least one perfect matching.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every perfect matching of a bipartite graph has integer total weight exactly when vertex potentials summing to zero make the reduced weight integral on every edge belonging to some perfect matching.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \left[\forall M\text{ perfect},\ \sum_{e\in M}w_e\in\mathbb{Z}\right]\iff\left[\exists b\in\mathbb{R}^{V}:\ \sum_{v\in V}b_v=0\ \land\ \forall uv\in E,\ \bigl(uv\text{ lies in a perfect matching}\Rightarrow w_{uv}-b_u-b_v\in\mathbb{Z}\bigr)\right]

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Criterion for k disjoint perfect matchings in a bipartite graph
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A multiplicity version of perfect-matching existence characterized by induced-edge inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be bipartite and let \(k\in\mathbb Z_{+}\). Then \(G\) has \(k\) pairwise edge-disjoint perfect matchings if and only if every \(X\subseteq V\) satisfies \[|E(G[X])|\geq k\left(|X|-\frac{|V|}{2}\right).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bipartite graph has k pairwise edge-disjoint perfect matchings exactly when every vertex subset X spans at least k(|X|-|V|/2) edges.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigl(G\text{ has }k\text{ pairwise edge-disjoint perfect matchings}\bigr)\iff\bigl(\forall X\subseteq V,\ |E(G[X])|\geq k(|X|-|V|/2)\bigr)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Triangular labeling for a uniquely matchable bipartite graph
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ordering representation implied by uniqueness of a perfect matching in a bipartite graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G_0=(U_0,W_0)\) be a bipartite graph with a unique perfect matching. Then its color classes can be labeled \(U_0=\{u_1,\ldots,u_m\}\) and \(W_0=\{w_1,\ldots,w_m\}\) so that every edge \(u_iw_j\in E(G_0)\) satisfies \(i\ge j\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bipartite graph with a unique perfect matching admits equal-size labelings of its two color classes in which every edge lies on or below the diagonal of the bipartite adjacency matrix.
assumptions_latex: G_0=(U_0,W_0)\text{ is a bipartite graph with a unique perfect matching.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Matching and Perfect Matching in a Bipartite Graph
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Vertex-incidence definitions and the cardinality consequence for perfect bipartite matchings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $G=(V^+,V^-;E)$ be a bipartite graph. A set $M\subseteq E$ is a matching if every vertex is incident to at most one edge of $M$, and it is a perfect matching if every vertex is incident to exactly one edge of $M$. If $M$ is perfect, then $|M|=|V^+|=|V^-|$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A matching is a set of edges using each vertex at most once. It is perfect when every vertex is used exactly once. A perfect bipartite matching has as many edges as either vertex class, so the two classes have equal size.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: M\text{ is perfect}\Rightarrow |M|=|V^+|=|V^-|

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bipartite Perfect-Matching Feasibility and Minimum-Weight Formulation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded statement retaining the unresolved source reference to formulation (5.8).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be a bipartite graph and \(c\in\mathbb{R}^{E}\). Then \(G\) has a perfect matching if and only if formulation \((5.8)\) has a feasible solution. Moreover, if \(G\) has a perfect matching, then its minimum perfect-matching weight equals the optimal value of \((5.8)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a bipartite graph with real edge weights, a perfect matching exists exactly when formulation (5.8) is feasible; when one exists, its minimum weight equals that formulation's optimal value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G\text{ has a perfect matching}\iff (5.8)\text{ is feasible},\qquad G\text{ has a perfect matching}\Rightarrow \min_{M\text{ perfect}}c(M)=\operatorname{opt}(5.8).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bipartite alternating-tree obstruction to perfect matching
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A perfect-matching nonexistence certificate obtained from an exhausted alternating tree in a bipartite graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be bipartite, let \(M\) be a matching of \(G\), and let \(T\) be an \(M\)-alternating tree. If no edge of \(G\) joins a vertex in \(B(T)\) to a vertex outside \(V(T)\), then \(T\) is frustrated and consequently \(G\) has no perfect matching.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a bipartite graph, an M-alternating tree with no edge from B(T) to a vertex outside the tree is frustrated and certifies that the graph has no perfect matching.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T\text{ is frustrated and }G\text{ has no perfect matching}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent perfect-matching criterion expressed through the sizes of all vertex covers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A bipartite graph \(G=(V,E)\) has a perfect matching if and only if every vertex cover \(C\subseteq V\) satisfies \(|C|\geq \tfrac12|V|\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Potential characterization of a unique minimum-weight perfect matching
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes uniqueness in a balanced weighted bipartite graph through an ordering and reduced-cost sign pattern.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V^+,V^-;E)\) be bipartite with \(|V^+|=|V^-|=m\), and let \(c:V^+\times V^-\to\mathbf R\cup\{+\infty\}\) satisfy \(c(u,v)<+\infty\iff (u,v)\in E\). A unique minimum-weight perfect matching exists if and only if there are a potential \(\widehat p:V^+\cup V^-\to\mathbf R\) and orderings \(V^+=\{u_1,\ldots,u_m\}\), \(V^-=\{v_1,\ldots,v_m\}\) such that \(c(u_i,v_j)+\widehat p(u_i)-\widehat p(v_j)=0\) for \(i=j\), is nonnegative for \(j<i\), and is strictly positive for \(i<j\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A balanced weighted bipartite graph has a unique minimum-weight perfect matching exactly when its two vertex classes can be ordered and assigned potentials so that diagonal reduced costs are zero, reduced costs below the diagonal are nonnegative, and those above the diagonal are strictly positive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists!\text{ minimum-weight perfect matching}\iff\exists\widehat p,(u_i)_{i=1}^m,(v_i)_{i=1}^m:\ c(u_i,v_j)+\widehat p(u_i)-\widehat p(v_j)\begin{cases}=0&i=j,\\ \geq0&j<i,\\ >0&i<j.\end{cases}

children.title: Neighborhood Surplus Regimes

assumptions_latex: \(G=(L\dot\cup R,E)\) is a finite bipartite graph with \(L\ne\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G\) has left neighborhood surplus at least \(k\) if and only if \(|N_G(X)|-|X|\ge k\) for every nonempty \(X\subseteq L\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform additive Hall surplus on a nonempty designated color class.

source_refs.locator: Section 10.1. Bipartite Matching p. 246

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(L\ne\varnothing\), define \[\sigma_L(G):=\min_{\varnothing\ne X\subseteq L}\bigl(|N_G(X)|-|X|\bigr).\] The neighborhood-surplus-\(k\) regime is the condition \(\sigma_L(G)\ge k\), equivalently \[|N_G(X)|\ge |X|+k\qquad\text{for every nonempty }X\subseteq L.\] For \(k=0\), this is Hall's condition for a matching saturating \(L\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonempty left color class, neighborhood surplus at least k means every nonempty left subset has at least k more neighbors than its own size.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Neighborhood Surplus and Surplus-Tight Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines set and graph surplus, records its sign relation to deficiency and its submodularity, and defines surplus-tight sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(A,B;E)\) be bipartite. For \(X\subseteq A\), define \(\sigma_G(X)=|\Gamma_G(X)|-|X|=-\operatorname{def}_G(X)\), and define \(\sigma(G)=\min_{\varnothing\neq Z\subseteq A}\sigma_G(Z)\). Then \(\operatorname{def}(G)=\max\{0,-\sigma(G)\}\). Moreover, for all \(X,Y\subseteq A\), \[\sigma_G(X\cup Y)+\sigma_G(X\cap Y)\leq \sigma_G(X)+\sigma_G(Y).\] A set \(X\subseteq A\) is \(\sigma\)-tight if \(\sigma_G(X)=\sigma(G)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set's surplus is its number of neighbors minus its size, while graph surplus is the minimum over nonempty subsets of side A. It is the negative of set deficiency, determines graph deficiency after truncation at zero, is submodular, and its minimizers are called sigma-tight.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sigma_G(X)=-\operatorname{def}_G(X),\quad \operatorname{def}(G)=\max\{0,-\sigma(G)\},\quad \sigma_G(X\cup Y)+\sigma_G(X\cap Y)\leq\sigma_G(X)+\sigma_G(Y),\quad X\text{ is }\sigma\text{-tight}\iff\sigma_G(X)=\sigma(G).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: König–Egerváry Theorem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bipartite matching–vertex-cover min–max equality, together with its equivalent binary-matrix formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every bipartite graph $G$, the maximum cardinality $\nu(G)$ of a matching equals the minimum cardinality $\tau(G)$ of a vertex cover. Equivalently, for every $A\in\{0,1\}^{m\times n}$, the maximum number of $1$-entries with no two in a common row or column equals the minimum number of rows and columns whose union contains every $1$-entry.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a bipartite graph, maximum matching size equals minimum vertex-cover size. Equivalently, in a binary matrix, the largest collection of 1s sharing no row or column has the same size as the smallest collection of rows and columns covering all 1s.
assumptions_latex: For the equivalent matrix formulation, $A\in\{0,1\}^{m\times n}$.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \nu(G)=\tau(G);\qquad \max\{|S|:S\subseteq\operatorname{supp}(A),\ S\text{ contains at most one entry from each row and column}\}=\min\{|L|:L\text{ is a collection of rows and columns covering }\operatorname{supp}(A)\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Egerváry’s weighted matching–cover theorem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted bipartite matching duality, including integral optimal covers for integral weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $G=(V,E)$ be bipartite and let $w:E\to\mathbb{R}_+$. Then
\[
\max\left\{\sum_{e\in M}w_e:M\text{ is a matching in }G\right\}
=
\min\left\{\sum_{v\in V}y_v:y\in\mathbb{R}_+^V,\ y_u+y_v\geq w_{uv}\ \forall uv\in E\right\}.
\]
If $w\in\mathbb{Z}_+^E$, the minimum admits an optimal solution in $\mathbb{Z}_+^V$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a bipartite graph with nonnegative edge weights, the maximum weight of a matching equals the minimum total nonnegative vertex weight whose endpoint sums dominate the edge weights. Integral edge weights admit an integral optimal vertex weighting.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \max_{M\text{ matching}}\sum_{e\in M}w_e=\min_{\substack{y\in\mathbb{R}_+^V\\y_u+y_v\geq w_{uv}\ \forall uv\in E}}\sum_{v\in V}y_v,\quad w\in\mathbb{Z}_+^E\Rightarrow\operatorname*{argmin}_{\substack{y\in\mathbb{R}_+^V\\y_u+y_v\geq w_{uv}}}\sum_{v\in V}y_v\cap\mathbb{Z}_+^V\neq\varnothing

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Matching Number, Vertex-Cover Number, and Weak Inequality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions of the two cardinality parameters, their universal weak inequality, and the failure of equality for general graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A vertex cover of a graph \(G\) is a set \(C\subseteq V(G)\) meeting every edge. Define \(
u(G)=\max\{|M|:M	ext{ is a matching in }G\}\) and \(	au(G)=\min\{|C|:C	ext{ is a vertex cover of }G\}\). For every graph \(G\), \(
u(G)\leq	au(G)\); equality need not hold, since \(
u(K_3)<	au(K_3)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vertex cover meets every edge. The matching number is the maximum matching size, and the vertex-cover number is the minimum cover size. Every graph has matching number at most its vertex-cover number, and the triangle shows that equality can fail.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \nu(G)\leq\tau(G),\qquad \nu(K_3)<\tau(K_3).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Allowed-edge components and their contracted bipartite graph
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Construction used to decompose a bipartite graph with a perfect matching into elementary components.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(U,W)\) be a bipartite graph with a perfect matching, and let \(L_1,\ldots,L_k\), where \(k\ge 1\), be the components of the subgraph consisting of all allowed edges of \(G\). Each \(L_i\) is elementary. Define \(S_i=U\cap V(L_i)\) and \(T_i=W\cap V(L_i)\). The graph \(G_0\) is obtained by shrinking every \(S_i\) and every \(T_i\) to a vertex and replacing each resulting set of parallel edges by one edge.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a bipartite graph with a perfect matching, the allowed-edge subgraph has elementary components. Contracting the two color-class portions of each component separately and suppressing parallel edges produces a bipartite quotient graph.
assumptions_latex: G=(U,W)\text{ is a bipartite graph with a perfect matching.}
L_1,\ldots,L_k\text{ are the components of the subgraph consisting of all allowed edges of }G.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall i\in\{1,\ldots,k\},\ L_i\text{ is elementary};\quad S_i=U\cap V(L_i),\ T_i=W\cap V(L_i),\text{ and }G_0\text{ is obtained by contracting all }S_i,T_i\text{ separately and suppressing parallel edges.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equivalent Characterizations of Elementary Bipartite Graphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes elementary bipartite graphs through minimum vertex covers, strict Hall expansion, opposite-color vertex deletion, and allowed edges.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be a bipartite graph with bipartition \((U,W)\). The following are equivalent: (i) \(G\) is elementary; (ii) \(G\) has exactly two minimum vertex covers, namely \(U\) and \(W\); (iii) \(|U|=|W|\) and \(|\Gamma(X)|\ge |X|+1\) for every nonempty proper subset \(X\subset U\); (iv) either \(G=K_2\), or \(|V(G)|\ge4\) and \(G-u-w\) has a perfect matching for every \(u\in U\) and \(w\in W\); (v) \(G\) is connected and every edge of \(G\) is allowed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a bipartite graph, being elementary is equivalent to having only its two color classes as minimum vertex covers, satisfying strict Hall expansion on every nonempty proper subset of one class, retaining a perfect matching after deletion of any opposite-color pair except for the stated K2 case, and being connected with every edge allowed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Conditions (i)--(v) are equivalent.}

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every subgraph G_0 without isolated vertices of an elementary bipartite graph G is contained in a nice elementary subgraph G' of G whose cyclomatic number is at most the number of edges of G_0 minus one.
assumptions_latex: $G_0\subseteq G$ is a subgraph without isolated vertices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists a nice elementary subgraph $G'$ with $G_0\subseteq G'\subseteq G$ and cyclomatic number at most $|E(G_0)|-1$.

children.title: Bipartite Ear Decompositions
children.top_down_role: Ear-based structural representations for elementary bipartite graphs.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(L\dot\cup R,E)\) is a finite bipartite graph with at least one edge.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G\) is elementary if and only if it has a spanning bipartite ear decomposition beginning with \(K_2\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Odd-ear characterization; conventions about surplus edges require source confirmation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A bipartite ear decomposition starts with \(G_0\cong K_2\) and, for \(i=1,\ldots,t\), forms \(G_i\) by adjoining an odd-length path \(P_i\) whose endpoints lie in opposite color classes of \(G_{i-1}\) and whose internal vertices are new. The characterization asserts that \(G\) is elementary if and only if some such sequence has \(V(G_t)=V(G)\) and \(G_t\) as a spanning subgraph of \(G\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Elementary bipartite graphs are characterized by construction from one edge through successive odd ears with new internal vertices.
knowledge_statements.title: Bipartite Ear Decompositions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The odd-ear characterization is convention-sensitive, particularly concerning initial graphs, admissible endpoints, single-edge ears, and whether the resulting sequence equals the graph or only a spanning subgraph. With no cited source, the exact theorem cannot be reliably accepted.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bipartite Ear Decomposition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the iterative odd-ear construction for bipartite graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Begin with an edge \(x\), and join its endpoints by an odd-length path \(P_1\). Inductively, if \(G_{r-1}=x+P_1+\cdots+P_{r-1}\), add an odd path \(P_r\) whose endpoints belong to different color classes of \(G_{r-1}\) and whose other vertices do not belong to \(G_{r-1}\). A representation \(G_r=x+P_1+\cdots+P_r\) obtained this way is a bipartite ear decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bipartite ear decomposition starts with an edge and an odd path joining its endpoints, then repeatedly adds an odd path between opposite color classes with all internal vertices new.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G_r=x+P_1+\cdots+P_r\text{ is a bipartite ear decomposition when every added ear satisfies the stated parity, endpoint, and disjointness conditions.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bipartite Ear Selection Lemma
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Selects an alternating relative ear with endpoints in prescribed bipartition classes under balance and separation conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose $G=(U,W)$ is a $1$-extendable bipartite graph, $H$ is a nice subgraph of $G$, $M$ is a perfect matching of $G-V(H)$, and $V(H)=V_1\mathbin{\dot\cup}V_2$. If $|V_1\cap U|\ge |V_1\cap W|$ and no edge of $H$ joins $V_1$ to $V_2$, then $G$ contains an ear relative to $H$ that alternates with respect to $M$ and joins $V_1\cap U$ to $V_2\cap W$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the stated balance and separation conditions, a 1-extendable bipartite graph has an alternating relative ear from the U-side of the first part to the W-side of the second part.
assumptions_latex: H\text{ is a nice subgraph of }G
M\text{ is a perfect matching of }G-V(H)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\text{ an }M\text{-alternating ear of }G\text{ relative to }H\text{ joining }V_1\cap U\text{ to }V_2\cap W.

children.title: Kuhn Search Method
children.top_down_role: Depth-first alternating search used in bipartite matching.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(U,V;E)\) is a finite bipartite graph represented by adjacency lists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M' = M\triangle E(P)\) when an augmenting path \(P\) is found; otherwise \(M'=M\).

notation.meaning: Visited marker for left vertices during one search

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Depth-first single-root augmenting search for unweighted bipartite matching.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given an exposed vertex \(u\in U\), initialize \(\operatorname{seen}(x)=0\) for every \(x\in U\). Define \(\operatorname{search}(x)\) to fail if \(\operatorname{seen}(x)=1\); otherwise set \(\operatorname{seen}(x)=1\) and inspect each \(y\in N(x)\). If \(y\) is exposed, match \(x\) to \(y\) and return success. If \(y\) is matched to \(z\) and \(\operatorname{search}(z)\) succeeds, replace \(zy\) by \(xy\) and return success. Return failure after all neighbors fail. The output is the resulting matching, enlarged by one exactly on success.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A depth-first search recursively reroutes matched edges until it reaches an exposed right vertex, producing one augmentation.
knowledge_statements.title: Kuhn Search Method

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role and depth-first augmentation description fit the leaf, but the recursive matching-update specification has no inspectable source.

children.title: Single-Augmentation Regime
children.top_down_role: Matching improvement organized around one augmenting path per search.

assumptions_latex: \(M\) is a matching and \(P\) is an \(M\)-augmenting path.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|M\triangle E(P)|=|M|+1\).

notation.meaning: Edge set of the augmenting path

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes the one-path-per-success regime of the Kuhn algorithm family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Because an \(M\)-augmenting path \(P\) begins and ends with unmatched edges and alternates between edges outside and inside \(M\), it contains exactly one more unmatched than matched edge. Consequently \(M\triangle E(P)\) is a matching of cardinality \(|M|+1\). A single-augmentation algorithm commits this update immediately and starts a fresh search rather than collecting several vertex-disjoint augmenting paths into one phase. Repeating successful searches terminates after at most \(\min\{|U|,|V|\}\) augmentations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each successful search flips one augmenting path and increases the matching size by exactly one before a new search begins.
knowledge_statements.title: Single-Augmentation Regime

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The one-augmentation property is standard and correctly scoped, but it lacks a citation and includes derivational proof-style text that should be removed when sourced.

assumptions_latex: Each root search uses a fresh visited set and explores every admissible neighbor before reporting failure.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates order-independent correctness from order-dependent DFS traces and running time.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Permuting the exposed roots or the adjacency lists may change which augmenting path a Kuhn search first discovers, the intermediate matchings, and the number of recursively inspected edges. It does not change the guarantee of maximum cardinality when every required search is complete and visited marks are reset for each new root. With adjacency lists, one root search costs \(O(m)\), so the single-augmentation implementation has the order-independent worst-case bound \(O(|U|m)\), although particular orders can require substantially less work.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Root and neighbor order can change augmenting paths and work, but complete searches still return a maximum matching.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The order-sensitivity claim is plausible, but the phrase “every required search” does not precisely specify the root-processing schedule needed for the maximum-matching guarantee, and no source resolves this ambiguity.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(U,V;E)\) is a finite bipartite graph with \(n=|U|+|V|\) and \(m=|E|\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\text{ is maximum and is computed in }O(m\sqrt n)\text{ time.}\)

notation.meaning: Shortest augmenting-path length in the current phase

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard unweighted bipartite Hopcroft–Karp algorithm and adjacency-list bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(M=\varnothing\). In each phase, breadth-first search the alternating graph from all exposed vertices of \(U\), retaining layers through the first exposed vertices of \(V\); let \(\ell\) be their common shortest augmenting-path length. Using depth-first searches restricted to consecutive layers, find a maximal family \(\mathcal P\) of pairwise vertex-disjoint augmenting paths of length \(\ell\), and set \(M\leftarrow M\triangle\bigcup_{P\in\mathcal P}E(P)\). Stop when breadth-first search reaches no exposed vertex of \(V\), and output \(M\). With adjacency lists, the total running time is \(O(m\sqrt n)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Hopcroft–Karp repeatedly augments along a maximal disjoint family of shortest layered augmenting paths in O(m square-root n) time.
knowledge_statements.title: Hopcroft–Karp Layered-Phase Methods

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The layered-phase algorithm and stated complexity are standard and appropriate for this topic container, but neither the algorithm nor the O(m sqrt(n)) bound has an inspectable citation.

children.title: Alternating-Path Certificates
children.top_down_role: Reachability structures certifying augmentability or maximality.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\text{ is maximum}\iff\text{there is no }M\text{-augmenting path}.\)

notation.meaning: Directed alternating graph associated with M
Vertices reachable from exposed vertices of U

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bipartite specialization of the augmenting-path optimality certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Orient every edge in \(E\setminus M\) from \(U\) to \(V\), and every edge in \(M\) from \(V\) to \(U\), obtaining \(D_M\). Let \(Z\) be the vertices reachable in \(D_M\) from the exposed vertices of \(U\). A directed path from such a root to an exposed vertex of \(V\) is an \(M\)-augmenting path and certifies that \(M\) is not maximum. Conversely, if no exposed vertex of \(V\) lies in \(Z\), the absence of an augmenting path certifies that \(M\) is maximum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reachability either exhibits an augmenting path proving nonoptimality or certifies maximum cardinality by showing none exists.
knowledge_statements.title: Alternating-Path Certificates

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The alternating-reachability certificate is correctly formulated and the certificate kind fits the leaf, but Berge’s augmenting-path characterization is uncited.

children.title: Vertex-Cover Certificates
children.top_down_role: Cover objects certifying bipartite matching optimality.

assumptions_latex: \(M\) has no augmenting path, and \(Z\) is alternating-reachable from the exposed vertices of \(U\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C=(U\setminus Z)\cup(V\cap Z)\text{ is a vertex cover and }|C|=|M|.\)
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constructive minimum-cover certificate obtained from a maximum matching search.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Form the alternating orientation relative to \(M\), and let \(Z\) be the vertices reachable from exposed vertices of \(U\). If no exposed vertex of \(V\) is reachable, define \(C=(U\setminus Z)\cup(V\cap Z)\). Every edge has an endpoint in \(C\), so \(C\) is a vertex cover. Moreover each edge of \(M\) has exactly one endpoint in \(C\), while every vertex of \(C\) is incident with an edge of \(M\). Hence \(|C|=|M|\), and the pair \((M,C)\) is directly verifiable as a maximum-matching and minimum-cover certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Alternating reachability constructs a vertex cover with one vertex per matching edge, certifying both objects as optimal.
knowledge_statements.title: Vertex-Cover Certificates

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The constructed cover and equality |C|=|M| are correctly scoped under the no-augmenting-path hypothesis, but the certificate construction has no source.

children.title: Matching–Cover Certificate Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Structural correspondence between optimal matchings plus minimum covers.

assumptions_latex: \(M\) is a matching and \(C\) is a vertex cover.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|M|=|C|\implies M\text{ is maximum and }C\text{ is minimum}.\)
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Kőnig matching–cover equality with mutually checkable primal and dual witnesses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Every vertex cover meets every matching edge, and distinct matching edges require distinct covering incidences; therefore \(|M|\le |C|\) for every matching \(M\) and vertex cover \(C\). In a bipartite graph, alternating reachability from any maximum matching constructs a vertex cover of the same cardinality. Consequently \(\nu(G)=\tau(G)\). In particular, presenting a matching \(M\) and a vertex cover \(C\) satisfying \(|M|=|C|\) simultaneously certifies that \(M\) is maximum and \(C\) is minimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In bipartite graphs, maximum matching size equals minimum vertex-cover size; equal-sized feasible witnesses certify each other.
knowledge_statements.title: Matching–Cover Certificate Correspondence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The duality role and equal-sized-witness certificate are mathematically correct, but Kőnig’s equality is uncited and the statement contains proof-style justification.

children.title: Square Assignment
children.top_down_role: Balanced assignment instances with equally sized vertex classes.

assumptions_latex: \(c=(c_{ij})\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) is a finite cost matrix.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min_{\pi\in S_n}\sum_{i=1}^n c_{i,\pi(i)}\).

source_refs.locator: Section 8. The Hungarian Method for Weighted Matching p. 201

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A square assignment instance has two sets of equal cardinality \(n\) and costs \(c_{ij}\) for assigning left item \(i\) to right item \(j\). A feasible assignment is a permutation \(\pi\in S_n\), equivalently a binary matrix \(x\) satisfying \(\sum_{j=1}^n x_{ij}=1\) for every \(i\), \(\sum_{i=1}^n x_{ij}=1\) for every \(j\), and \(x_{ij}\in\{0,1\}\). The minimum-cost square assignment minimizes \(\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^n c_{ij}x_{ij}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A square assignment bijectively pairs n agents with n tasks while minimizing total pair cost.
knowledge_statements.title: Square Assignment

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(m\le n\), a rectangular assignment assigns every left item to a distinct right item. knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A maximum-weight assignment is a bijection \(\pi:L\to R\), identified with a permutation \(\pi\in S_n\), that maximizes total assigned weight. Its optimal value is
\[
W^*=\max_{\pi\in S_n}\sum_{i=1}^n w_{i,\pi(i)}.
\]
Equivalently, using variables \(x_{ij}\in\{0,1\}\), it maximizes \(\sum_{i,j}w_{ij}x_{ij}\) subject to \(\sum_jx_{ij}=1\) for every \(i\in L\) and \(\sum_ix_{ij}=1\) for every \(j\in R\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose one distinct right vertex for each left vertex so that the sum of selected edge weights is maximum.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Symmetric maximum-weight assignment
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines admissible assignments, complete and partial assignments, and the symmetric maximum-benefit assignment model; it also identifies the asymmetric cardinality regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let there be $n$ persons and $n$ objects, with nonempty admissible-object sets $A(i)$ and benefits $a_{ij}$ for $j\in A(i)$. Define $\mathcal A=\{(i,j):i=1,\ldots,n,\ j\in A(i)\}$. An assignment is a set $S\subseteq\mathcal A$ containing at most one pair for each person and at most one pair for each object. It is complete or feasible when $|S|=n$ and partial otherwise. The symmetric assignment problem maximizes $\sum_{(i,j)\in S}a_{ij}$ over complete assignments. The corresponding regime with fewer persons than objects is called asymmetric.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An assignment is a matching of admissible person–object pairs. With equally many persons and objects it is complete when it has n pairs, and the symmetric maximum-weight problem maximizes total benefit over such assignments. Fewer persons than objects gives the asymmetric regime.
assumptions_latex: a_{ij}\text{ is specified for every }(i,j)\in\mathcal A
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \max\left\{\sum_{(i,j)\in S}a_{ij}:S\subseteq\mathcal A\text{ is an assignment and }|S|=n\right\}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Balanced Minimum-Cost Assignment and Its Transportation LP Relaxation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Formulates balanced minimum-cost assignment and states the integrality guarantee of its unit-supply, unit-demand transportation relaxation, including the solver-output boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let |\mathcal S|=|\mathcal D|=m, with assignment costs c_{ij}. The balanced assignment problem is \(\min \sum_{i\in\mathcal S}\sum_{j\in\mathcal D}c_{ij}x_{ij}\), subject to \(\sum_{j\in\mathcal D}x_{ij}=1\) for every \(i\in\mathcal S\), \(\sum_{i\in\mathcal S}x_{ij}=1\) for every \(j\in\mathcal D\), and \(x_{ij}\in\{0,1\}\). Replacing \(x_{ij}\in\{0,1\}\) by \(x_{ij}\ge 0\) yields a Hitchcock transportation LP with unit supplies and demands. Every assignment is feasible for the relaxation, and every integral relaxation-feasible point is an assignment. Network simplex produces an integral optimal solution of this relaxation and therefore solves the assignment problem. Without a unique optimum, an interior-point method is not guaranteed to return an integral optimal point; if the optimum is unique, every LP solver returns that integral optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For equal-sized sets of people and tasks, balanced minimum-cost assignment assigns each person to exactly one task and covers each task exactly once. Dropping binary restrictions gives a transportation LP with unit supplies and demands. Network simplex returns an integral optimum and thus solves the assignment problem. When alternate optima exist, an interior-point method is not guaranteed to return an integral optimum; a unique optimum is integral and common to all LP solvers.
assumptions_latex: x_{ij}\ge 0\quad\forall(i,j)\in\mathcal S\times\mathcal D\ \text{in the LP relaxation}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Network simplex obtains an integral optimum of the assignment LP relaxation; interior-point output is not guaranteed integral when the optimal face is non-singleton.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Square Minimum-Cost Assignment Formulation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the balanced one-to-one minimum-cost assignment problem, its binary-matrix formulation, and the associated doubly stochastic and permutation matrix classes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For costs \(c_{ij}\) on \(n\) persons and \(n\) jobs, a feasible assignment is a permutation \((p_1,\ldots,p_n)\) of \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with cost \(\sum_{i=1}^n c_{i p_i}\). Equivalently, it is represented by \(X=(x_{ij})\in\{0,1\}^{n\times n}\) satisfying \(\sum_{j=1}^n x_{ij}=1\) for every \(i\) and \(\sum_{i=1}^n x_{ij}=1\) for every \(j\), and minimizes \(\sum_{i,j}c_{ij}x_{ij}\). A nonnegative square matrix whose row and column sums are all one is doubly stochastic; such a matrix is a permutation matrix when all entries are binary. The permutation formulation has \(n!\) feasible assignments.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A square minimum-cost assignment pairs each of n persons with exactly one of n jobs and minimizes total selected cost. Feasible assignments are permutations, equivalently binary matrices with every row and column sum equal to one. Nonnegative matrices with these sums are doubly stochastic, and binary ones are permutation matrices. There are n! possible assignments.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min_{X\in\{0,1\}^{n\times n}}\left\{\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^n c_{ij}x_{ij}:\sum_{j=1}^n x_{ij}=1\ \forall i,\ \sum_{i=1}^n x_{ij}=1\ \forall j\right\}

children.title: Objective-Convention Equivalence
children.top_down_role: Transformations connecting reward-maximization with cost-minimization formulations.

assumptions_latex: There are \(n\) assigned edges in every feasible assignment.
Weights \(w_{ij}\in\mathbb{R}\) are converted to costs by \(c_{ij}=K-w_{ij}\), where \(K\in\mathbb{R}\) is fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The maximum-weight and transformed minimum-cost problems have identical optimal assignments, with \(C^*=nK-W^*\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine conversion for fixed-cardinality perfect assignments.

source_refs.locator: 1.2.1 The Minimum Cost Flow Problem p. 9
source_refs.source_title: Network Optimization: Continuous and Discrete Models

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every feasible assignment \(\pi\in S_n\), define \(W(\pi)=\sum_iw_{i,\pi(i)}\) and \(C(\pi)=\sum_ic_{i,\pi(i)}\). If \(c_{ij}=K-w_{ij}\), then
\[
C(\pi)=nK-W(\pi).
\]
Consequently, \(W(\pi)\geq W(\sigma)\) if and only if \(C(\pi)\leq C(\sigma)\) for all \(\pi,\sigma\in S_n\). Thus the maximizers of \(W\) are exactly the minimizers of \(C\), and their optimal values satisfy \(C^*=nK-W^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Subtracting every weight from one fixed constant converts maximization to minimization without changing the optimal perfect assignments.
knowledge_statements.title: Objective-Convention Equivalence

children.title: Bottleneck Assignment
children.top_down_role: Assignment quality governed by the worst selected edge value.

assumptions_latex: The bipartite graph is complete and balanced, with finite edge costs \(c_{ij}\in\mathbb{R}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A bottleneck-optimal assignment minimizes \(\max_i c_{i,\pi(i)}\) over \(\pi\in S_n\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimization form of the bottleneck assignment problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For an assignment \(\pi\in S_n\), its bottleneck cost is
\[
b(\pi)=\max_{1\leq i\leq n}c_{i,\pi(i)}.
\]
The bottleneck assignment problem seeks
\[
b^*=\min_{\pi\in S_n}b(\pi).
\]
An assignment \(\pi^*\) is bottleneck-optimal precisely when \(b(\pi^*)=b^*\). Unlike the ordinary minimum-cost assignment, this objective depends only on the largest selected edge cost and does not distinguish assignments having the same largest cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimize the largest edge cost appearing in a perfect assignment, without regard to the sum of its selected costs.
knowledge_statements.title: Bottleneck Assignment

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The minimax definition is precise and standard, but the record supplies no citation supporting the selected minimization convention for bottleneck assignment.

children.title: Lexicographic Assignment
children.top_down_role: Assignment quality governed by an ordered hierarchy of selected values.

assumptions_latex: The bipartite graph is complete and balanced, with finite edge costs \(c_{ij}\in\mathbb{R}\).
Selected costs are sorted in nonincreasing order before comparison.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A lexicographically optimal assignment minimizes its nonincreasing sorted cost vector in lexicographic order.

notation.meaning: nonincreasing rearrangement of the costs selected by \(\pi\)

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lexicographic bottleneck minimization of sorted selected costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(\pi\in S_n\), let \(s(\pi)=(s_1(\pi),\ldots,s_n(\pi))\) be the costs \(c_{i,\pi(i)}\) sorted so that \(s_1(\pi)\geq\cdots\geq s_n(\pi)\). An assignment \(\pi^*\) is lexicographically optimal when
\[
s(\pi^*)\leq_{\mathrm{lex}}s(\pi)\qquad\text{for every }\pi\in S_n.
\]
Thus it first minimizes the largest selected cost; subject to that, it minimizes the second largest selected cost, and continues through all coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sort each assignment's selected costs from largest to smallest, then minimize the resulting vector lexicographically.
knowledge_statements.title: Lexicographic Assignment

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The nonincreasing-vector lexicographic minimization variant is internally correct, but no source supports this specific assignment convention.

children.title: Bottleneck–Lexicographic Refinement
children.top_down_role: Refinement relationships between worst-value optimization plus lexicographic comparison.

assumptions_latex: Assignments are compared through their selected costs sorted in nonincreasing order.
The bottleneck objective minimizes the first coordinate of that sorted vector.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every lexicographically optimal assignment is bottleneck-optimal, and subsequent coordinates refine ties successively.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relation between bottleneck and lexicographic minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Because \(s_1(\pi)=\max_i c_{i,\pi(i)}\), any assignment minimizing \(s(\pi)\) lexicographically also minimizes the bottleneck value. More precisely, let \(\mathcal{P}_0=S_n\) and recursively define
\[
\alpha_k=\min_{\pi\in\mathcal{P}_{k-1}}s_k(\pi),\qquad
\mathcal{P}_k=\{\pi\in\mathcal{P}_{k-1}:s_k(\pi)=\alpha_k\}.
\]
Then \(\alpha_1=b^*\), \(\mathcal{P}_1\) is the set of bottleneck-optimal assignments, and \(\mathcal{P}_n\) is exactly the set of lexicographically optimal assignments.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lexicographic optimization first solves the bottleneck problem, then successively breaks ties using the next-largest selected costs.
knowledge_statements.title: Bottleneck–Lexicographic Refinement

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The refinement relation is correct under the preceding nonincreasing minimization convention, but neither that convention nor the refinement claim has cited support.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The linear-programming dual of the maximum-weight assignment problem is
\[
\min\left\{\sum_{i\in L}u_i+\sum_{j\in R}v_j: u_i+v_j\geq w_{ij}\text{ for all }(i,j)\in L\times R\right\},
\]
where \(u_i,v_j\in\mathbb{R}\) are unrestricted. Every feasible pair \((u,v)\) gives an upper bound on every assignment weight. A feasible assignment and feasible potentials are simultaneously optimal when each assigned edge satisfies \(u_i+v_j=w_{ij}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Vertex potentials dominate every edge weight; minimizing their total gives the dual assignment problem, with equality on optimally assigned edges.
knowledge_statements.title: Assignment Dual Potentials

children.title: Reduced-Cost Geometry
children.top_down_role: Geometric structure induced by reduced edge costs.

assumptions_latex: Potentials \((u,v)\) satisfy \(u_i+v_j\geq w_{ij}\) for every edge.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every reduced cost \(r_{ij}=u_i+v_j-w_{ij}\) is nonnegative, and zero reduced cost identifies the equality graph.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual-slack geometry under the maximum-weight convention.

source_refs.locator: 1.3.2 Dual Cost Improvement p. 24
source_refs.source_title: Network Optimization: Continuous and Discrete Models

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For feasible dual potentials, define the reduced-cost slack of edge \((i,j)\) by
\[
r_{ij}=u_i+v_j-w_{ij}\geq0.
\]
The equality graph is
\[
E_0(u,v)=\{(i,j)\in L\times R:r_{ij}=0\}.
\]
Thus dual feasibility places every weighted edge on or below the additive potential surface \(u_i+v_j\); equality edges lie on that surface. For any assignment \(\pi\), its duality gap equals \(\sum_i r_{i,\pi(i)}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reduced costs are nonnegative dual slacks; zero-slack edges form the equality graph, and assigned slacks sum to the duality gap.
knowledge_statements.title: Reduced-Cost Geometry

children.title: Tight-Edge Structure
children.top_down_role: Edges selected by equality between primal costs plus dual potentials.

assumptions_latex: An assignment \(\pi\) and dual potentials \((u,v)\) are feasible for the maximum-weight primal-dual pair.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The pair is optimal exactly when every assigned edge is tight; hence any perfect matching contained in the equality graph is optimal.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complementary-slackness certificate for assignment optimality.

source_refs.locator: 1.3.2 Dual Cost Improvement p. 24

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every feasible assignment \(\pi\),
\[
\sum_i u_i+\sum_jv_j-\sum_iw_{i,\pi(i)}=
\sum_i\bigl(u_i+v_{\pi(i)}-w_{i,\pi(i)}\bigr)=\sum_i r_{i,\pi(i)}.
\]
All terms are nonnegative. Therefore the primal and dual objectives agree exactly when \(r_{i,\pi(i)}=0\) for every \(i\). Consequently, feasible potentials together with a perfect matching wholly contained in \(E_0(u,v)\) form a directly checkable optimality certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible perfect matching is optimal exactly when all its edges have zero reduced cost under feasible dual potentials.
knowledge_statements.title: Tight-Edge Structure

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(S\) with the unmatched vertices of \(L\) and set \(T=\varnothing\). Repeatedly traverse an equality edge \((i,j)\in E_0(u,v)\setminus M\) from \(i\in S\) to \(j\notin T\), add \(j\) to \(T\), and record its predecessor. If \(j\) is unmatched, output the resulting alternating augmenting path. Otherwise, if \((i',j)\in M\), add \(i'\) to \(S\). Stop with boundary \((S,T)\) when no further equality edge leaves \(S\) toward \(R\setminus T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Search the equality graph by alternating unmatched and matched edges, producing either an augmenting path or a stalled reachable boundary.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given an equality-graph augmenting path \(P\), update the matching by
\[
M' = M\triangle E(P).
\]
That is, remove from \(M\) the matched edges of \(P\) and insert the previously unmatched edges of \(P\). Because \(P\) alternates and both endpoints are unmatched, \(M'\) is a matching with \(|M'|=|M|+1\). Every edge of \(P\) is tight, so \(M'\subseteq E_0(u,v)\); the potentials remain unchanged. Stop when the matching is perfect, otherwise restart equality-graph search.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Flip matching status along a tight augmenting path; the matching grows by one while every matched edge remains tight.
knowledge_statements.title: Equality-Graph Augmentation

children.title: Stalled-Search Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Search configurations requiring a change to the current tight-edge structure.

assumptions_latex: The graph is complete bipartite, potentials are dual feasible, and \(M\) is a nonperfect matching of equality edges.
Equality-graph search stalls with reachable sets \(S\subseteq L\) and \(T\subseteq R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The minimum boundary slack is positive, and the stated potential update preserves feasibility while creating a new equality edge from \(S\) to \(R\setminus T\).

notation.meaning: reachable left and right sets at a stalled search
minimum slack across the stalled boundary

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
At a stalled search, no equality edge joins \(S\) to \(R\setminus T\). Set
\[
\delta=\min\{r_{ij}:i\in S,\ j\in R\setminus T\}>0.
\]
Update potentials by \(u'_i=u_i-\delta\) for \(i\in S\), \(v'_j=v_j+\delta\) for \(j\in T\), and leave all other potentials unchanged. Then every dual inequality remains feasible: slacks across \(S\times(R\setminus T)\) decrease by \(\delta\), while no other slack becomes negative. At least one boundary edge becomes tight, so equality-graph search can resume.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When tight-edge search stalls, shift reachable potentials by the smallest boundary slack, preserving feasibility and exposing a new tight edge.
knowledge_statements.title: Stalled-Search Boundaries

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(\operatorname{OPT}=\max_{\pi}\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{i,\pi(i)}\), where the maximum is over all permutations \(\pi\) of \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\). Initialize prices \(p_j=0\) and leave all bidders unassigned. While some bidder \(i\) is unassigned, choose an object \(j^*\) maximizing \(a_{ij}-p_j\), let \(w_i\) be the second-largest value in \(\{a_{ij}-p_j:j=1,\ldots,n\}\), and replace \(p_{j^*}\) by \(p_{j^*}+a_{ij^*}-p_{j^*}-w_i+\varepsilon\). Assign \(j^*\) to \(i\), displacing its previous bidder if necessary. Stop when every bidder is assigned and output the resulting permutation \(\sigma\). The output obeys \(\varepsilon\)-complementary slackness and therefore has benefit at least \(\operatorname{OPT}-n\varepsilon\). If all \(a_{ij}\) are integers and \(\varepsilon<1/n\), the output is optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly raise the price of an unassigned bidder's best object and displace its owner. For at least two bidders and objects, the final assignment is within n epsilon of optimal and is exact when benefits are integral and epsilon is less than 1/n.
knowledge_statements.title: Auction Methods for Assignment

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Auction iteration for the assignment problem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Specifies initialization, bidding, object-price updates, reassignment, and the singleton-admissible-set convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Start an iteration with a partial assignment $S$ and prices $p$ satisfying $\epsilon$-CS; $S=\varnothing$ with arbitrary prices is a valid initialization. Choose a nonempty set $I$ of unassigned persons. For each $i\in I$, choose
\[
 j_i\in\arg\max_{j\in A(i)}(a_{ij}-p_j),\qquad v_i=\max_{j\in A(i)}(a_{ij}-p_j),
\]
define
\[
 w_i=\max_{j\in A(i),\,j\ne j_i}(a_{ij}-p_j),\qquad b_{ij_i}=p_{j_i}+v_i-w_i+\epsilon=a_{ij_i}-w_i+\epsilon,
\]
where $w_i=-\infty$, or a sufficiently small computational surrogate, if $A(i)=\{j_i\}$. For every object $j$ receiving bids from the nonempty set $P(j)$, set
\[
 p_j:=\max_{i\in P(j)}b_{ij},
\]
remove the previous pair incident to $j$ if one exists, and add $(i_j,j)$ for a bidder $i_j\in P(j)$ attaining the maximum. Iterate until the assignment is complete.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Selected unassigned persons bid for their best benefit-minus-price objects, raising each bid enough to exceed the second-best value by epsilon. Each object adopts its highest bid as its new price, evicts any former assignee, and is assigned to a highest bidder.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: p_j\leftarrow\max_{i\in P(j)}b_{ij},\qquad S\leftarrow\bigl(S\setminus\{(h,j)\in S\}\bigr)\cup\{(i_j,j)\}\quad\text{for every }P(j)\ne\varnothing

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Epsilon-Auction Algorithm and Termination Guarantee
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Perturbed forward-auction bidding that prevents zero increments, preserves epsilon-complementary slackness, and terminates when a feasible assignment exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix $\epsilon>0$. In each iteration, an unassigned person $i$ selects a best object $j_i$ and raises its price by $\gamma_i=v_i-w_i+\epsilon$. This is the largest increment preserving $\epsilon$-complementary slackness for the new pair; an increment satisfying $\epsilon\le\gamma_i\le v_i-w_i+\epsilon$ also preserves that condition. If at least one feasible assignment exists, the auction terminates with a feasible assignment and prices satisfying $\epsilon$-complementary slackness. The final assignment value is within $n\epsilon$ of the optimal assignment value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The epsilon-auction adds epsilon to the best-versus-second-best value gap when raising the selected object's price. Positive bids prevent zero-increment cycling; provided a feasible assignment exists, the method terminates with epsilon-complementary slackness and an assignment value within n epsilon of optimal.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \gamma_i=v_i-w_i+\epsilon\ge\epsilon;\qquad\text{the process terminates with a feasible }\epsilon\text{-CS assignment, and }0\le\operatorname{OPT}_{\rm primal}-V_{\rm assignment}\le n\epsilon.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Termination and approximation guarantee of the assignment auction algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gives termination, feasibility, additive optimality, and the integer-data exactness boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If the assignment instance has at least one complete assignment and the auction algorithm is run with $\epsilon>0$, then it terminates with a complete assignment $S$ satisfying
\[
 \operatorname{OPT}-\sum_{(i,j)\in S}a_{ij}\leq n\epsilon.
\]
If the problem data are integer and $\epsilon<1/n$, the returned assignment is optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a complete assignment exists, the auction algorithm terminates with one whose total benefit is at most n epsilon below optimum. For integer data, epsilon below 1/n guarantees exact optimality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{OPT}-\sum_{(i,j)\in S}a_{ij}\leq n\epsilon;\qquad \text{integer problem data and }\epsilon<1/n\Longrightarrow S\text{ is optimal}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Naive Auction Algorithm for Assignment
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unperturbed assignment-auction iterations that preserve exact complementary slackness but carry no termination guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Starting with a partial assignment and prices satisfying complementary slackness on all assigned pairs, while the assignment is incomplete select an unassigned person $i$, choose $j_i\in\arg\max_{j\in A(i)}\{a_{ij}-p_j\}$, assign $i$ to $j_i$ and unassign any former occupant of $j_i$, and update $p_{j_i}\leftarrow p_{j_i}+\gamma_i$, where $\gamma_i=v_i-w_i$, $v_i=\max_{j\in A(i)}\{a_{ij}-p_j\}$, and $w_i=\max_{j\in A(i),\,j\ne j_i}\{a_{ij}-p_j\}$. If all persons become assigned, the algorithm terminates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The naive auction repeatedly assigns an unassigned person to a best object, displaces any incumbent, and raises the object's price by the gap between the person's best and second-best net values. The update preserves exact complementary slackness, but this extract supplies no termination guarantee.
assumptions_latex: \text{At the start of each iteration, every assigned pair satisfies complementary slackness.}
\text{The assignment is incomplete and an unassigned person }i\text{ is selected.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \gamma_i=v_i-w_i\ge 0,\qquad p_{j_i}\leftarrow p_{j_i}+\gamma_i,\qquad a_{ij_i}-p_{j_i}=\max_{j\in A(i)}\{a_{ij}-p_j\}\text{ after the update.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Primal and dual error bounds from epsilon-complementary slackness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Approximate primal-dual optimality certificate for the asymmetric assignment problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If a feasible asymmetric assignment \(S\), with \(m\) persons, satisfies all three \(\epsilon\)-complementary-slackness conditions with \((\pi,p)\), then \(S\) is within \(m\epsilon\) of primal optimality. Define \(\lambda=\min_{k:\,k\text{ assigned under }S}p_k\), \(\widehat\pi_i=\pi_i+\epsilon\) for \(i=1,\ldots,m\), and \(\widehat p_j=p_j\) for assigned objects and \(\widehat p_j=\lambda\) for unassigned objects. Then \((\widehat\pi,\widehat p,\lambda)\) is within \(m\epsilon\) of an optimal solution of the associated dual problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible asymmetric assignment satisfying epsilon-complementary slackness is within m epsilon of optimality. Raising each person potential by epsilon and replacing each unassigned-object price by the minimum assigned-object price also produces a dual solution within m epsilon of dual optimality.
assumptions_latex: S\text{ is a feasible asymmetric assignment with }m\text{ persons}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{OPT}_{P}-\operatorname{val}(S)\le m\epsilon,\qquad \operatorname{val}_{D}(\widehat\pi,\widehat p,\lambda)-\operatorname{OPT}_{D}\le m\epsilon.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Profit-price formulation of approximate complementary slackness for an assignment and its admissible pairs.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Epsilon-scaling for the assignment auction algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines successive auction phases, warm-started prices, and geometric reduction of the approximation parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Choose an initial value $\epsilon^0>0$ and an integer $\theta>1$. Apply the auction algorithm in successive scaling phases, using the prices produced by one phase to initialize the next, and update
\[
 \epsilon^{k+1}=\frac{\epsilon^k}{\theta},\qquad k=0,1,\ldots.
\]
Stop at a chosen final value $\bar\epsilon$ for which $n\bar\epsilon$ is deemed sufficiently small.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Epsilon-scaling repeatedly applies the auction algorithm, warm-starting each phase with prices from the preceding phase and reducing epsilon geometrically by an integer factor greater than one until the desired final error scale is reached.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \epsilon^{k+1}=\epsilon^k/\theta\quad(k=0,1,\ldots)\text{ until the selected final phase with parameter }\bar\epsilon

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Consequences of joint epsilon-complementary slackness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Derivation of the two one-sided auction conditions and the feasible-assignment approximation guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose an assignment \(S\) and profit-price pair \((\pi,p)\) satisfy joint \(\epsilon\)-complementary slackness. Then, for every \((i,j)\in S\), \(a_{ij}-\pi_i\ge\max_{k\in B(j)}\{a_{kj}-\pi_k\}-\epsilon\) and \(a_{ij}-p_j\ge\max_{k\in A(i)}\{a_{ik}-p_k\}-\epsilon\). If \(S\) is feasible, then \(S\) is within \(n\epsilon\) of an optimal assignment.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Joint epsilon-complementary slackness implies both one-sided epsilon-complementary-slackness conditions on assigned pairs. If the assignment is feasible, it also gives an additive optimality gap of at most n epsilon.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \begin{aligned}&\forall(i,j)\in S:\quad a_{ij}-\pi_i\ge\max_{k\in B(j)}\{a_{kj}-\pi_k\}-\epsilon,\\&\forall(i,j)\in S:\quad a_{ij}-p_j\ge\max_{k\in A(i)}\{a_{ik}-p_k\}-\epsilon,\\&S\text{ feasible}\Rightarrow \operatorname{OPT}-\operatorname{val}(S)\le n\epsilon.\end{aligned}

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose \(\varepsilon_0\geq C\), initialize object prices, and set \(k=0\). In phase \(k\), starting from the preceding prices and assignment, repeatedly apply admissible price and reassignment updates until every bidder \(i\) satisfies \(a_{i,\sigma(i)}-p_{\sigma(i)}\geq\max_j(a_{ij}-p_j)-\varepsilon_k\). If \(\varepsilon_k<1/n\), stop and output \(\sigma\); otherwise set \(\varepsilon_{k+1}=\varepsilon_k/\theta\), retain the current prices as warm-start dual variables, and refine again. Every completed phase produces an assignment within \(n\varepsilon_k\) of optimum. Because assignment values are integral, the stopping phase is exactly optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Solve a sequence of increasingly accurate auction or primal-dual subproblems, reusing prices between phases. Integral costs make the final sufficiently accurate assignment exactly optimal.

children.title: Assignment Postoptimality
children.top_down_role: Optimal-solution behavior after modifications to a solved assignment instance.

assumptions_latex: The balanced assignment instance is represented by a finite bipartite graph \(G=(U,V;E)\) with edge-cost vector \(c\in\mathbb{R}^{E}\), and \(M\subseteq E\) is a minimum-cost perfect matching.
The costs are perturbed to \(c'=c+d\), where \(d\in\mathbb{R}^{E}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The old assignment remains optimal exactly when \(\sum_{e\in M}d_e\leq c(M')-c(M)+\sum_{e\in M'}d_e\) for every perfect matching \(M'\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact global postoptimality condition for a fixed perfect assignment under arbitrary cost perturbations.

source_refs.locator: Section 13. Duality Theory p. 53

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every perfect matching \(M'\) of \(G\), define \(c(M')=\sum_{e\in M'}c_e\) and \(d(M')=\sum_{e\in M'}d_e\). The previously optimal matching \(M\) is optimal for the perturbed costs \(c'=c+d\) if and only if \[d(M)-d(M')\leq c(M')-c(M)\qquad\text{for every perfect matching }M'.\] For a perfect matching \(M'\neq M\), equality holds precisely when \(M'\) is also optimal under the perturbed costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An old optimal assignment survives a cost change exactly when no competing assignment gains more from the perturbation than its original optimality gap permits. A distinct competitor is tied after the perturbation exactly when the corresponding inequality is tight.
knowledge_statements.title: Assignment Postoptimality

children.title: Assignment Cost Sensitivity
children.top_down_role: Stability of optimal assignments under changes to edge costs.

assumptions_latex: The cost-minimizing perfect matching \(M\) has value \(z=c(M)\).
Only one edge \(e\) has its cost changed, from \(c_e\) to \(c_e+\delta\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(e\notin M\), stability is equivalent to \(\delta\geq-\alpha_e\); if \(e\in M\), it is equivalent to \(\delta\leq\beta_e\).

notation.meaning: minimum original penalty for forcing edge e
minimum original penalty for excluding edge e

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact one-edge allowable cost interval for a fixed optimal assignment.

source_refs.locator: Section 13. Duality Theory p. 53

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(e\notin M\), set \(\alpha_e=\min\{c(M')-z:M'\text{ is a perfect matching and }e\in M'\}\). Then \(M\) remains optimal after changing only \(c_e\) by \(\delta\) if and only if \(\delta\geq-\alpha_e\). For \(e\in M\), set \(\beta_e=\min\{c(M')-z:M'\text{ is a perfect matching and }e\notin M'\}\). Then \(M\) remains optimal if and only if \(\delta\leq\beta_e\). A minimum over an empty family is \(+\infty\). At a finite boundary, a competing perfect matching becomes co-optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The allowable change of one edge cost equals the cheapest replacement gap: decreases are bounded for unused edges, while increases are bounded for used edges.
knowledge_statements.title: Assignment Cost Sensitivity

children.title: Assignment Structural Sensitivity
children.top_down_role: Effects of adding, removing, or restricting assignment edges.

assumptions_latex: The bipartite graph \(G=(U,V;E)\) admits a cost-minimizing perfect matching \(M\) of value \(z\).
A single edge is inserted into or deleted from \(G\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Insertion preserves optimality of \(M\) exactly when the best assignment using the new edge costs at least \(z\); deletion preserves value \(z\) exactly when an old optimum avoids the deleted edge.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Single-edge insertion and deletion sensitivity for minimum-cost perfect assignments.

source_refs.locator: 3.3 Weighted matchings of bipartite graphs p. 111

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If a new edge \(e\notin E\) with cost \(c_e\) is inserted, define \(z_e=\min\{c(M'):M'\text{ is a perfect matching in }G+e,\ e\in M'\}\). The old matching \(M\) remains optimal precisely when \(z_e\geq z\). If an edge \(f\in E\) is deleted, the optimum value remains \(z\) precisely when some original optimal perfect matching excludes \(f\); in particular, deleting \(f\notin M\) leaves \(M\) feasible and optimal. Deleting an edge belonging to every optimum either destroys perfect-matchability or raises the optimum value to the cheapest feasible assignment avoiding that edge.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A new edge matters only if it creates a cheaper assignment. Deleting an edge preserves the optimum exactly when some old optimal assignment did not use it.
knowledge_statements.title: Assignment Structural Sensitivity

children.title: Optimal-Basis Stability
children.top_down_role: Ranges over which a selected optimal assignment remains valid.

assumptions_latex: The assignment linear program is written as \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\geq0\}\).
A nonsingular basis \(B\) is primal feasible and optimal for cost vector \(c\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The basis \(B\) remains optimal under \(c'=c+d\) if and only if \(c'_N-A_N^{\mathsf T}A_B^{-\mathsf T}c'_B\geq0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reduced-cost stability cone for a fixed assignment LP basis.

source_refs.locator: Section 13. Duality Theory p. 53

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A_B\) be nonsingular, let \(N\) index the nonbasic columns, and suppose \(x_B=A_B^{-1}b\geq0\). Cost perturbations do not change this primal basic solution. For \(c'=c+d\), define the associated dual vector \(y'=A_B^{-\mathsf T}c'_B\). The same basis \(B\) is optimal if and only if every perturbed nonbasic reduced cost is nonnegative: \[r'_N=c'_N-A_N^{\mathsf T}y'=c'_N-A_N^{\mathsf T}A_B^{-\mathsf T}c'_B\geq0.\] Strict positivity of all components of \(r'_N\), together with nondegeneracy, places \(c'\) in the relative interior of the basis-stability region.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed assignment LP basis stays optimal precisely while every nonbasic reduced cost computed from the perturbed objective remains nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.title: Optimal-Basis Stability

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Integral LP formulation of minimum-weight bipartite matching
knowledge_statements.scope_note: LP representation of a not-necessarily-perfect minimum-weight matching; with unrestricted real weights, the empty matching remains feasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(N_1,N_2,A)\) be a finite bipartite graph with edge weights \(w_{jk}\). Its minimum-weight matching LP is \[\min\sum_{(j,k)\in A}w_{jk}x_{jk}\] subject to \[\sum_{k:(j,k)\in A}x_{jk}\le1\quad(j\in N_1),\qquad \sum_{j:(j,k)\in A}x_{jk}\le1\quad(k\in N_2),\qquad x_{jk}\ge0.\] Every extreme point of this polytope is integral, so an integral optimum exists without explicitly imposing \(x_{jk}\in\{0,1\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimum-weight bipartite matching can be represented by one nonnegative variable per edge and at-most-one-edge constraints at each vertex. The resulting polytope is integral, so the LP has a zero-one optimum without explicit binary restrictions. This formulation permits the empty matching unless additional coverage constraints are imposed.
assumptions_latex: G=(N_1,N_2,A)\text{ is a finite bipartite graph}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{ext}\left\{x\ge0:\sum_{k:(j,k)\in A}x_{jk}\le1,\ \sum_{j:(j,k)\in A}x_{jk}\le1\right\}\subseteq\{0,1\}^{A}.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Construct a directed network with arcs \(s\to u\) for \(u\in U\), arcs \(u\to v\) for \(uv\in E\), and arcs \(v\to t\) for \(v\in V\), each having capacity \(1\). Every matching \(M\) induces an integral \(s\)-\(t\) flow of value \(|M|\) by sending one unit along \(s\to u\to v\to t\) for each \(uv\in M\). Conversely, the middle arcs carrying one unit in any integral flow form a matching. Consequently, \[\max\{|M|:M\text{ is a matching of }G\}=\max\{\operatorname{val}(f):f\text{ is a feasible }s\text{-}t\text{ flow}\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Connect a source to the left class and the right class to a sink with unit capacities. Integral flow paths correspond exactly to matched edges.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Assignment Problem as a Minimum-Cost Flow Linear Program
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Flow representation of minimum-weight perfect matching in a balanced bipartite graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $G=(N_1\cup N_2,A)$ be a weighted bipartite graph with $|N_1|=|N_2|$ and costs $c_{ij}$, with every edge oriented from $N_1$ to $N_2$. The minimum-weight perfect-matching problem, called the assignment problem, is represented by
\[\min\sum_{(i,j)\in A}c_{ij}x_{ij}\]
subject to
\[\sum_{j:(i,j)\in A}x_{ij}=1\quad(i\in N_1),\qquad \sum_{j:(j,i)\in A}x_{ji}=1\quad(i\in N_2),\qquad x_{ij}\ge 0\quad((i,j)\in A).\]
This is a special minimum-cost-flow formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a balanced weighted bipartite graph, minimum-weight perfect matching—the assignment problem—has a minimum-cost-flow linear formulation in which every vertex has assignment value one and all assignment variables are nonnegative.
assumptions_latex: G=(N_1\cup N_2,A)\text{ is a weighted bipartite graph}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min\left\{\sum_{(i,j)\in A}c_{ij}x_{ij}:\sum_{j:(i,j)\in A}x_{ij}=1\ (i\in N_1),\ \sum_{j:(j,i)\in A}x_{ji}=1\ (i\in N_2),\ x\ge0\right\}\text{ is a minimum-cost-flow formulation of the assignment problem.}

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Create arcs \(s\to u\) for \(u\in U\), \(u\to v\) for \(uv\in E\), and \(v\to t\) for \(v\in V\), all with capacity \(1\). Give each middle arc \(u\to v\) cost \(c_{uv}\) and every other arc cost \(0\). Add a return arc \(t\to s\) with lower and upper bound both equal to \(n\). Flow conservation forces every integral feasible circulation to use exactly one middle arc incident with each vertex. Thus its positive middle arcs form a perfect matching, every perfect matching induces such a circulation, and circulation cost equals assignment cost. Minimum-cost feasible circulation therefore solves minimum-cost perfect assignment.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Force n units around a source-left-right-sink-return network. Integral feasible circulations then correspond exactly, and cost-preservingly, to perfect assignments.

If the network system is feasible, its feasible polyhedron has integral extreme points; if a finite linear optimum exists, an integral optimum \(f^*\) exists. Under the standard reduction, define \(x^*_{uv}=f^*_{uv}\) on arcs corresponding to bipartite edges. Unit capacities and flow conservation imply \(x^*_{uv}\in\{0,1\}\) and the matching degree constraints. Hence projection preserves integrality and objective value, yielding an integral maximum matching or minimum-cost assignment solution.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Linear-programming duality gives \[\max\left\{\sum_{e\in E}w_ex_e:x\geq0,\ \sum_{e\in\delta(v)}x_e\leq1\ \text{for all }v\right\}=\min\left\{\sum_{v\in U\cup V}y_v:y\geq0,\ y_u+y_v\geq w_{uv}\ \text{for all }uv\in E\right\}.\] Because the bipartite incidence system is integral, an optimal primal solution is a matching incidence vector. If \(w\) is integral, an integral optimal dual potential may also be chosen. For \(w_e=1\) on every edge, the dual integral solutions are vertex covers, yielding equality between maximum matching cardinality and minimum vertex-cover cardinality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maximum-weight bipartite matching is dual to minimum vertex potentials covering every edge weight. With unit weights this becomes the matching–vertex-cover min-max equality.

knowledge_statements.title: Bipartite Incidence Matrices
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unsigned vertex-edge incidence represented as a signed directed incidence matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite bipartite graph \(G=(U\mathbin{\dot\cup}W,E)\), its unsigned vertex-edge incidence matrix is \(A\in\{0,1\}^{(U\cup W)\times E}\), where \(A_{v,e}=1\) exactly when \(v\in e\). Let \(D\) be diagonal with \(D_{vv}=1\) for \(v\in U\) and \(D_{vv}=-1\) for \(v\in W\). Then every column of \(DA\) has one entry \(1\), one entry \(-1\), and all other entries zero; thus \(DA\) is the node-arc incidence matrix obtained by orienting every edge from \(W\) to \(U\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Signing one bipartition class converts the unsigned incidence matrix of a bipartite graph into a directed node-arc incidence matrix.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(DA\) is a directed node-arc incidence matrix.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\) be the unsigned vertex-edge incidence matrix of a finite bipartite graph. knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Integrality Consequences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integral right-hand sides yield integral bipartite degree-constraint polyhedra.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\) be the unsigned vertex-edge incidence matrix of a finite bipartite graph and let \(b\in\mathbb{Z}^{V}\). The polyhedron \[P(b)=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{E}:Ax\leq b,\ x\geq 0\}\] is integral whenever it is nonempty: every extreme point of \(P(b)\) belongs to \(\mathbb{Z}^{E}\). In particular, for \(b=\mathbf{1}\), every extreme point is a zero-one vector and therefore the incidence vector of a matching.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Total unimodularity makes bipartite degree-constraint polyhedra integral for integral capacities; unit capacities recover matching vectors.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) is a bipartite vertex-edge incidence matrix.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{ext}P(b)\subseteq\mathbb{Z}^{E}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Nonbipartite Matrix Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The triangle witnesses failure of incidence-matrix unimodularity and degree-only matching integrality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=K_3\), order its vertices and edges cyclically, and let \[A=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&1\\1&1&0\\0&1&1\end{pmatrix}.\] Then \(A\) is the unsigned vertex-edge incidence matrix of \(G\) and \(\det(A)=2\), so \(A\) is not totally unimodular. Moreover, \(x=(1/2,1/2,1/2)\) is an extreme point of \(\{x\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq0}^{3}:Ax\leq\mathbf{1}\}\), but it is not the incidence vector of a matching.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A triangle has incidence determinant two and a half-integral extreme point, so bipartite matrix integrality does not extend to nonbipartite graphs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A\) is not totally unimodular, and the degree-only matching relaxation is not integral.
