knowledge_statements.title: Permutation-Matrix Decomposition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Birkhoff–von Neumann decomposition theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(X\in\mathcal{B}_n\), there exist permutation matrices \(P_1,\ldots,P_m\) and coefficients \(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_m>0\) such that \[X=\sum_{k=1}^{m}\lambda_kP_k,\qquad \sum_{k=1}^{m}\lambda_k=1.\] Conversely, every such convex combination is doubly stochastic. Hence \(\mathcal{B}_n\) is the convex hull of the \(n\times n\) permutation matrices, and those permutation matrices are exactly its extreme points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every doubly stochastic matrix is a convex combination of permutation matrices, which are exactly the Birkhoff polytope's extreme points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal{B}_n=\operatorname{conv}\{P:P\text{ is an }n\times n\text{ permutation matrix}\}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Convex Bipartite Graphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-sided convex bipartite graphs with consecutive neighborhoods in a fixed order.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite bipartite graph \(G=(U\mathbin{\dot\cup}W,E)\) is convex on \(W\) if there is a linear order \(w_1<\cdots<w_q\) of \(W\) such that, for every \(u\in U\), its neighborhood is an interval in that order: either \(N(u)=\varnothing\), or there exist \(1\leq \ell(u)\leq r(u)\leq q\) with \[N(u)=\{w_j:\ell(u)\leq j\leq r(u)\}.\] It is called a convex bipartite graph if it is convex on at least one bipartition class.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bipartite graph is convex when one side can be ordered so that every vertex on the other side has a consecutive neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G\) is convex on \(W\) exactly when every \(N(u)\) is an interval in one common order of \(W\).

children.title: Monge Assignment Structure
children.top_down_role: Assignment instances governed by Monge-type cost organization.

knowledge_statements.title: Monge Assignment Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Monge inequality for a minimization-form rectangular assignment cost array.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=(c_{ij})\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), with rows and columns carrying their natural linear orders. The array \(C\) is Monge if, for every \(1\leq i<k\leq m\) and \(1\leq j<\ell\leq n\), \[c_{ij}+c_{k\ell}\leq c_{i\ell}+c_{kj}.\] Equivalently, every ordered two-by-two subarray has the sum on its northwest-to-southeast diagonal no greater than the sum on its northeast-to-southwest diagonal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cost array is Monge when every ordered two-by-two subarray favors its aligned diagonal over its crossed diagonal.
assumptions_latex: Rows and columns have fixed linear orders.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(c_{ij}+c_{k\ell}\leq c_{i\ell}+c_{kj}\) for all \(i<k\) and \(j<\ell\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed inequality is the standard minimization-form Monge condition and fits the condition leaf, but no source confirms the terminology and sign convention.

children.title: Ordered Assignment Structure
children.top_down_role: Assignment instances whose vertex order constrains optimal pairings.

knowledge_statements.title: Ordered Assignment Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Assignments between equally sized linearly ordered sets, classified by inversions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U=\{u_1<\cdots<u_n\}\) and \(W=\{w_1<\cdots<w_n\}\). A perfect assignment is represented by a permutation \(\pi\in S_n\), matching \(u_i\) to \(w_{\pi(i)}\). A pair \((i,k)\) with \(i<k\) is an inversion when \(\pi(i)>\pi(k)\). The assignment is order-compatible when it has no inversions, equivalently when \(i<k\) implies \(\pi(i)<\pi(k)\). For equal finite chains, the unique order-compatible perfect assignment is \(\pi(i)=i\) for every \(i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An ordered perfect assignment is order-compatible when matched indices never cross; for two equal chains this is the identity assignment.
assumptions_latex: \(U\) and \(W\) are linearly ordered sets of the same finite cardinality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\pi\) is order-compatible if and only if \(\pi(i)=i\) for every \(i\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The inversion-based formulation is internally correct, including uniqueness of the increasing permutation, but the locally introduced term “order-compatible” lacks a cited source.

children.title: Order-Compatible Optimal Matchings
children.top_down_role: Optimal matching patterns supported by compatible ordering.

knowledge_statements.title: Order-Compatible Optimal Matchings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uncrossing theorem for square Monge minimization assignments.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=(c_{ij})\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) satisfy the Monge inequalities. For a permutation \(\pi\in S_n\), define its assignment cost by \(F(\pi)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}c_{i,\pi(i)}\). If \(\pi\) has an inversion, exchanging the two inverted images produces a permutation \(\pi'\) with \(F(\pi')\leq F(\pi)\). Repeated exchanges therefore yield the order-compatible permutation \(\operatorname{id}\), and \[F(\operatorname{id})=\sum_{i=1}^{n}c_{ii}\leq F(\pi)\qquad\text{for every }\pi\in S_n.\] Thus an order-compatible optimal perfect matching exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a square Monge cost matrix, uncrossing inversions never increases cost, so the identity matching is optimal.
assumptions_latex: The objective is to minimize total assignment cost.

notation.meaning: total cost of permutation assignment π

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The uncrossing statement is correct for square minimization-form Monge arrays and fits the theorem leaf, but neither the theorem nor its convention has an inspectable source locator.

children.title: Monge Structure Violations
children.top_down_role: Instance features that destroy Monge-based simplifications.

knowledge_statements.title: Monge Structure Violations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A violated two-by-two Monge inequality defeats guaranteed order-compatible optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a two-by-two minimization assignment array \(C=(c_{ij})\). If \[c_{11}+c_{22}>c_{12}+c_{21},\] then the Monge inequality is violated. The order-compatible assignment has cost \(c_{11}+c_{22}\), whereas the crossed assignment has strictly smaller cost \(c_{12}+c_{21}\). Hence the order-compatible assignment is not optimal. More generally, a violated ordered two-by-two inequality reverses the local uncrossing comparison on those rows and columns, so Monge-based order-compatible optimality is no longer guaranteed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A single reversed two-by-two Monge inequality can make the crossed assignment cheaper than the order-compatible assignment.
assumptions_latex: The objective is to minimize assignment cost.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{id}\) is not an optimal assignment for \(C\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The two-by-two failure example is mathematically correct and appropriately classified as a failure boundary, but it has no source confirming the Monge sign convention or claim context.

knowledge_statements.title: Regular Bipartite Graphs

knowledge_statements.title: Edge-Coloring Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Correspondence between one-factorizations and optimal edge colorings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite \(r\)-regular bipartite graph \(G=(V,E)\), a labeled partition \(E=M_1\mathbin{\dot\cup}\cdots\mathbin{\dot\cup}M_r\) into perfect matchings corresponds bijectively to a proper edge coloring \(\kappa:E\to\{1,\ldots,r\}\), with \(\kappa(e)=k\) exactly when \(e\in M_k\). knowledge_statements.title: Hall-Deficiency Obstructions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deficient vertex sets as certificates against left-saturating matchings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite bipartite graph \(G=(L\mathbin{\dot\cup}R,E)\), define \[\delta_L(G)=\max_{S\subseteq L}\bigl(|S|-|N(S)|\bigr).\] Every matching leaves at least \(\delta_L(G)\) vertices of \(L\) unmatched, and a maximum matching leaves exactly that many. Hence any \(S\subseteq L\) with \(|S|>|N(S)|\) is a directly verifiable certificate that no matching saturates \(L\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set with fewer neighbors than vertices certifies failure of a left-saturating matching; maximum matching size is governed exactly by maximum Hall deficiency.

children.title: Odd-Cycle Obstructions

knowledge_statements.title: Odd-Cycle Obstructions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Odd cycles mark failure of the bipartite matching relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) contain an odd cycle \(C\). Set \(x_e=1/2\) for \(e\in E(C)\) and \(x_e=0\) otherwise. Then \(x\ge0\) and \(x(\delta(v))\le1\) for every \(v\in V\), but \[x(E(C))=|C|/2>(|C|-1)/2.\] Thus the degree-only matching relaxation admits a point excluded by every convex combination of matchings.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Half-weighting every edge of an odd cycle satisfies degree constraints but violates the matching bound for that odd vertex set.

knowledge_statements.title: Bipartite Integrality Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Degree description of the bipartite matching polytope.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite bipartite graph \(G=(V,E)\), the matching polytope is \[P_M(G)=\left\{x\in\mathbb R_{}^{E}:x_e\ge0\ \text{for all }e\in E,\quad x(\delta(v))\le1\ \text{for all }v\in V\right\}.\] Every extreme point of this polytope is the incidence vector of a matching; hence every linear objective over the displayed relaxation has an integral optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In bipartite graphs, nonnegativity and vertex-degree inequalities describe exactly the convex hull of matchings.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The degree relaxation equals \(\operatorname{conv}\{\mathbf 1_M:M\text{ is a matching of }G\}\) and is integral.

knowledge_statements.title: Fractional Nonbipartite Behavior
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Half-integral extreme point on an odd cycle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the cycle \(G=C_{2k+1}\) with \(k\ge1\), define \(x_e=1/2\) for every edge. This vector satisfies \(x_e\ge0\) and \(x(\delta(v))=1\) at every vertex. It is an extreme point of the degree-only relaxation, yet it is not integral and cannot be a convex combination of matching incidence vectors because \(x(E)=k+1/2>k=\nu(G)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The all-one-half vector on an odd cycle is a fractional extreme point of the degree relaxation and lies outside the matching polytope.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The degree-only matching relaxation has the nonintegral extreme point \(x=\tfrac12\mathbf 1_E\).

knowledge_statements.title: Odd-Set Repair Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Edmonds's odd-set description of the general matching polytope.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every finite undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\), its matching polytope equals the set of \(x\in\mathbb R^{E}\) satisfying \[x_e\ge0,\qquad x(\delta(v))\le1\quad(v\in V),\qquad x(E(S))\le\frac{|S|-1}{2}\quad(S\subseteq V,\ |S|\text{ odd}).\] Thus adding all odd-set inequalities repairs the degree relaxation and yields precisely the convex hull of matching incidence vectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For general graphs, degree constraints become exact after adding one matching-capacity inequality for every odd vertex set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed system equals \(\operatorname{conv}\{\mathbf 1_M:M\text{ is a matching of }G\}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Assignment Degeneracy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Degeneracy understood locally as nonuniqueness of the optimal assignment face, rather than basic-solution degeneracy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(n\in\mathbb Z_{\ge 1}\), let \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and let \(C=(c_{ij})\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\). Define \(B_n=\{x\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^{n\times n}:\sum_{j\in[n]}x_{ij}=1\text{ for every }i\in[n],\ \sum_{i\in[n]}x_{ij}=1\text{ for every }j\in[n]\}\) and \(F^*=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in B_n}\langle C,x\rangle\). In the optimal-face sense used here, the assignment instance is degenerate if \(F^*\) is not a singleton. Equivalently, \(\dim F^*\ge1\), or at least two distinct permutation matrices attain the minimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the local optimal-face convention, an assignment instance is degenerate when its optimal face is not a singleton, equivalently when it has at least two distinct optimal permutation matrices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Optimal-face degeneracy means \(|F^*|>1\), equivalently \(\dim F^*\ge1\).

notation.meaning: The Birkhoff polytope of n by n doubly stochastic matrices.
The optimal face for cost matrix C.

children.title: Multiple Optimal Assignments
children.top_down_role: Instances admitting more than one optimal assignment.

knowledge_statements.title: Multiple Optimal Assignments
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Alternating-cycle criterion in the zero-reduced-cost graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(n\in\mathbb Z_{\ge1}\), let \(C=(c_{ij})\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\), and consider the minimum-cost perfect-matching problem on the complete bipartite graph with vertex classes \(L=R=[n]\). Let \(M\) be an optimal perfect matching and let \((u,v)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^n\) be an optimal dual solution satisfying \(u_i+v_j\le c_{ij}\) for every \((i,j)\in L\times R\). Define the equality graph \(H=(L\mathbin{\dot\cup}R,E_H)\) by \(E_H=\{ij:c_{ij}-u_i-v_j=0\}\). A distinct optimal assignment exists if and only if \(H\) contains an \(M\)-alternating cycle.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Given an optimal assignment and optimal dual potentials, a second optimal assignment exists exactly when the zero-reduced-cost equality graph contains an alternating cycle relative to the first assignment.
assumptions_latex: \((u,v)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^n\) is an optimal dual solution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There are multiple optimal assignments if and only if \(H\) contains an \(M\)-alternating cycle.

notation.meaning: Optimal row and column dual potentials.

children.title: Optimal-Face Structure
children.top_down_role: Geometric organization of all optimal assignment solutions.

knowledge_statements.title: Optimal-Face Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimal assignment face represented by the equality graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(n\in\mathbb Z_{\ge1}\), let \([n]=\{1,ldots,n\}\), and let \(C=(c_{ij})\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\). Define \(B_n=\{x\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^{n\times n}:\sum_{j\in[n]}x_{ij}=1\text{ for every }i\in[n],\ \sum_{i\in[n]}x_{ij}=1\text{ for every }j\in[n]\}\). For any optimal dual solution \((u,v)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^n\), let \(H\) be the bipartite graph on two copies of \([n]\) with \(E(H)=\{ij:c_{ij}=u_i+v_j\}\). The optimal face is \[F^*=\{x\in B_n:x_{ij}=0\text{ whenever }ij\notin E(H)\}=\operatorname{conv}\{\mathbf 1_M:M\text{ is a perfect matching of }H\}.\] Consequently, \(F^*\) is the perfect-matching polytope of \(H\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For any optimal dual solution, the optimal assignment face consists exactly of the doubly stochastic matrices supported on zero-reduced-cost edges, and it is the convex hull of the perfect matchings in that equality graph.
assumptions_latex: \((u,v)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^n\) is an optimal dual solution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F^*\) is the perfect-matching polytope of the equality graph \(H\).

notation.meaning: The optimal face of the assignment polytope.

children.title: Tie-Breaking Stability
children.top_down_role: Effects of perturbations or selection rules on tied optima.

knowledge_statements.title: Tie-Breaking Stability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lexicographic perturbation of a finite assignment problem without changing its primary optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal A\) be the finite set of feasible assignments, let \(c:\mathcal A\to\mathbb R\), and order the assignment edges as \(e_1,\ldots,e_m\). Define \(c_\varepsilon(A)=c(A)+\sum_{e_i\in A}\varepsilon^i\). There exists \(\varepsilon_0>0\) such that, for every \(0<\varepsilon<\varepsilon_0\), every minimizer of \(c_\varepsilon\) minimizes \(c\); moreover, the perturbed problem has the unique minimizer whose incidence vector is lexicographically smallest among the \(c\)-optimal assignments, with respect to the stated edge order.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For all sufficiently small positive perturbation parameters, primary optimality is preserved and the unique selected assignment is the one with lexicographically smallest incidence vector among the original cost-optimal assignments.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname*{argmin}_{A\in\mathcal A}c_\varepsilon(A)=\{A^{\mathrm{lex}}\}\subseteq\operatorname*{argmin}_{A\in\mathcal A}c(A)

knowledge_statements.title: Maximum-Cardinality Matching
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unweighted matching optimization in a finite undirected graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\), a matching is a set \(M\subseteq E\) whose edges have pairwise disjoint endpoint sets. A maximum-cardinality matching is a matching \(M^*\) satisfying \[|M^*|=\nu(G):=\max\{|M|:M\subseteq E\text{ is a matching}\}.\] It maximizes the number of selected edges, equivalently the number \(2|M|\) of covered vertices.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A maximum-cardinality matching is a matching containing as many edges, and hence covering as many vertices, as any matching in the graph.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Augmenting paths and maximum matchings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Augmenting-path terminology, matching coverage terminology, and the maximum-cardinality criterion for simple graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $G=(V,E)$ be a simple graph and let $M\subseteq E$ be a matching. A path $P$ is $M$-augmenting if it has odd length, joins two vertices not covered by $M$, and its edges alternate between $E\setminus M$ and $M$. A vertex is covered by $M$ if it is incident with an edge of $M$, and otherwise is missed by $M$. Then $M$ has maximum cardinality if and only if no $M$-augmenting path exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a simple graph, an M-augmenting path is an odd-length path joining two vertices missed by M, with edges alternating outside and inside M. A vertex is covered when it is incident with a matching edge and missed otherwise. A matching is maximum exactly when it has no augmenting path.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: M\text{ has maximum cardinality}\iff\text{there is no }M\text{-augmenting path}.

knowledge_statements.title: Perfect General-Graph Matching
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Perfect matchings in finite undirected graphs, including nonbipartite graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph. A matching \(M\subseteq E\) is perfect if every vertex of \(G\) is incident with exactly one edge of \(M\). Equivalently, the endpoint sets of the edges in \(M\) partition \(V\), so \[|M|=|V|/2.\] Consequently, existence of a perfect matching requires \(|V|\) to be even.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A perfect matching consists of vertex-disjoint edges covering every vertex exactly once; therefore the graph must have even order.
assumptions_latex: G=(V,E)\text{ is a finite undirected graph}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: V=\biguplus_{e\in M}e\quad\text{and}\quad |M|=|V|/2

knowledge_statements.title: Near-Perfect General-Graph Matching
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Near-perfect matchings under the one-exposed-vertex convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph. A matching \(M\subseteq E\) is near-perfect if exactly one vertex is not incident with an edge of \(M\). Thus \(|V|\) is odd and \[|M|=(|V|-1)/2.\] If \(v\) is the unique exposed vertex, then \(M\) is a perfect matching of the vertex-deleted graph \(G-v\); conversely, every perfect matching of \(G-v\) is near-perfect in \(G\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A near-perfect matching leaves exactly one vertex exposed, equivalently becoming perfect after that vertex is deleted.
assumptions_latex: G=(V,E)\text{ is a finite undirected graph}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: M\text{ is near-perfect with exposed vertex }v\iff M\text{ is perfect in }G-v

knowledge_statements.title: Parity-Controlled Coverage
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parity restriction on the vertices left uncovered by a matching.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) be a matching in a finite undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\), and let \(U(M)\) be the set of vertices not covered by \(M\). Since every matching edge covers exactly two vertices, \[|U(M)|=|V|-2|M|\quad\text{and hence}\quad |U(M)|\equiv |V|\pmod 2.\] Therefore a perfect matching can occur only when \(|V|\) is even, while a matching with exactly one exposed vertex can occur only when \(|V|\) is odd.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every matching leaves a number of exposed vertices having the same parity as the graph order.
assumptions_latex: G=(V,E)\text{ is a finite undirected graph}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: |U(M)|=|V|-2|M|\equiv |V|\pmod 2

knowledge_statements.title: Weighted General-Graph Matching
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Maximum-weight matching without a prescribed cardinality in a general graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph and let \(w:E\to\mathbb R\). The weight of a matching \(M\) is \(w(M)=\sum_{e\in M}w(e)\). A maximum-weight matching is any matching \(M^*\) satisfying \[w(M^*)=\max\left\{\sum_{e\in M}w(e):M\subseteq E\text{ is a matching}\right\}.\] Under this unconstrained convention, negative-weight edges need not be selected and the empty matching is feasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A maximum-weight matching maximizes the sum of selected edge weights; its cardinality is not fixed.
assumptions_latex: G=(V,E)\text{ is a finite undirected graph}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: w(M^*)=\max\{w(M):M\text{ is a matching in }G\}

notation.meaning: sum of weights of matching edges

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Weighted matching, completion reductions, and bipartite versus general-graph formulations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines maximum-weight matching under nonnegative edge weights and records objective-preserving completion, fixed-cardinality cost conversion, and the algorithmic distinction between bipartite and nonbipartite instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a graph \(G=(V,E)\) with weights \(w_e\ge 0\), the weighted matching problem is \(\max\{\sum_{e\in M}w_e:M\subseteq E\text{ is a matching}\}\); maximum-cardinality matching is the special case \(w_e=1\) for every \(e\in E\). Assigning weight zero to missing edges, adding a zero-weight dummy vertex when necessary, and, in the bipartite case, balancing the two parts produce complete even-order or complete balanced-bipartite instances without changing the optimal value. An optimal matching in the completed instance can be chosen perfect. For perfect matchings, replacing \(w_e\) by \(c_e=W-w_e\), where \(W>\max_e w_e\), converts weight maximization into equivalent cost minimization. The bipartite case is the assignment problem and is solvable by the Hungarian method in \(O(n^3)\) arithmetic operations for two parts of size \(n\). In general nonbipartite graphs, the elementary bipartite matching linear formulation is not exact: it has basic feasible solutions that do not represent matchings, so blossom structure must be handled. The described general-graph primal-dual algorithm has complexity \(O(|V|^4)\), while the source notes refinements to \(O(|V|^3)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weighted matching maximizes the total nonnegative weight of selected, vertex-disjoint edges; unit weights recover maximum-cardinality matching. Zero-weight missing edges and dummy vertices permit reduction to complete perfect-matching instances, after which subtracting weights from a sufficiently large constant converts maximization to minimum cost. The bipartite case is assignment and admits a cubic Hungarian algorithm. For nonbipartite graphs, the elementary bipartite LP is not exact because of blossom structure; the described primal-dual algorithm is quartic, with cubic refinements noted by the source.
assumptions_latex: \text{The cost transformation is applied after reduction to perfect matchings of fixed cardinality.}
\text{For the assignment specialization, the completed bipartite graph has two parts of equal size }n.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \max_{M\text{ matching}}\sum_{e\in M}w_e;\qquad w_e\equiv1\Rightarrow\text{maximum-cardinality matching};\qquad \arg\max_{M\text{ perfect}}\sum_{e\in M}w_e=\arg\min_{M\text{ perfect}}\sum_{e\in M}(W-w_e);\qquad T_{\mathrm{Hungarian}}(n)=O(n^3),\quad T_{\mathrm{general}}(|V|)=O(|V|^4).

knowledge_statements.title: Minimum-Cost General-Graph Matching
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimum-cost matching over an explicitly specified feasible matching family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph, let \(c:E\to\mathbb R\), and let \(\mathcal F\) be a nonempty family of matchings encoding the required cardinality or coverage. For \(M\in\mathcal F\), set \(c(M)=\sum_{e\in M}c(e)\). A minimum-cost matching is any \(M^*\in\mathcal F\) satisfying \[c(M^*)=\min_{M\in\mathcal F}c(M).\] Specifying \(\mathcal F\) is essential because the unconstrained empty matching may otherwise be optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A minimum-cost matching minimizes total edge cost within a stated nonempty family that fixes the intended cardinality or coverage regime.
assumptions_latex: G=(V,E)\text{ is a finite undirected graph}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: M^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{M\in\mathcal F}\sum_{e\in M}c(e)

knowledge_statements.title: Weight–Cost Transformation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine equivalence of weight maximization and cost minimization at fixed cardinality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be finite, let \(w:E\to\mathbb R\), fix \(k\ge 0\), and define \(c(e)=C-w(e)\) for a constant \(C\in\mathbb R\). For every matching \(M\) with \(|M|=k\), \[c(M)=\sum_{e\in M}(C-w(e))=kC-w(M).\] Hence, over the family \(\mathcal M_k\) of size-\(k\) matchings, maximizing \(w(M)\) and minimizing \(c(M)\) have exactly the same optimizers.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For fixed-size matchings, replacing each weight by a constant minus that weight converts maximum weight into minimum cost without changing optimizers.
assumptions_latex: G=(V,E)\text{ is a finite undirected graph}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname*{argmax}_{M\in\mathcal M_k}w(M)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{M\in\mathcal M_k}c(M)

knowledge_statements.title: Cardinality-Constrained Weighting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Maximum-weight optimization restricted to matchings of a prescribed size.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph, let \(w:E\to\mathbb R\), and choose an integer \(k\) with \(0\le k\le\nu(G)\). A cardinality-constrained maximum-weight matching is a matching \(M_k^*\) satisfying \[|M_k^*|=k\quad\text{and}\quad w(M_k^*)=\max\{w(M):M\text{ is a matching and }|M|=k\}.\] The constraint prevents changes in cardinality from being traded against edge weight.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The problem selects a maximum-weight matching among exactly those matchings containing a prescribed number of edges.
assumptions_latex: G=(V,E)\text{ is a finite undirected graph}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: M_k^*\in\operatorname*{argmax}\{w(M):M\text{ is a matching},\ |M|=k\}

knowledge_statements.title: Matching with Prescribed Vertex Coverage
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact characterization of a prescribed set as the covered vertices of a matching.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph and let \(S\subseteq V\). A matching \(M\) covers exactly \(S\) when the union of the endpoint sets of its edges equals \(S\). Such a matching exists if and only if the induced subgraph \(G[S]\) has a perfect matching. Equivalently, there is a matching \(M\subseteq E(G[S])\) with \[|M|=|S|/2.\] In particular, \(|S|\) must be even.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exactly the vertices in S can be covered by a matching precisely when the induced graph on S has a perfect matching.
assumptions_latex: G=(V,E)\text{ is a finite undirected graph}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists M\text{ with covered vertex set }S\iff G[S]\text{ has a perfect matching}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Alternating and augmenting paths in matching optimality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions of matching-alternating and augmenting paths, their bipartite flow correspondence, and the general maximum-matching criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) be a matching in a graph \(G\). A path is \(M\)-alternating if its edges alternate between membership and nonmembership in \(M\), with no prescribed membership status for its first or last edge. It is \(M\)-augmenting if its endpoints are distinct and both are \(M\)-exposed. For the integral-flow formulation of bipartite matching, flow-augmenting paths correspond to \(M\)-augmenting paths. In every graph, \(M\) is maximum if and only if no \(M\)-augmenting path exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An M-alternating path alternates between matched and unmatched edges, without prescribing the status of its first or last edge. It is augmenting when its distinct endpoints are exposed. These paths correspond to flow-augmenting paths in the bipartite flow formulation, and a matching in any graph is maximum exactly when no augmenting path exists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: M\text{ is maximum}\iff\nexists\text{ an }M\text{-augmenting path};\qquad G\text{ bipartite}\Rightarrow\text{flow-augmenting paths correspond to }M\text{-augmenting paths}.

knowledge_statements.title: Berge Augmenting-Path Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Berge’s optimality criterion for matchings in finite general graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph and let \(M\subseteq E\) be a matching. An \(M\)-augmenting path is a simple path whose endpoints are uncovered by \(M\) and whose edges alternate between \(E\setminus M\) and \(M\), beginning and ending outside \(M\). Then \(M\) is a maximum-cardinality matching if and only if no \(M\)-augmenting path exists in \(G\). If such a path \(P\) exists, \(M\triangle E(P)\) is a matching of cardinality \(|M|+1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A matching is maximum exactly when it admits no alternating path joining two exposed vertices; flipping such a path increases cardinality by one.
assumptions_latex: G=(V,E)\text{ is a finite undirected graph}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: M\text{ is maximum-cardinality}\iff G\text{ has no }M\text{-augmenting path}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Alternating Paths and Alternating Cycles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parity and cycle terminology for paths alternating relative to a matching.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a matching \(M\), a path \(P=i_1-i_2-\cdots-i_k\) is alternating with respect to \(M\) if every consecutive pair of edges on \(P\) contains one edge in \(M\) and one edge outside \(M\). children.title: Alternating Paths

knowledge_statements.title: Alternating Paths
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Alternation is defined relative to a fixed matching in a finite undirected graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph and \(M\subseteq E\) a matching. A simple path \(P=(v_0,e_1,v_1,\ldots,e_k,v_k)\) with \(k\ge 1\) is \(M\)-alternating if consecutive edges alternate between \(M\) and \(E\setminus M\); equivalently, for every \(1\le i<k\), exactly one of \(e_i,e_{i+1}\) belongs to \(M\). It is \(M\)-augmenting if both endpoints are unmatched by \(M\) and \(e_1,e_k\notin M\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive-length alternating path switches between matching and nonmatching edges. It is augmenting when both endpoints are unmatched and its first and last edges are outside the matching.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is a simple path of length \(k\ge 1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\text{ is }M\text{-alternating}\iff |\{e_i,e_{i+1}\}\cap M|=1\text{ for every }1\le i<k.\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Alternating, Exposed, and Augmenting Paths
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions and the elementary augmentation consequence for matchings in arbitrary graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be a graph and \(M\) a matching in \(G\). A path \(P=v_1,v_2,\ldots,v_m\) is \(M\)-alternating if every two consecutive edges of \(P\) have opposite membership in \(M\). A vertex is \(M\)-exposed if no edge of \(M\) is incident with it. An \(M\)-alternating path joining two exposed vertices is an \(M\)-augmenting path. If \(P\) is augmenting, then \(M'=(M\setminus E(P))\cup(E(P)\setminus M)\) is a matching with \(|M'|=|M|+1\), so \(M\) is not maximum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An alternating path relative to a matching has consecutive edges alternately in and outside the matching. A vertex is exposed when it is incident with no matching edge. An alternating path joining two exposed vertices is augmenting, and exchanging matching and nonmatching edges along it increases the matching size by one.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P\text{ is }M\text{-augmenting}\implies M'=(M\setminus E(P))\cup(E(P)\setminus M)\text{ is a matching with }|M'|=|M|+1.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Alternating and augmenting paths relative to a matching
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Alternating-search terminology relative to a fixed matching; broad matching variants and the illustrated examples are excluded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $M$ be a matching in a graph $G$. Edges in $M$ are matched, edges outside $M$ are free, and a vertex incident to no edge of $M$ is exposed. A path $p=[u_1,\ldots,u_k]$ is alternating with respect to $M$ if its successive edges alternate between free and matched, beginning with a free edge. On such a path beginning at an exposed vertex, vertices in odd positions are outer and vertices in even positions are inner. An alternating path is augmenting if both endpoints are exposed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relative to a fixed matching, an alternating path begins with a free edge and alternates between free and matched edges. On one starting at an exposed vertex, odd-position vertices are outer and even-position vertices are inner. It is augmenting when both endpoints are exposed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: p\text{ is augmenting with respect to }M\iff p\text{ is alternating with respect to }M\text{ and both endpoints of }p\text{ are exposed}.

knowledge_statements.title: Alternating Cycles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The cycle is simple and alternates relative to a fixed matching.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph and \(M\subseteq E\) a matching. A simple cycle \(C=(v_0,e_1,v_1,\ldots,e_k,v_0)\) is \(M\)-alternating if, cyclically, exactly one edge of every consecutive pair belongs to \(M\). Consequently \(k\) is even and \(|E(C)\cap M|=|E(C)\setminus M|=k/2\). Replacing \(M\cap E(C)\) by \(E(C)\setminus M\) yields another matching of the same cardinality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An alternating cycle has matching and nonmatching edges in cyclic alternation. It is even, and flipping all its edges preserves matching feasibility and cardinality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M' = M\mathbin{\triangle}E(C)\text{ is a matching and }|M'|=|M|.\)

knowledge_statements.title: Symmetric-Difference Decompositions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Component decomposition for two matchings in a finite graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M,N\) be matchings in a finite undirected graph \(G\). Every nontrivial connected component of the spanning subgraph \((V,M\mathbin{\triangle}N)\) is either a path or an even cycle, and its edges alternate between \(M\setminus N\) and \(N\setminus M\). Cycle components contain equally many edges of both matchings. A path component has equal counts or has one more edge from exactly one of \(M\) and \(N\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The symmetric difference of two matchings decomposes into edge-alternating paths and even cycles, with each path having matching-edge counts differing by at most one.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\mathbin{\triangle}N\text{ is a vertex-disjoint union of alternating paths and even alternating cycles.}\)

notation.meaning: edges belonging to exactly one of the two matchings

knowledge_statements.title: Matching-Exchange Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasible exchanges are obtained by flipping alternating components.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M,N\) be matchings of a finite graph \(G\), and let \(K\) be a connected component of \(M\mathbin{\triangle}N\). Then \(M_K=M\mathbin{\triangle}E(K)\) is a matching. Moreover, \(|M_K|-|M|=|E(K)\cap N|-|E(K)\cap M|\), which belongs to \(\{-1,0,1\}\). In particular, a component beginning and ending with edges of \(N\setminus M\) is an \(M\)-augmenting path and its flip increases cardinality by one.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Flipping any component of the symmetric difference of two matchings remains feasible; its cardinality change is minus one, zero, or one according to the component endpoints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\mathbin{\triangle}E(K)\text{ is a matching and }|M\mathbin{\triangle}E(K)|-|M|\in\{-1,0,1\}.\)

notation.meaning: matching obtained by flipping the edges of the component

children.title: Odd-Cycle Structure
children.top_down_role: Odd cycles relevant to alternating search in general graphs.

knowledge_statements.title: Odd-Cycle Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Odd alternating cycles are expressed as blossoms with a distinguished base.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) be a matching in a finite graph \(G\). An \(M\)-blossom cycle is a simple odd cycle \(C\) with a distinguished vertex \(b\), called its base, such that \(M\cap E(C)\) matches every vertex of \(V(C)\setminus\{b\}\) within \(C\). Thus the two cycle edges incident with \(b\) lie outside \(M\), while all remaining cycle edges alternate between outside and inside \(M\). The cycle minus \(b\) has a perfect matching supplied by \(M\cap E(C)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A blossom cycle is odd and has one base vertex; all other cycle vertices are paired by alternating matching edges within the cycle.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\cap E(C)\text{ is a perfect matching of }C-b.\)

notation.meaning: base vertex of the blossom cycle

children.title: Blossom Obstructions
children.top_down_role: Odd alternating structures that obstruct direct augmenting-path search.

knowledge_statements.title: Blossom Obstructions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The obstruction concerns uncontracted alternating-tree search in nonbipartite graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T\) be an \(M\)-alternating search forest rooted at vertices exposed by \(M\). If an edge joins two even-level vertices in the same tree, their tree paths to the least common ancestor together with that edge form an odd \(M\)-blossom cycle. Unlike the bipartite case, this edge need not yield an augmenting path: the two paths can meet at the blossom base. Treating the cycle as an ordinary alternating path therefore makes the uncontracted search criterion invalid.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An edge between even-level vertices of one alternating tree can close an odd blossom rather than produce an augmenting path, invalidating the bipartite search rule.
assumptions_latex: \(T\) is an alternating forest rooted at exposed vertices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{An even--even search edge within one tree may certify an odd blossom, not an }M\text{-augmenting path.}\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Opposite-Parity Alternating Paths Within a Blossom
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The two alternating routes from the root or blossom base to each nonbase blossom vertex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every nonbase vertex \(i\) of a blossom, there are two distinct alternating paths from the root to \(i\), equivalently two routes from the blossom base after removing the common stem. knowledge_statements.statement_title: Matching Flowers and Associated Blossoms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines an odd alternating flower and its associated terminal blossom circuit relative to a matching.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) be a matching, let \(X\) be the set of vertices missed by \(M\), and let \(P=(v_0,v_1,\ldots,v_t)\) be an \(M\)-alternating walk. The walk \(P\) is an \(M\)-flower if and only if \(t\) is odd, \(v_0,\ldots,v_{t-1}\) are distinct, \(v_0\in X\), and \(v_t=v_i\) for some even \(i<t\). For such an index \(i\), the circuit \((v_i,v_{i+1},\ldots,v_t)\) is the associated \(M\)-blossom.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An M-alternating walk is an M-flower exactly when it starts at a vertex missed by M, has odd length, has distinct vertices before its endpoint, and ends by repeating a vertex in an even position. The resulting terminal circuit is its associated M-blossom.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P\text{ is an }M\text{-flower}\iff\bigl[t\text{ is odd},\ v_0,\ldots,v_{t-1}\text{ are distinct},\ v_0\in X,\ \exists\text{ even }i<t:\ v_t=v_i\bigr],\quad (v_i,\ldots,v_t)\text{ is the associated }M\text{-blossom}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Blossom with Base and Stem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition of a blossom relative to a matching, including its base, stem, and internal alternating paths.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a matching in \(G=(N,A)\). For \(N_B\subseteq N\) with \(|N_B|=2r+1\), \(r\geq 1\), let \(B\) be the set of edges whose endpoints both lie in \(N_B\). Then \(B\) is a blossom with respect to \(X\) if: (i) \(|X\cap B|=r\), leaving a unique vertex \(b\in N_B\) exposed by \(X\cap B\), called the base; (ii) there is an even-length \(X\)-alternating path \(S\), with \(S\cap B=\varnothing\), from \(b\) to a vertex exposed by \(X\), called the root of the stem; and (iii) for every \(i\in N_B\), there is an even-length \(X\)-alternating path \(S_{b,i}\subseteq B\) between \(b\) and \(i\). Consequently, concatenating \(S\) and \(S_{b,i}\) gives an alternating path from the root to \(i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relative to a matching X, a blossom consists of an odd vertex set with exactly r internal matching edges and hence one internally exposed base. An even alternating stem, edge-disjoint from the blossom, connects the base to an X-exposed root, and every blossom vertex has an even alternating path to the base using blossom edges.
assumptions_latex: B=\{e\in A:\text{both endpoints of }e\text{ lie in }N_B\}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: B\text{ is a blossom with respect to }X\iff \text{conditions (i)--(iii) hold}.

knowledge_statements.title: Nested Blossom Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Laminarity applies to blossoms maintained by recursive contraction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In a recursive blossom-contraction regime, regard each contracted blossom as the union of its represented original vertices. If a new blossom is formed in the current contracted graph, then every previously contracted blossom is either wholly contained in the new blossom or disjoint from it. Hence the represented blossom sets form a laminar family \(\mathcal B\): for all \(B_1,B_2\in\mathcal B\), either \(B_1\cap B_2=\varnothing\), \(B_1\subseteq B_2\), or \(B_2\subseteq B_1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recursive contraction maintains blossoms as a laminar family: any two represented blossom sets are disjoint or one contains the other.
assumptions_latex: Blossoms are created after contracting all currently active blossoms.
Each contracted vertex represents its full set of original vertices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal B\text{ is laminar.}\)

notation.meaning: family of represented blossom vertex sets

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Matching Defect and Graph Deficiency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions for a general graph, not assumed bipartite.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a graph \(G\) and a matching \(M\) in \(G\), the defect of \(M\) is the number of vertices not covered by \(M\), namely \(|V(G)|-2|M|\). The deficiency of \(G\) is \[\operatorname{def}(G)=|V(G)|-2\nu(G),\] equivalently the number of vertices left uncovered by a maximum matching and the minimum defect over all matchings of \(G\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The defect of a matching is the number of vertices it leaves unmatched. The deficiency of a graph is the minimum matching defect, equal to the number of vertices minus twice the maximum-matching size.
assumptions_latex: G\text{ is a general graph, not assumed bipartite}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{def}(G)=|V(G)|-2\nu(G)=\min_{M'\text{ matching in }G}\bigl(|V(G)|-2|M'|\bigr)

knowledge_statements.title: Tutte One-Factor Theory
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tutte's criterion for perfect matchings in finite undirected graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph, and for \(S\subseteq V\) let \(q(G-S)\) denote the number of connected components of \(G-S\) having odd order. Then \(G\) has a one-factor, equivalently a perfect matching, if and only if \(q(G-S)\le |S|\) for every \(S\subseteq V\). In particular, taking \(S=\varnothing\) shows that every connected component of a graph having a perfect matching has even order.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite graph has a perfect matching exactly when deleting any vertex set leaves no more odd components than the number of deleted vertices. In particular, each connected component of such a graph has even order.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G\text{ has a perfect matching}\iff q(G-S)\le |S|\text{ for every }S\subseteq V.\)

notation.meaning: number of odd-order components of the vertex-deleted graph

knowledge_statements.title: Tutte–Berge Maximum-Matching Min–Max Theory
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cardinality and deficiency forms of the finite-graph Tutte–Berge formula.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph, let \(\nu(G)\) be its maximum matching cardinality, and let \(q(G-S)\) count the odd-order components of \(G-S\). Then
\[|V|-2\nu(G)=\max_{S\subseteq V}\bigl(q(G-S)-|S|\bigr).\]
Equivalently,
\[\nu(G)=\frac12\min_{S\subseteq V}\bigl(|V|+|S|-q(G-S)\bigr).\]
Thus a maximizing set \(S\) certifies the number of vertices necessarily exposed by every matching.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The maximum matching size equals half the minimum of vertex count plus deleted-set size minus the number of resulting odd components.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|V|-2\nu(G)=\max_{S\subseteq V}\{q(G-S)-|S|\}.\)

notation.meaning: maximum cardinality of a matching in the graph
number of odd-order components after deleting the vertex set

knowledge_statements.title: Matching Barriers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Barriers are maximizers in the Tutte–Berge deficiency formula.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a finite graph \(G=(V,E)\), define \(\operatorname{def}(G)=|V|-2\nu(G)\). A set \(S\subseteq V\) is a matching barrier if
\[q(G-S)-|S|=\operatorname{def}(G),\]
where \(q(G-S)\) is the number of odd-order components of \(G-S\). Thus a barrier attains the Tutte–Berge maximum. When \(G\) has a perfect matching, this reduces to \(q(G-S)=|S|\); conventions that require nonempty \(S\) should be stated separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A matching barrier is a vertex set attaining the maximum odd-component excess in the Tutte–Berge formula, and therefore witnessing the graph's matching deficiency.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S\text{ is a barrier}\iff q(G-S)-|S|=|V|-2\nu(G).\)

notation.meaning: number of vertices left exposed by a maximum matching
number of odd-order components after deleting the set

knowledge_statements.title: Odd-Component Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Odd components after vertex deletion provide a verifiable deficiency lower bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be finite, let \(S\subseteq V\), and let \(Q_1,\ldots,Q_q\) be the odd-order components of \(G-S\). For every matching \(M\), at most \(|S|\) of these components can send an \(M\)-edge to \(S\). Each remaining odd component has at least one vertex unmatched by \(M\). Consequently every matching exposes at least \(q-|S|\) vertices, and
\[|M|\le \frac{|V|-q+|S|}{2}.\]
The listed components and set \(S\) therefore form a directly checkable deficiency certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Deleting a set that creates many odd components certifies unmatched vertices: every matching exposes at least the number of odd components minus the deleted-set size.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|V|-2|M|\ge q(G-S)-|S|\text{ for every matching }M.\)

notation.meaning: odd-order components of the vertex-deleted graph

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Tutte–Berge Theorem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Min–max characterization of maximum matching cardinality using odd components remaining after vertex deletion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\), let \(\operatorname{odd}(G-S)\) be the number of connected components of \(G-S\) having an odd number of vertices. Then
\[
\nu(G)=\min_{S\subseteq V}\frac{|V|+|S|-\operatorname{odd}(G-S)}{2},
\]
where \(\nu(G)\) is the maximum cardinality of a matching in \(G\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For any undirected graph, the maximum matching size equals the minimum, over all vertex sets S, of one half of the number of vertices plus the size of S minus the number of odd components left after deleting S.
assumptions_latex: \operatorname{odd}(G-S)=\#\{C:C\text{ is a component of }G-S,\ |V(C)|\text{ is odd}\}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \nu(G)=\min_{S\subseteq V}\frac{|V|+|S|-\operatorname{odd}(G-S)}{2}

knowledge_statements.title: General-Graph Deficiency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tutte–Berge representation of cardinality-matching deficiency in a finite undirected graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a finite undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\), let \(\nu(G)\) be the maximum cardinality of a matching and let \(o(G-U)\) count the odd-order connected components of the vertex-deleted graph \(G-U\). The matching deficiency, equal to the minimum number of vertices left uncovered by a matching, satisfies
\[
\operatorname{def}(G):=|V|-2\nu(G)=\max_{U\subseteq V}\bigl(o(G-U)-|U|\bigr).
\]
Thus every set \(U\subseteq V\) gives the lower bound \(\operatorname{def}(G)\ge o(G-U)-|U|\), and at least one set attains equality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The minimum number of unmatched vertices equals the maximum, over deleted vertex sets, of the number of resulting odd components minus the number deleted.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite undirected graph; parallel edges are allowed and loops are irrelevant.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{def}(G)=|V|-2\nu(G)=\max_{U\subseteq V}(o(G-U)-|U|)\).

notation.meaning: number of odd-order components of the vertex-deleted graph
minimum number of vertices uncovered by a matching

knowledge_statements.title: Maximum-Deficiency Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal–dual certificate for the Tutte–Berge deficiency value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A certificate that a matching \(M\) of a finite graph \(G=(V,E)\) is maximum consists of a set \(U\subseteq V\) such that
\[
|V|-2|M|=o(G-U)-|U|.
\]
The matching verifies \(\operatorname{def}(G)\le |V|-2|M|\), while the odd components verify \(\operatorname{def}(G)\ge o(G-U)-|U|\): after matching vertices of \(U\), at least \(o(G-U)-|U|\) odd components must retain an uncovered vertex. Equality certifies both that \(M\) is maximum and that \(U\) maximizes the deficiency expression.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A matching and a deleted vertex set certify optimality when their numbers of uncovered vertices and excess odd components are equal.
assumptions_latex: \(M\subseteq E\) is a matching and \(U\subseteq V\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(|V|-2|M|=o(G-U)-|U|\), then \(M\) is maximum and \(U\) is a maximum-deficiency set.

notation.meaning: vertex set furnishing the odd-component bound
number of odd-order components after deleting U

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Gallai–Edmonds decomposition theorem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical vertex decomposition and the resulting structure and cardinality of maximum matchings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be a graph. Let \(Y\) be the set of vertices exposed by at least one maximum matching, let \(X\) be the set of neighbors of \(Y\) in \(V(G)\setminus Y\), and let \(W=V(G)\setminus(X\cup Y)\). Every maximum matching in \(G\) contains a perfect matching of \(G[W]\), near-perfect matchings of the connected components of \(G[Y]\), and edges matching all vertices of \(X\) to distinct connected components of \(G[Y]\). Every connected component of \(G[Y]\) is factor-critical, and \(2\nu(G)=|V(G)|-q_G(X)+|X|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Gallai–Edmonds partition consists of vertices exposed by some maximum matching, their outside neighbors, and the remaining vertices. Every maximum matching is perfect on the remaining part, near-perfect on each exposed-part component, and matches each neighboring vertex into a distinct such component. Those components are factor-critical, and the stated formula gives twice the maximum-matching cardinality.
assumptions_latex: Y=\{v\in V(G):v\text{ is exposed by at least one maximum matching}\}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \begin{aligned}&\text{Every maximum matching contains a perfect matching of }G[W]\text{ and near-perfect matchings of every component of }G[Y],\\&\text{and matches all vertices of }X\text{ to distinct components of }G[Y];\\&\text{every component of }G[Y]\text{ is factor-critical};\\&2\nu(G)=|V(G)|-q_G(X)+|X|.\end{aligned}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equivalence Relation on Vertices Exposable by Maximum Matchings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A structural relation on the set of vertices missed by at least one maximum matching.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be a graph and let \(D=\{u\in V(G):u\text{ is missed by some maximum matching of }G\}\). For \(u,v\in D\), define \(u\sim v\) if and only if \(u=v\) or no maximum matching of \(G\) misses both \(u\) and \(v\). Then \(\sim\) is an equivalence relation on \(D\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Among vertices that can be missed by a maximum matching, two vertices are related when they are equal or no maximum matching misses them both. This is an equivalence relation.
assumptions_latex: D=\{u\in V(G):u\text{ is missed by some maximum matching of }G\}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sim\text{ is an equivalence relation on }D

knowledge_statements.title: Canonical Vertex Partition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical Gallai–Edmonds partition determined by all maximum matchings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph. Define \(D\) to be the set of vertices that are uncovered by at least one maximum matching of \(G\). Define
\[
A:=N_G(D)\setminus D,
\qquad
C:=V\setminus(A\cup D).
\]
The ordered triple \((D,A,C)\) is the Gallai–Edmonds partition. It is canonical because its definition depends only on \(G\), not on a selected maximum matching. Here \(N_G(D)\) comprises all vertices outside or inside \(D\) adjacent to a vertex of \(D\), with subtraction ensuring \(A\cap D=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Vertices exposable by maximum matchings form D; their external neighbors form A; all remaining vertices form C.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((D,A,C)\) is a uniquely determined partition of \(V\).

notation.meaning: vertices missed by at least one maximum matching
neighbors of D lying outside D
vertices in neither D nor A

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Gallai–Edmonds Canonical Vertex Partition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the three canonical vertex classes through exposure by maximum matchings and adjacency to exposed vertices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a graph \(G=(V,E)\), let \(N(W)=\{v\in V\setminus W:\exists w\in W,\;vw\in E\}\). Define \(D(G)=\{v\in V:\text{there exists a maximum-size matching of }G\text{ that misses }v\}\), \(A(G)=N(D(G))\), and \(C(G)=V\setminus(D(G)\cup A(G))\). The partition \((D(G),A(G),C(G))\) is the Gallai\text{--}Edmonds decomposition of \(G\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Gallai–Edmonds decomposition partitions the vertices into D, the vertices missed by some maximum matching; A, the neighbors of D outside D; and C, all remaining vertices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: V=D(G)\mathbin{\dot\cup}A(G)\mathbin{\dot\cup}C(G)\text{ with the three classes defined above.}

knowledge_statements.title: Factor-Critical Components
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Factor-critical portion of the Gallai–Edmonds structure theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((D,A,C)\) be the Gallai–Edmonds partition of a finite graph \(G\). Every connected component \(H\) of the induced subgraph \(G[D]\) is factor-critical: for every vertex \(v\in V(H)\), the graph \(H-v\) has a perfect matching. Consequently, every maximum matching of \(G\) restricts to a near-perfect matching in each component of \(G[D]\), except that components receiving a matching edge from \(A\) can expose the endpoint incident with that edge before the edge is added.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every component induced by D remains perfectly matchable after deletion of any one of its vertices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every component \(H\) of \(G[D]\) and every \(v\in V(H)\), the graph \(H-v\) has a perfect matching.

notation.meaning: subgraph induced by the Gallai–Edmonds set D

knowledge_statements.title: Decomposition-Based Matching Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Construction of a maximum matching from the Gallai–Edmonds decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input \(G\) and its Gallai–Edmonds partition \((D,A,C)\). Find a perfect matching of \(G[C]\). In the bipartite incidence graph between \(A\) and the components of \(G[D]\), find a matching saturating \(A\). For each assigned pair \((a,H)\), choose an edge \(av\) with \(v\in V(H)\) and a perfect matching of \(H-v\). In every unassigned component \(H\), choose any vertex \(w\) and a perfect matching of \(H-w\). Output the union of these edges and matchings. The output is a maximum matching of \(G\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Match C perfectly, assign each A vertex to a distinct D-component, and use near-perfect matchings inside the factor-critical components.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a finite undirected graph with Gallai–Edmonds partition \((D,A,C)\).
The component-incidence matching records an actual edge from each assigned \(a\in A\) to its assigned component.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The constructed union is a matching of cardinality \(\nu(G)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Alternating-Forest Blossom Search
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Alternating-forest search for augmenting a matching or certifying maximum cardinality in a general graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Maintain an \(M\)-alternating forest \(F\), initially \(F:=M\), and the classes \(\operatorname{even}(F)\), \(\operatorname{odd}(F)\), and \(\operatorname{free}(F)\). Repeatedly choose an edge \(uv\) with \(u\in\operatorname{even}(F)\) and \(v\in\operatorname{even}(F)\cup\operatorname{free}(F)\). If \(v\in\operatorname{free}(F)\), extend the forest using \(uv\) and the edge of \(M\) incident with \(v\). If \(v\in\operatorname{even}(F)\), the forest paths from \(X\) to \(u\) and \(v\), together with \(uv\), either form an \(M\)-augmenting path when the paths are disjoint or contain an \(M\)-blossom, which is contracted, when they intersect. There are at most \(|V|\) iterations. The search terminates with an augmentation or, if no edge joins \(\operatorname{even}(F)\) to \(\operatorname{even}(F)\cup\operatorname{free}(F)\), with the conclusion that \(M\) has maximum size; the overall search work is \(O(n^2)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The algorithm grows an alternating forest from even vertices. An edge to a free vertex extends the forest, while an edge between even vertices produces either an augmenting path or a blossom to contract. It performs at most n iterations and in quadratic time either augments the matching or concludes that it is maximum.
assumptions_latex: G=(V,E)\text{ is a finite graph with }n=|V|
F\text{ is maintained as an }M\text{-alternating forest rooted at }X
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The search finds an }M\text{-augmentation or concludes that }M\text{ is maximum in }O(n^2)\text{ time.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nonbipartite Cardinality Matching Algorithm with Blossoms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded summary of a blossom-based maximum-cardinality matching algorithm for general graphs; blossom membership and base determination rely on procedures defined elsewhere in the source.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a graph $G=(N,A)$ and an initial matching $X$ (possibly empty), initialize $b(i)=i$ for every $i\in N$ and label every exposed vertex $S:\varnothing$. Repeatedly scan an unmatched edge $(i,j)\notin X$ incident to an $S$-labeled vertex, or the unique matched edge $(i,j)\in X$ incident to a $T$-labeled vertex, ignoring the edge when $b(i)=b(j)$. An unlabeled encountered vertex receives the corresponding alternating-tree label. If the relevant backtraces reach distinct exposed roots, augment $X$, remove all labels, reset $b(i)=i$ for all $i$, and restart. If they reach the same root, form the blossom, determine its membership and base, complete its labels, update its blossom numbers, and continue. If no label remains unscanned, then no augmenting path exists, $X$ has maximum cardinality, and the final labels and blossom numbers can be used to construct an optimal dual solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Start with any matching in a general graph, label all exposed vertices as roots, and grow labeled alternating trees while treating each current blossom as a unit. An encounter whose backtraces reach different exposed roots produces an augmenting path; augment the matching, clear the labels, restore singleton blossom numbers, and restart. An encounter whose backtraces reach the same root produces a blossom, which is formed and labeled before scanning continues. If all labels have been scanned without finding an augmentation, no augmenting path exists, the matching is maximum-cardinality, and the labels and blossom numbers provide an optimal-dual certificate.
assumptions_latex: G=(N,A)\text{ is a general, not necessarily bipartite, graph}
X\subseteq A\text{ is an initial matching, possibly }X=\varnothing
b(i)=i\quad\forall i\in N\text{ initially and after every augmentation}
\text{Blossom membership, base selection, labeling, and backtracing are performed as specified by the surrounding method}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{If the labeling process terminates with no unscanned labels, then no augmenting path exists, }X\text{ is maximum-cardinality, and the labels and blossom numbers construct an optimal dual solution.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Edmonds Blossom Matching Algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Alternating-forest procedure using scanning, augmentation, blossom contraction, and forest growth to obtain a maximum matching in a general graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize $\mu=\phi=\rho=\operatorname{id}$ and $\sigma=\mathrm{UNSCANNED}$. Repeatedly select an UNSCANNED blossom point $x$. Mark $x$ SCANNED when every neighbor is inner or has the same $\rho$-representative. For a blossom-point neighbor $y$ with $\rho(y)\ne\rho(x)$, augment and reinitialize when $S(x)\cap S(y)=\varnothing$; otherwise shrink the blossom determined by the first common base point by updating $\phi$ and $\rho$. For an out-of-forest neighbor $y$, grow the forest by setting $\phi(y)=x$. Stop when every blossom is SCANNED; then the edges represented by $\{x\mu(x)\}$ form a maximum matching in $G$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Initialize the matching, forest, and blossom-representative maps and mark all blossoms unscanned. Scanning either closes a search point, augments along disjoint alternating paths, contracts a blossom when the paths meet, or grows the forest through a new neighbor. When every blossom is scanned, the matching encoded by the matching map is maximum.
assumptions_latex: S(\cdot),\rho,\phi,\mu,\sigma\text{ have the meanings fixed by the preceding algorithmic setup}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Upon termination, the edges represented by }\{x\mu(x)\}\text{ form a maximum matching in }G

knowledge_statements.title: Alternating Forests
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Search forest used by the cardinality version of Edmonds' blossom algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a matching \(M\) in a finite undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\), an alternating forest \(F\) is a rooted forest in which every root is uncovered by \(M\), and every root-to-vertex path alternates between edges outside \(M\) and edges in \(M\), beginning with an edge outside \(M\). Vertices at even depth are outer and vertices at odd depth are inner. Every inner vertex is covered by \(M\), and its unique incident edge in \(M\) joins it to its outer child; equivalently, every nonroot outer vertex is joined to its inner parent by an edge in \(M\). During search growth from an outer vertex, an unmatched edge to an unreached matched vertex adds that vertex as inner and its mate as outer. An unmatched edge to an exposed vertex instead yields an augmenting path and does not add that exposed vertex as an inner vertex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An alternating forest grows from exposed roots through unmatched-then-matched edge pairs; even-depth vertices are outer, odd-depth vertices are inner, and reaching another exposed vertex produces an augmenting path.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every root-to-outer path has even length, every root-to-inner path has odd length, and every inner vertex has a unique matched outer child.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Alternating Forest
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Alternating-search forest relative to a fixed matching.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be a graph and \(M\) a matching in \(G\). An alternating forest with respect to \(M\) is a forest \(F\subseteq G\) such that: (i) \(V(F)\) contains every vertex exposed by \(M\), and every component contains exactly one exposed vertex, called its root; (ii) a vertex is outer or inner according as its distance from its component root is even or odd, respectively, and every inner vertex has degree \(2\) in \(F\); and (iii) for every \(v\in V(F)\), the unique path from \(v\) to its component root is \(M\)-alternating.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An alternating forest contains all exposed vertices and exactly one exposed root per component. Vertices are outer or inner according to even or odd root distance, every inner vertex has degree two, and every vertex-to-root path alternates with respect to the matching.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F\text{ is an alternating forest with respect to }M\text{ exactly when conditions (i)--(iii) hold.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Matching-Alternating Forest and Its Vertex Classes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines an alternating-search forest and its even, odd, and free vertex classes relative to a designated root set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\), let \(M\subseteq E\) be a matching, and let \(X\subseteq V\). An \(M\)-alternating forest is a set \(F\subseteq E\) such that \(F\) is a forest, \(M\subseteq F\), every component of \((V,F)\) either contains exactly one vertex of \(X\) or consists of one edge of \(M\), and every path in \(F\) starting in \(X\) is \(M\)-alternating. Define \(\operatorname{even}(F)=\{v\in V: F\text{ contains an even-length }X\!\text{-}v\text{ path}\}\), \(\operatorname{odd}(F)=\{v\in V: F\text{ contains an odd-length }X\!\text{-}v\text{ path}\}\), and \(\operatorname{free}(F)=\{v\in V: F\text{ contains no }X\!\text{-}v\text{ path}\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An M-alternating forest contains M, has each component rooted at exactly one vertex of X or consisting of a single matching edge, and has alternating paths from X. Vertices are classified as even, odd, or free according to the parity or absence of a path from X.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F\text{ is an }M\text{-alternating forest, with }\operatorname{even}(F),\operatorname{odd}(F),\operatorname{free}(F)\text{ defined as above.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Alternating forest with respect to a matching
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Search forest rooted at all exposed vertices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a matching \(S\) of a graph \(G\), an alternating forest is a subgraph \(H\) such that \(E(H)\) is a forest; each component contains exactly one exposed vertex as its root and every exposed vertex is a root; vertices are classified as even or odd by their distance from the root; and every odd vertex has degree \(2\) in \(H\), with one of its two incident forest edges belonging to \(S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An alternating forest for a matching is a forest with exactly one exposed root in each component and with every exposed vertex included as a root. Vertex parity is determined by distance from the root, and every odd vertex has two forest edges, one of which is a matching edge.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: H\text{ is an alternating forest with respect to }S\iff\begin{cases}E(H)\text{ is a forest},\\\text{each component has exactly one exposed root and every exposed vertex is a root},\\\text{each odd vertex has degree }2\text{ in }H\text{ and one incident forest edge lies in }S.\end{cases}

children.title: Blossom Detection
children.top_down_role: Recognition of odd alternating structures during forest search.

knowledge_statements.title: Blossom Detection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Same-tree outer–outer collision criterion for detecting a blossom.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) be an alternating forest for matching \(M\). Suppose a searched edge \(xy\notin M\) joins distinct outer vertices in the same tree, and let \(b\) be their lowest common ancestor in \(F\). The union of \(xy\), the tree path from \(b\) to \(x\), and the tree path from \(b\) to \(y\) is an odd cycle \(B\). Its edges alternate with respect to \(M\), except that the two cycle edges incident with the base \(b\) are outside \(M\). This cycle, together with base \(b\), is the detected blossom.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An edge joining two outer vertices in one search tree creates an odd alternating cycle based at their lowest common ancestor.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is an alternating forest for a matching \(M\).
\(x\) and \(y\) are distinct outer vertices in the same tree and \(xy\notin M\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The two tree paths to their lowest common ancestor together with \(xy\) form an \(M\)-blossom.

notation.meaning: lowest common ancestor and blossom base

children.title: Forest Label Structure
children.top_down_role: Parity-based organization of vertices within alternating forests.

knowledge_statements.title: Forest Label Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parity and mate invariants maintained by an Edmonds alternating search forest.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In an alternating forest \(F\) for matching \(M\), each root is exposed and outer. Every nonroot outer vertex has an inner parent joined to it by an edge of \(M\); every inner vertex has an outer parent joined to it by an edge outside \(M\), and its unique \(M\)-mate is its outer child. Hence an outer vertex has an even-length alternating path from its root, while an inner vertex has an odd-length alternating path. These labels are relative to the current contracted search graph and must be recomputed or inherited consistently after contraction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Outer and inner labels encode path parity, with matched edges linking each inner vertex to its unique outer child.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is an alternating forest generated from exposed roots for matching \(M\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Outer vertices have even alternating root paths; inner vertices have odd alternating root paths and a unique matched outer child.

children.title: Search-Collision Regimes
children.top_down_role: Forest interactions that reveal augmentation or blossom formation.

knowledge_statements.title: Search-Collision Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Case distinction for an unmatched edge scanned from an outer search vertex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: When an edge \(xy\notin M\) is scanned from an outer vertex \(x\), apply the following cases. If \(y\) is unreached and matched, add \(y\) as inner and its mate as outer; if \(y\) is unreached and exposed, the root-to-\(x\) path followed by \(xy\) is augmenting. If \(y\) is outer in a different tree, concatenate the two root paths with \(xy\) to obtain an augmenting path. If \(y\) is outer in the same tree, detect and contract the resulting blossom. Edges to inner vertices require no growth under this scan rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An outer-edge scan either grows the forest, finds an augmenting path, detects a blossom, or produces no search change.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is an alternating forest for matching \(M\).
\(x\) is outer and \(xy\notin M\) is being scanned.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The status of \(y\) determines growth, augmentation, blossom contraction, or no action.

notation.meaning: opposite endpoint of the scanned edge

children.title: Blossom Contraction
children.top_down_role: Reduced-graph representation obtained by shrinking a blossom.

knowledge_statements.title: Blossom Contraction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shrinking a detected alternating blossom during augmenting-path search.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a graph \(G\), matching \(M\), and a detected blossom \(B\) with base \(b\). Replace all vertices of \(B\) by one pseudovertex \(\beta\); delete loops and retain each edge between \(B\) and \(V(G)\setminus B\) as an edge incident with \(\beta\), preserving its original endpoint in \(B\) as metadata. Replace the internal matched edges of \(B\) by nothing and map any matching edge leaving the base to its corresponding edge at \(\beta\). In the contracted search, treat \(\beta\) as having the outer status formerly held by \(b\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Shrink the odd alternating cycle to an outer pseudovertex while retaining boundary-edge endpoints for later expansion.
assumptions_latex: \(B\) is an odd alternating blossom detected relative to matching \(M\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The procedure produces the contracted graph \(G/B\) and induced matching \(M/B\) used for continued search.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Graph Obtained by Blossom Contraction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the graph obtained by shrinking a blossom to a single vertex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\), let \(M\) be a matching, and let \(b\) be a blossom with respect to \(M\). The contraction \(G/b=(V/b,E/b)\) replaces the vertices of \(b\) by a new vertex \(v_b\), omits every edge having both endpoints in \(b\), and replaces each edge \([v,u]\) with \(u\in V(b)\) and \(v\notin V(b)\) by \([v,v_b]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Shrinking a blossom replaces its vertices by one new vertex, removes its internal edges, and redirects its boundary edges to the new vertex.
assumptions_latex: b\text{ is a blossom with respect to }M
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: V/b=(V\setminus V(b))\cup\{v_b\},\quad E/b\text{ is obtained by omitting the internal edges of }b\text{ and redirecting its boundary edges to }v_b

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Blossom contraction operation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Construction of a contracted graph and an even pseudonode during cardinality-matching search.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a blossom \(B=(i_1,i_2,\ldots,i_k,i_1)\) relative to the current matching and rooted search, introduce a pseudonode \(b\), set \(A^c(b)=\bigcup_{i\in B}A(i)\), add \(b\) to the adjacency list of every vertex adjacent to \(B\), retain the cyclic order of the blossom vertices in a circular doubly linked list, and delete the blossom vertices and their incident edges. The pseudonode is even, and scanning its adjacency list exposes the external adjacencies of the blossom.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Contract a blossom by replacing its vertices with an even pseudonode whose adjacency list combines their adjacencies, updating neighboring lists, recording the blossom cycle for recovery, and deleting the original vertices and incident edges.
assumptions_latex: B=(i_1,i_2,\ldots,i_k,i_1)\text{ is a blossom relative to the current matching and rooted search}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G^c\text{ represents }B\text{ by an even pseudonode }b\text{ with }A^c(b)=\bigcup_{i\in B}A(i).
