knowledge_statements.title: Total Dual Integrality for b-Matching Systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: TDI criterion for a chosen rational b-matching inequality system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A rational inequality system \(Ax\le d\) describing a \(b\)-matching polyhedron is totally dual integral if, for every integral objective vector \(c\in\mathbb Z^{E}\) for which the primal optimum is finite, the dual program \[\min\{d^\top y:A^\top y=c,\ y\ge0\}\] has an integral optimal solution \(y\). When additionally \(d\) is integral, total dual integrality implies that the polyhedron \(\{x:Ax\le d\}\) is integral. TDI is a property of the displayed system, not merely of the polyhedron it represents.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A b-matching inequality system is TDI when every finite dual with an integral objective admits an integral optimal multiplier vector.
assumptions_latex: \(c\in\mathbb Z^{E}\) and the corresponding primal optimum is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Ax\le d\) is TDI exactly when the displayed dual has an integral optimum for every such \(c\).

children.title: Expansion Reductions

knowledge_statements.title: Expansion Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parallel-copy expansion of integral edge capacities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a finite capacitated instance \((G,b,u,w)\). For each edge \(e\in E\), create \(u_e\) labeled parallel copies, each having the endpoints and weight of \(e\); retain every vertex bound \(b_v\). Solve the resulting simple \(b\)-matching instance and output \(x_e=\sum_{i=1}^{u_e}y_{e,i}\). Conversely, represent any feasible \(x\) by choosing \(x_e\) copies of each edge. The reduction preserves feasibility and objective value, but its expanded size is \(\sum_{e\in E}u_e\), so it is generally pseudopolynomial when capacities are binary encoded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Expand each capacity-u edge into u parallel copies, solve a simple b-matching instance, and project selected copies back to edge multiplicities.
assumptions_latex: The target matching model permits parallel labeled edges.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(w^\top x=\sum_{e\in E}\sum_{i=1}^{u_e}w_e y_{e,i}\), with expanded edge count \(\sum_{e\in E}u_e\).

notation.meaning: selection indicator for copy i of edge e

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The expansion algorithm and pseudopolynomial binary-encoding boundary are plausible and well stated, but no source supports either the exact reduction or its complexity qualification.

knowledge_statements.title: Vertex-Splitting Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reduction of uncapacitated multiplicity b-matchings to ordinary matchings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a finite loopless graph \(G=(V,E)\) and \(b\in\mathbb Z_{ge0}^{V}\), replace each vertex \(v\) by labeled slots \(v^1,\ldots,v^{b_v}\). For every edge \(e=uv\), join every pair \(u^i v^j\) and give the new edge weight \(w_e\). Any ordinary matching \(M'\) projects to \(x_e\), the number of selected slot edges originating from \(e\); then \(x(\delta(v))\le b_v\). Conversely, every integer-multiplicity \(b\)-matching admits such a slot assignment. The projection preserves weight, although the construction may have \(\sum_{uv\in E}b_u b_v\) edges.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Split each vertex into b_v unit slots and connect compatible slot pairs; ordinary matchings then project exactly to uncapacitated integer-multiplicity b-matchings.
assumptions_latex: \(b\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^{V}\); repeated use of an original edge is allowed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_e=|M'\cap\{u^iv^j:1\le i\le b_u,\ 1\le j\le b_v\}|\) preserves feasibility and total weight.

notation.meaning: ordinary matching in the split graph
number of matched slot edges representing e

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The slot construction is coherent for the explicitly stated integer-multiplicity model and the representation kind fits the reduction leaf, but the exact bidirectional correspondence and size bound have no citation.

children.title: Ordinary-Matching Reductions
children.top_down_role: Reductions from b-matching instances to ordinary matching instances.

assumptions_latex: \(b:V\to\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}\) satisfies \(b(v)\le d_G(v)\) for every \(v\in V\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G\) has a \(b\)-factor if and only if \(H_b\) has a perfect matching.

notation.meaning: Incidence-slack expansion of the input graph
Degree of vertex v in G

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Incidence-slack reduction of exact \(b\)-factors to perfect matching.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every incidence \((v,e)\), create a vertex \(v_e\). For each edge \(e=uv\), add the edge \(u_ev_e\). For every \(v\), create \(d_G(v)-b(v)\) slack vertices and join each of them to every incidence vertex \(v_e\). Call the resulting graph \(H_b\). Then \(G\) contains a spanning subgraph \(F\) with \(d_F(v)=b(v)\) for all \(v\) if and only if \(H_b\) has a perfect matching. Under this correspondence, \(e=uv\) belongs to \(F\) exactly when \(u_ev_e\) belongs to the perfect matching.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines b-factors, identifies the uniform degree-one and degree-two cases, and records the stated bipartite flow reductions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) and \(b\in\mathbf Z^V\). A \(b\)-factor is a set \(M\subseteq E\) such that \(|M\cap\delta(v)|=b_v\) for every \(v\in V\). A \(1\)-factor is a perfect matching, while a \(2\)-factor is a collection of circuits covering every vertex exactly once. The minimum-weight \(2\)-factor problem is a relaxation of the traveling-salesman problem. If \(G\) is bipartite, existence of a \(b\)-factor can be decided by network-flow methods, and a minimum-weight \(b\)-factor can be found as a minimum-cost-flow problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A b-factor selects edges so that each vertex has exactly its prescribed incident degree. Degree one gives a perfect matching and degree two gives a vertex-covering collection of circuits. Minimum-weight 2-factor relaxes TSP; for bipartite graphs, feasibility and minimum weight reduce to flow and minimum-cost flow, respectively.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: H-factor definition and tractability boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Graph-family factors, the perfect-matching specialization, and the stated fixed-family complexity classifications.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal H\) be a family of connected graphs. An \(\mathcal H\)-factor of \(G\) is a spanning subgraph of \(G\) whose components are isomorphic to members of \(\mathcal H\). Every graph has a \(\{K_1\}\)-factor, and a \(\{K_2\}\)-factor is a perfect matching. For a fixed connected graph \(F\not\cong K_1,K_2\), deciding whether \(G\) has a \(\{F\}\)-factor is NP-complete. If \(\mathcal H=\{K_2\}\cup\mathcal H'\), where \(\mathcal H'\) is any finite family of factor-critical graphs, the \(\mathcal H\)-factor problem is polynomial-time solvable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An H-factor is a spanning subgraph whose components have types from H. The K2 case is perfect matching. Every other nontrivial fixed singleton component type gives an NP-complete problem, while K2 together with finitely many factor-critical component types gives a polynomial-time problem.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal H\text{ is a family of connected graphs}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \{F\}\text{-Factor is NP-complete for fixed connected }F\not\cong K_1,K_2;\qquad \left(\{K_2\}\cup\mathcal H'\right)\text{-Factor is polynomial-time solvable when }\mathcal H'\text{ is finite and every member is factor-critical}.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Disjoint-set parity criterion for exact \(f\)-factors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For disjoint \(S,T\subseteq V\), let \(q_f(S,T)\) be the number of components \(C\) of \(G-(S\cup T)\) for which \(f(C)+e_G(C,T)\) is odd, and define
\[\Delta_f(S,T)=f(S)+\sum_{v\in T}d_{G-S}(v)-f(T)-q_f(S,T).\]
Then \(G\) has an \(f\)-factor if and only if \(\Delta_f(S,T)\ge 0\) for every disjoint pair \(S,T\). Moreover, each \(\Delta_f(S,T)\) has the same parity as \(f(V)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Tutte f-Factor Theorem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary and sufficient component-parity inequalities for the existence of a prescribed-degree factor.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G\) be a graph and let \(f:V(G)\to\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}\) satisfy \(f(v)\le \deg_G(v)\) for every \(v\in V(G)\), with \(\widehat f(v)=\deg_G(v)-f(v)\). Then \(G\) has an \(f\)-factor if and only if, for every pair of disjoint sets \(X,Y\subseteq V(G)\),
\[
\left|\left\{K\in\operatorname{comp}(G-X-Y): f(V(K))+|\nabla(V(K),Y)|\equiv 1\pmod 2\right\}\right|
\le f(X)+\widehat f(Y)-|\nabla(X,Y)|.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Let f assign each vertex a nonnegative prescribed degree not exceeding its degree in G, and define f-hat(v)=deg_G(v)−f(v). The graph G has an f-factor exactly when, for every two disjoint vertex sets X and Y, the number of components K of G−X−Y for which f(V(K))+|∇(V(K),Y)| is odd is at most f(X)+f-hat(Y)−|∇(X,Y)|.

knowledge_statements.title: Factor Deficiency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tutte deficiency for prescribed-degree factors in finite undirected graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be finite, let \(f:V\to\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}\) satisfy \(f(v)\le d_G(v)\), and assume \(f(V)\) is even. For disjoint \(S,T\subseteq V\), let \(q_f(S,T)\) count the components \(C\) of \(G-(S\cup T)\) for which \(f(C)+|E(C,T)|\) is odd, and set \[\delta_f(S,T)=f(S)-f(T)+\sum_{v\in T}d_{G-S}(v)-q_f(S,T).\] The Tutte \(f\)-factor deficiency is \[\operatorname{def}_f(G)=\max\bigl\{0,\max_{S\cap T=\varnothing}(-\delta_f(S,T))\bigr\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Factor deficiency is the greatest violation, over disjoint vertex sets, of the Tutte inequalities governing existence of a spanning subgraph with degrees exactly f.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{def}_f(G)\) is a nonnegative integer measuring the maximum violated Tutte \(f\)-factor inequality.

notation.meaning: The sum of f(v) over vertices v in X.
Number of parity-obstructing components outside S union T.
Degree of v after deleting S.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The formula is a plausible maximum-violation convention for the Tutte f-factor inequalities, but no inspectable source establishes that this normalization is called the f-factor deficiency.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Existence of an upper-bound-normalized optimal (f,g)-subgraph
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A normal-form existence result for minimum-deficiency generalized factors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let G be a graph and let f,g satisfy f,g\ge 0 and f+g\ge\deg_G pointwise. Then there exists an (f,g)-optimal spanning subgraph H such that \deg_H(v)\le f(v) for every v\in V(G).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For nonnegative f and g whose sum dominates the vertex degrees of G, some minimum-deficiency spanning subgraph satisfies every f upper bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists H:\ \delta(H;f,g)=\delta(f,g)\ \text{and}\ \deg_H\le f.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Min–Max Formula for \((f,g)\)-Factor Deficiency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Min–max characterization of \((f,g)\)-factor deficiency, using the section's definitions of \(\delta(f,g)\), \(\tau(X,Y)\), and \(\nabla(X,Y)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G\) be a graph and let \(f,g:V(G)\to\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}\) satisfy \(f(v)+g(v)\ge \deg_G(v)\) for every \(v\in V(G)\). Then
\[
\delta(f,g)=\max_{\substack{X,Y\subseteq V(G)\\X\cap Y=\varnothing}}\left\{\tau(X,Y)+|\nabla(X,Y)|-f(X)-g(Y)\right\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For nonnegative integer-valued vertex functions f and g whose pointwise sum dominates the vertex degrees, the (f,g)-factor deficiency equals the maximum, over all disjoint vertex sets X and Y, of the number of contextually defined (X,Y)-odd components plus the number of edges between X and Y, minus f(X) and g(Y).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \delta(f,g)=\max_{\substack{X,Y\subseteq V(G)\\X\cap Y=\varnothing}}\left\{\tau(X,Y)+|\nabla(X,Y)|-f(X)-g(Y)\right\}

knowledge_statements.title: Factor Barriers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Barriers witnessing or maximizing violations of Tutte’s prescribed-degree inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the preceding finite-graph and parity conventions, an ordered pair of disjoint sets \((S,T)\) is an \(f\)-barrier if \(\delta_f(S,T)<0\), where \[\delta_f(S,T)=f(S)-f(T)+\sum_{v\in T}d_{G-S}(v)-q_f(S,T).\] It is a maximum \(f\)-barrier if \(-\delta_f(S,T)=\operatorname{def}_f(G)\). Thus every \(f\)-barrier identifies a parity-and-cut obstruction to an \(f\)-factor, while a maximum barrier attains the largest such obstruction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An f-barrier is a disjoint pair of vertex sets violating a Tutte f-factor inequality; a maximum barrier realizes the graph’s factor deficiency.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\delta_f(S,T)<0\) certifies that \(G\) has no \(f\)-factor.

notation.meaning: Tutte deficiency expression for the ordered pair (S,T).
Number of parity-obstructing components of the remaining graph.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The obstruction implication is mathematically plausible, but the definition of every negatively valued pair as an f-barrier and the maximum-barrier convention require an authoritative locator.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Odd components relative to disjoint vertex sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the parity-sensitive components counted in lower–upper factor obstruction formulas and records their symmetry and canonical-decomposition specialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be a graph, let \(f,g:V(G)\to\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\), and let \(X,Y\subseteq V(G)\) be disjoint. A connected component \(K\) of \(G-X-Y\) is \((X,Y)\)-odd with respect to \((f,g)\) if \[f(v)=\widehat g(v)\quad\text{for every }v\in V(K),\] and \[f(V(K))+|\nabla(V(K),Y)|\equiv1\pmod2.\] This is equivalent to \(K\) being \((Y,X)\)-odd with respect to \((g,f)\). Let \(\tau(X,Y)\) denote the number of \((X,Y)\)-odd components. Every connected component of \(G[D]\) is \((A,B)\)-odd, and hence \[\tau(A,B)=\#\operatorname{comp}(G[D]).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An (X,Y)-odd component is a component outside disjoint sets X and Y on which the bounds are complementary and whose total f-value plus its number of edges to Y is odd. The definition is symmetric under swapping X with Y and f with g. At the canonical pair (A,B), the count equals the number of D-components.
assumptions_latex: K\text{ is a connected component of }G-X-Y
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: K\text{ is }(X,Y)\text{-odd w.r.t. }(f,g)\iff\left(\forall v\in V(K),\ f(v)=\widehat g(v)\right)\land\left(f(V(K))+|\nabla(V(K),Y)|\equiv1\pmod2\right);\quad K\text{ is }(X,Y)\text{-odd w.r.t. }(f,g)\iff K\text{ is }(Y,X)\text{-odd w.r.t. }(g,f);\quad \tau(A,B)=\#\operatorname{comp}(G[D])

knowledge_statements.title: Deficiency–Barrier Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Infeasibility certificates supplied by violated Tutte inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) and \(f:V\to\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\) satisfy the stated feasibility and parity assumptions. A certificate of nonexistence of an \(f\)-factor is a disjoint pair \((S,T)\) together with the component list defining \(q_f(S,T)\), such that \[q_f(S,T)>f(S)-f(T)+\sum_{v\in T}d_{G-S}(v).\] Every quantity in this inequality is computable directly from \(G,f,S,T\). Tutte’s \(f\)-factor criterion asserts that such a certificate exists exactly when \(G\) has no \(f\)-factor; a maximum certificate has violation \(\operatorname{def}_f(G)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A violated Tutte inequality, with its parity-obstructing components listed, is a directly checkable certificate that no f-factor exists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G\) has an \(f\)-factor if and only if no deficiency–barrier certificate exists.

notation.meaning: Disjoint vertex sets forming the certificate.
Count of components satisfying the defining odd-parity condition.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The certificate kind fits the leaf, but the asserted equivalence is Tutte's f-factor theorem and requires a source with a specific theorem or section locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Factor Canonical Decompositions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Decomposition induced by edges occurring in prescribed-degree factors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a finite graph \(G=(V,E)\), a demand \(f:V\to\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\), and the nonempty family \(\mathcal F_f(G)\) of all \(f\)-factors. Call an edge \(f\)-allowed if it belongs to some \(F\in\mathcal F_f(G)\), and let \(G_f=(V,E_f)\) be the spanning subgraph of all allowed edges. The canonical allowed-edge decomposition is the partition of \(V\) into the connected components of \(G_f\). Every \(f\)-factor uses only edges within these components, and each allowed edge is realized by at least one \(f\)-factor.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The allowed-edge decomposition partitions the vertices into components connected by edges that occur in at least one f-factor.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The connected components of \(G_f\) form a uniquely determined partition associated with \((G,f)\).

notation.meaning: Family of all f-factors of G.
Edges occurring in at least one f-factor.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Allowed-edge connected components give a well-defined factor-component decomposition, but the broad title may denote a finer canonical decomposition. An authoritative definition is needed to resolve the intended local sense.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Monotonicity of Canonical Classes Under Ordered Parameters
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The sets \(A(f,g),B(f,g),D(f,g)\) retain their source-defined meanings in the canonical structure of (f,g)-optimal subgraphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be a graph and let \(f_1,f_2,g_1,g_2:V(G)\to\mathbb Z\). If \(f_1\leq f_2\), \(g_1\leq g_2\), and \(f_1+g_1\geq\deg_G\), then \(A(f_1,g_1)\supseteq A(f_2,g_2)\), \(B(f_1,g_1)\supseteq B(f_2,g_2)\), and \(D(f_1,g_1)\supseteq D(f_2,g_2)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When both integer-valued parameter functions increase pointwise and the first pair's sum dominates the vertex degrees, each canonical class A, B, and D can only shrink.

knowledge_statements.title: Tutte Reduction to Perfect Matching
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unweighted gadget reduction from exact prescribed degrees to perfect matching.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(G=(V,E)\) and \(f:V\to\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\) with \(f(v)\le d_G(v)\), create one incidence vertex \((v,e)\) for every \(e\in\delta_G(v)\). For each \(v\), create \(d_G(v)-f(v)\) dummy vertices and join each to every incidence vertex at \(v\). For every edge \(e=uv\), join \((u,e)\) to \((v,e)\). Compute a perfect matching \(M\) in the resulting graph. Output \[F=\{e=uv:(u,e)(v,e)\in M\}.\] If no perfect matching exists, report that no \(f\)-factor exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An incidence-and-dummy gadget converts f-factor existence into perfect-matching existence, with cross-gadget matching edges selecting the factor.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a finite undirected loopless graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The auxiliary graph has a perfect matching if and only if \(G\) has an \(f\)-factor, and the displayed extraction maps one to the other.

notation.meaning: Set of edges incident with v.
Perfect matching in the auxiliary graph.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Clone-expansion reduction of perfect f-matching to perfect matching
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reduction of perfect f-matching existence to ordinary perfect-matching existence by replacing each vertex with the prescribed number of clones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be a graph and let \(f:V(G)\to\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}\). For each \(v\in V(G)\), let \(U_v\) be a set of \(f(v)\) elements, with the sets \(U_v\) pairwise disjoint. Define \(G'\) on \(\bigcup_{v\in V(G)}U_v\) by joining every element of \(U_v\) to every element of \(U_w\) whenever \(vw\in E(G)\). Then \(G'\) has a perfect matching if and only if \(G\) has a perfect \(f\)-matching.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Replace every vertex v by f(v) clones and completely join the clone sets corresponding to adjacent vertices. The resulting graph has a perfect matching if and only if the original graph has a perfect f-matching.
assumptions_latex: \text{Every element of }U_v\text{ is adjacent to every element of }U_w\text{ whenever }vw\in E(G)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G'\text{ has a perfect matching}\iff G\text{ has a perfect }f\text{-matching}

knowledge_statements.title: Weighted Factor Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weight-preserving extension of the incidence-and-dummy matching reduction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an edge-weighted instance \((G,f,w)\), construct the Tutte auxiliary graph. Give each cross edge \((u,e)(v,e)\), where \(e=uv\), weight \(w(e)\), and give every incidence-to-dummy edge weight zero. Compute a minimum-weight perfect matching \(M\) and return \[F=\{e=uv:(u,e)(v,e)\in M\}.\] Every perfect matching selects exactly \(f(v)\) cross edges incident with each original vertex \(v\), and \[w(M)=\sum_{e\in F}w(e).\] Infeasibility of perfect matching is equivalent to infeasibility of the \(f\)-factor instance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Assigning original costs to cross-gadget edges makes the Tutte construction preserve feasibility and total weight.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Minimum-weight perfect matchings in the auxiliary graph correspond weight-for-weight to minimum-weight \(f\)-factors of \(G\).

notation.meaning: Perfect matching of the auxiliary graph.

children.title: Direct f-Factor Methods
children.top_down_role: Direct approaches specialized to prescribed-degree f-factor problems.

knowledge_statements.title: Direct f-Factor Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Direct solution through maximum-cardinality capacitated matching.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \((G,f)\), run a direct capacitated blossom algorithm for a maximum-cardinality integral \(b\)-matching with vertex capacities \(b(v)=f(v)\) and edge capacities one. Let its output be \(F\subseteq E\). Since \(d_F(v)\le f(v)\), one has \[2|F|=\sum_{v\in V}d_F(v)\le f(V).\] Stop and output \(F\) as an \(f\)-factor exactly when \(|F|=f(V)/2\); otherwise report that no \(f\)-factor exists. For weighted factors, optimize weight subject to this maximum-cardinality requirement.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A direct capacitated-blossom method finds a maximum b-matching; it is an f-factor exactly when every vertex capacity is saturated.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is an \(f\)-factor if and only if \(|F|=f(V)/2\).

notation.meaning: Vertex capacity, set equal to f(v).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Saturation of all capacities is correctly characterized by cardinality f(V)/2, but the claimed direct capacitated-blossom algorithm and weighted extension require an authoritative locator.

children.title: Degree-Constrained Subgraph Methods
children.top_down_role: Direct approaches for broader degree-constrained subgraph models.

knowledge_statements.title: Degree-Constrained Subgraph Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary formulation of lower–upper degree-constrained spanning subgraphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be finite and let \(g,f:V\to\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\) satisfy \(g(v)\le f(v)\le d_G(v)\). A spanning subgraph \(H\) is a \((g,f)\)-factor precisely when its incidence vector \(x\in\{0,1\}^{E}\) satisfies \[g(v)\le\sum_{e\in\delta_G(v)}x_e\le f(v)\qquad(v\in V).\] Thus a degree-constrained subgraph method may optimize \(\sum_{e\in E}w_ex_e\) over these integral constraints, using augmenting-trail or matching-polytope machinery to enforce integrality rather than accepting the bare linear relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lower and upper degree bounds become binary incidence constraints; direct methods optimize over their integral feasible set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Feasible binary vectors are in one-to-one correspondence with spanning \((g,f)\)-factors.

notation.meaning: Indicator that edge e belongs to the chosen subgraph.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The binary formulation correctly represents (g,f)-factors, but the additional assertion about direct augmenting-trail or matching-polytope methods is nontrivial and unsupported.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local-augmentation alignment with a prescribed optimal (f,g)-subgraph
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transforms an arbitrary spanning subgraph to an optimum agreeing with a prescribed optimum outside edges induced by C.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume f,g\ge 0 and f+g\ge\deg_G pointwise, and let C=C(G;f,g). If J is an (f,g)-optimal spanning subgraph and H is any spanning subgraph of G, then H can be transformed by local augmentations into an (f,g)-optimal spanning subgraph H_0 such that E(J)\mathbin{\triangle}E(H_0)\subseteq E(G[C]).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Given an optimal subgraph J, every spanning subgraph can be locally augmented to an optimal subgraph H0 that differs from J only on edges having both endpoints in the canonical class C.
assumptions_latex: H\text{ is a spanning subgraph of }G
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: H\leadsto H_0\text{ by local augmentations},\qquad \delta(H_0;f,g)=\delta(f,g),\qquad E(J)\triangle E(H_0)\subseteq E(G[C]).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local augmentations for (f,g)-factor deficiency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines single-edge local augmentations and records their deficiency and optimality invariants.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume f,g\ge 0 and f+g\ge \deg_G pointwise. If H is spanning and \deg_H(v)>f(v), deleting any edge vw\in E(H) gives H' with \delta(v;H';f,g)=\delta(v;H;f,g)-1, \delta(w;H';f,g)\le \delta(w;H;f,g)+1, and unchanged local deficiency at every u\notin\{v,w\}; hence \delta(H';f,g)\le\delta(H;f,g). Dually, if \deg_{\bar H}(v)>g(v), adding any edge vw\in E(\bar H) incident with v also does not increase total deficiency. An edge addition or deletion that strictly decreases local deficiency at some vertex is called a local augmentation. If H is (f,g)\text{-optimal} and H' is obtained by a local augmentation, then H' is optimal and H is obtainable from H' by a local augmentation. No local augmentation of an optimal subgraph changes an edge incident with C. Local augmentations can transform any spanning subgraph into one satisfying \deg_H\le f.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Deleting an incident edge at a vertex exceeding its f-bound, or adding a missing incident edge at a vertex exceeding its complementary g-bound, does not increase total deficiency. Such single-edge changes are local augmentations. On optimal subgraphs they preserve optimality, are reversible, and do not change edges incident with C. Local augmentations can also enforce all f upper bounds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \delta(H';f,g)\le\delta(H;f,g),\qquad H\text{ optimal}\Longrightarrow H'\text{ optimal},\qquad \text{local augmentations can attain }\deg_H\le f.

children.title: Direct-Method Tractability Regimes

knowledge_statements.title: Direct-Method Tractability Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polynomial-time regimes for exact and interval degree constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite graph with binary-encoded integral edge weights, exact degree sets \(D_v=\{f(v)\}\) and interval degree sets \(D_v=\{g(v),g(v)+1,\ldots,f(v)\}\) admit polynomial-time feasibility and optimization algorithms via factor or capacitated-matching methods. Polynomiality is measured in \(|V|+|E|\) and the encoding length of the weights and bounds. This conclusion does not extend merely from these regimes to arbitrary allowed-degree sets \(D_v\subseteq\{0,\ldots,d_G(v)\}\), whose gaps can destroy the exchange structure used by direct methods.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact and interval degree constraints are polynomially tractable; arbitrary gapped degree lists require separate complexity analysis.
assumptions_latex: Degree bounds and edge weights have finite binary encodings.
Allowed degrees are singletons or integer intervals.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Feasibility and minimum- or maximum-weight optimization are solvable in time polynomial in the input encoding length.

notation.meaning: Allowed degree set at vertex v.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity-bound kind fits the tractability leaf, but polynomial-time weighted optimization for exact and interval degree constraints requires a precise algorithmic theorem and complexity-model citation.

children.title: Fractional Matching Relaxations
children.top_down_role: Fractional relaxations originating from ordinary matching models.

knowledge_statements.title: Fractional Matching Relaxations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Vertex-capacity relaxation of the matching incidence formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite loopless graph \(G=(V,E)\), the fractional matching relaxation is \[P_{\mathrm{FM}}(G)=\left\{x\in\mathbb R_{\ge 0}^{E}:\sum_{e\in\delta_G(v)}x_e\le 1\text{ for every }v\in V\right\}.\] For weights \(w:E\to\mathbb R\), the relaxation maximizes \(\sum_{e\in E}w_ex_e\) over \(P_{\mathrm{FM}}(G)\). Incidence vectors of matchings are feasible, but without odd-set inequalities the polytope can also contain fractional points supported on odd cycles.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The fractional matching relaxation imposes nonnegativity and unit vertex capacities but omits the odd-set inequalities needed for the matching polytope.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every matching incidence vector belongs to \(P_{\mathrm{FM}}(G)\), while the relaxation need not be integral.

notation.meaning: Fractional matching polytope with only vertex constraints.

children.title: 2-Matching Relaxations
children.top_down_role: Relaxation structures associated with 2-matching models.

knowledge_statements.title: 2-Matching Relaxations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Degree-two relaxation allowing paths and cycles as integral supports.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite loopless graph \(G=(V,E)\), the simple fractional \(2\)-matching relaxation is \[P_2(G)=\left\{y\in[0,1]^E:\sum_{e\in\delta_G(v)}y_e\le2\text{ for every }v\in V\right\}.\] Its integral points are incidence vectors of subgraphs having maximum degree at most two, hence disjoint unions of paths, cycles, and isolated vertices. Requiring equality \(y(\delta_G(v))=2\) for every vertex instead gives the fractional \(2\)-factor relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The simple 2-matching relaxation bounds every edge by one and every vertex degree by two; its integral supports are paths and cycles.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_2(G)\cap\{0,1\}^E\) consists exactly of incidence vectors of simple \(2\)-matchings.

notation.meaning: Sum of incident edge variables at v.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed relaxation and its integral-support characterization are coherent, and definition is an appropriate kind, but a source is needed for the chosen simple 2-matching convention.

children.title: Half-Integral Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Half-integral structural links between fractional matchings and 2-matching objects.

knowledge_statements.title: Half-Integral Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extreme-point structure connecting fractional matchings with capacitated integral 2-matchings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Every extreme point \(x\) of \(P_{\mathrm{FM}}(G)\) is half-integral: \(x_e\in\{0,\tfrac12,1\}\) for every edge \(e\in E\). Moreover, the edges with value \(1\) form a matching, and the edges with value \(\tfrac12\) form vertex-disjoint odd cycles that are vertex-disjoint from that matching. Consequently, \(y=2x\) is an integral capacitated \(2\)-matching satisfying \(y_e\in\{0,1,2\}\) and \(y(\delta_G(v))\le 2\) for every \(v\in V\). Conversely, if an integral vector \(y\in\{0,1,2\}^{E}\) has its value-\(2\) edges forming a matching and its value-\(1\) edges forming vertex-disjoint odd cycles that are vertex-disjoint from that matching, then \(x=y/2\) is an extreme point of \(P_{\mathrm{FM}}(G)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fractional-matching extreme points consist of matching edges valued one and vertex-disjoint odd cycles valued one-half; doubling gives a capacitated integral 2-matching, and vectors with exactly this support structure yield extreme points when halved.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The extreme points of \(P_{\mathrm{FM}}(G)\) have values in \(\{0,\tfrac12,1\}\), with fractional support equal to a vertex-disjoint union of odd cycles.

notation.meaning: Sum of the variables on edges incident with v.

children.title: Odd-Cycle Interface Boundary
children.top_down_role: Odd-cycle regimes governing the limits of the fractional-to-2-matching correspondence.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite undirected simple graph.
\(x\) is an extreme point of \(\{z\in\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}^{E}:z(\delta(v))\le 1\text{ for every }v\in V\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(E_{1/2}=\{e\in E:x_e=\tfrac12\}\) is a vertex-disjoint union of odd cycles, while \(E_1=\{e\in E:x_e=1\}\) is a matching disjoint from those cycles.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extreme-point boundary under the degree-only fractional matching relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Every coordinate of \(x\) belongs to \(\{0,\tfrac12,1\}\). The edges in \(E_1\) form a matching. The subgraph \((V,E_{1/2})\) is a disjoint union of odd cycles, and no vertex on such a cycle is incident with an edge of \(E_1\). Thus doubling every half-valued cycle edge produces a degree-two cycle component, whereas an integral fractional matching contains no such odd-cycle interface.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Extreme fractional matchings consist of disjoint unit matching edges and half-valued odd cycles; the odd cycles are precisely the nonintegral interface with degree-two structures.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Min–Max Formula for Maximum Simple 2-Matching Size
knowledge_statements.scope_note: For each component \(K\) of \(G-U-S\), \(E[K,S]\) is the set of edges joining \(K\) and \(S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every graph \(G=(V,E)\), the maximum size of a simple 2-matching equals
\[
\min_{\substack{U,S\subseteq V,
U\cap S=\varnothing\\ S\text{ stable}}}\left(|V|+|U|-|S|+\sum_{K\in\operatorname{comp}(G-U-S)}\left\lfloor\frac{|E[K,S]|}{2}\right\rfloor\right).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: 2-Covers and Basic 2-Covers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines integral vertex-weighted 2-covers, their minimum-size parameter and basic form, together with elementary bounds and existence of a basic optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A 2-cover of a graph \(G\) is a function \(y:V(G)\to\{0,1,2\}\) such that \(y(u)+y(v)\ge 2\) for every edge \(uv\in E(G)\). Its size is \(\sum_{v\in V(G)}y(v)\), and \(\tau_2(G)\) is the minimum size of a 2-cover. If \(p=|V(G)|\) and \(\tau(G)\) is the minimum vertex-cover cardinality, then \(\tau_2(G)\le p\) and \(\tau_2(G)\le 2\tau(G)\). A 2-cover is basic if every component of the subgraph induced by its weight-\(1\) vertices is non-bipartite. Every graph has a minimum 2-cover that is basic.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A 2-cover assigns every vertex weight 0, 1, or 2 so that the endpoint weights of each edge total at least 2. Its size is the total weight, and τ₂(G) is the minimum size. Assigning weight 1 everywhere gives τ₂(G)≤|V(G)|, while adding two ordinary vertex covers gives τ₂(G)≤2τ(G). A 2-cover is basic when every component induced by its weight-1 vertices is non-bipartite, and every graph has a basic minimum 2-cover.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \tau_2(G)\le p,\qquad \tau_2(G)\le 2\tau(G),\qquad \exists\text{ a basic minimum 2-cover of }G.

knowledge_statements.title: Interval Degree Constraints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The standard finite undirected ((g,f))-factor formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph, and let \(g,f:V\to\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}\) satisfy \(g(v)\le f(v)\) for every \(v\in V\). An interval degree-constrained factor, or \((g,f)\)-factor, is a spanning subgraph \(H=(V,F)\) with \(F\subseteq E\) such that
\[
g(v)\le d_H(v)\le f(v)\qquad\text{for every }v\in V.
\]
The instance is feasible precisely when at least one such edge set \(F\) exists.

knowledge_statements.title: Degree-Sequence Realization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Erdős–Gallai characterization for simple undirected graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(d_1\ge d_2\ge\cdots\ge d_n\ge0\) be integers. There exists a simple undirected graph on labeled vertices \(v_1,\ldots,v_n\) with \(d_G(v_i)=d_i\) for every \(i\) if and only if \(\sum_{i=1}^n d_i\) is even and, for every \(k\in\{1,
\ldots,n\}\),
\[
\sum_{i=1}^k d_i\le k(k-1)+\sum_{i=k+1}^n\min\{d_i,k\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonincreasing nonnegative integer sequence is realizable as the degrees of a simple graph exactly when it has even sum and satisfies every Erdős–Gallai inequality.
assumptions_latex: The realizing graph is finite, simple, and undirected.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The sequence is graphical if and only if its sum is even and all displayed Erdős–Gallai inequalities hold.

knowledge_statements.title: Regularizable Graphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the strictly positive edge-weighting convention; literature also permits nonnegative weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A finite undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) is positively regularizable if there exist a scalar \(r>0\) and edge weights \(x:E\to\mathbb R_{>0}\) such that
\[
\sum_{e\in\delta(v)}x(e)=r\qquad\text{for every }v\in V.
\]
Equivalently, if \(A\) is the unsigned vertex-edge incidence matrix of \(G\), then positive regularizability means that \(Ax=r\mathbf 1\) has a solution \(x>0\) and \(r>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A graph is positively regularizable when strictly positive edge weights can make every vertex have the same positive weighted degree.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Positive regularizability is equivalent to solvability of \(Ax=r\mathbf1\) with \(x>0\) and \(r>0\).

notation.meaning: set of edges incident with v

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The positive-weight formulation is internally correct, but “regularizable” is also used for nonnegative-weight conventions. A source is needed to establish the intended local convention.

knowledge_statements.title: Minimum-Cardinality Edge Covers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gallai’s matching–edge-cover identity for graphs without isolated vertices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph with no isolated vertices. If \(\nu(G)\) is the maximum matching cardinality and \(\rho(G)\) is the minimum edge-cover cardinality, then
\[
\rho(G)=|V|-\nu(G).
\]
Moreover, from any maximum matching \(M\), a minimum edge cover is obtained by adding, for each vertex not saturated by \(M\), one incident edge. The resulting cover has \(|M|+|V|-2|M|=|V|-|M|\) edges.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a graph without isolated vertices, the minimum edge-cover size equals the number of vertices minus the maximum matching size.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is finite, undirected, and has no isolated vertices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\rho(G)=|V|-\nu(G)\), and a maximum matching extends directly to a minimum edge cover.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Gallai’s matching–edge-cover identity and its construction are correctly stated for graphs without isolated vertices, but no authoritative theorem locator is supplied.

children.title: Minimum-Weight Edge Covers

knowledge_statements.title: Minimum-Weight Edge Covers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite simple edge covers with arbitrary real edge costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph without isolated vertices, and let \(c:E\to\mathbb R\). An edge cover is a set \(F\subseteq E\) satisfying \(d_F(v)\ge1\) for every \(v\in V\). A minimum-weight edge cover is any feasible set \(F^*\) such that
\[
\sum_{e\in F^*}c(e)=\min\left\{\sum_{e\in F}c(e):F\subseteq E,\ d_F(v)\ge1\text{ for all }v\in V\right\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A minimum-weight edge cover is an edge set incident to every vertex and having least total edge cost among all such sets.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite undirected graph without isolated vertices.
\(c:E\to\mathbb R\) assigns a finite cost to each edge.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F^*\) minimizes \(\sum_{e\in F}c(e)\) over all edge covers \(F\subseteq E\).

notation.meaning: number of selected edges incident with v

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The optimization definition is precise and fits the minimum-weight edge-cover container, but it has no cited source or inspectable locator.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Reduction of minimum-weight edge cover to perfect matching
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Perfect-matching reduction for graphs without isolated vertices and nonnegative rational edge weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $G=(V,E)$ have no isolated vertices and let $w:E\to\mathbb{Q}_+$. Form $G'$ from disjoint copies $G$ and $\widetilde G$ by adding $v\widetilde v$ for each $v\in V$. Define $w'(e)=w'(\widetilde e)=w(e)$ and $w'(v\widetilde v)=2\mu(v)$, where $\mu(v)=\min\{w(e):e\in\delta(v)\}$. Given a minimum-weight perfect matching $M$ in $G'$, replace each $v\widetilde v\in M$ by a minimum-weight edge of $G$ incident with $v$, and delete the edges in $M\cap\widetilde E$. The resulting edge set $F$ is a minimum-weight edge cover of $G$ and $w(F)=\tfrac12w'(M)$. Moreover, $G$ bipartite implies $G'$ bipartite.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Duplicate the graph, connect every vertex to its copy, and assign the specified weights. Transforming a minimum-weight perfect matching of this auxiliary graph produces a minimum-weight edge cover whose weight is half the matching weight. The construction preserves bipartiteness.
assumptions_latex: M\text{ is a minimum-weight perfect matching in }G'
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F\text{ is a minimum-weight edge cover of }G,\quad w(F)=\frac12w'(M),\quad G\text{ bipartite}\Rightarrow G'\text{ bipartite}

knowledge_statements.title: Weight-Sensitive Edge-Cover Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform, weight-first, and cardinality-first objective regimes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal C\) be the edge covers of a finite graph and let \(c:E\to\mathbb R\). If \(c(e)=\alpha>0\) for all \(e\), minimizing \(c(F)\) over \(F\in\mathcal C\) is equivalent to minimizing \(|F|\). For arbitrary costs, weight-first optimization minimizes \(c(F)\) regardless of cardinality. Cardinality-first lexicographic optimization is represented by minimizing
\[
M|F|+c(F)
\]
whenever \(M>\sum_{e\in E}|c(e)|\); every minimizer then first minimizes \(|F|\) and, among minimum-cardinality covers, minimizes \(c(F)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform positive weights reproduce minimum cardinality, arbitrary weights define weight-first optimization, and a sufficiently large cardinality penalty realizes cardinality-first lexicographic optimization.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is finite and admits an edge cover.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Uniform costs yield cardinality minimization, while \(M|F|+c(F)\) with \(M>\sum_e|c(e)|\) yields cardinality-first lexicographic minimization.

notation.meaning: family of edge covers of G

knowledge_statements.title: Simple b-Edge Covers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uncapacitated simple-edge selection with vertex demands.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph and let \(b:V\to\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\). A simple \(b\)-edge cover is a set \(F\subseteq E\) such that
\[
d_F(v)=|F\cap\delta(v)|\ge b(v)
\qquad\text{for every }v\in V.
\]
Each edge may be selected at most once. The family is nonempty only if the simultaneous degree-demand inequalities can be satisfied; in particular, feasibility requires \(b(v)\le d_G(v)\) for every \(v\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A simple b-edge cover selects each edge at most once and supplies every vertex with at least its prescribed number of incident selected edges.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\subseteq E\) is feasible exactly when \(d_F(v)\ge b(v)\) for every \(v\in V\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: natural lower-degree generalization of an edge cover
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The lower-degree formulation is coherent and fits the simple b-edge-cover container, but the terminology and convention require an authoritative source locator.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Min–Max Formula for Simple b-Edge Covers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact minimum-cardinality characterization over disjoint vertex sets and components of an induced subgraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a graph and let \(b\in\mathbb Z_+^V\) satisfy \(b(v)\le\deg_G(v)\) for every \(v\in V\). The minimum size of a simple \(b\)-edge cover equals \[\max_{\substack{T,U\subseteq V\\T\cap U=\varnothing}}\left\{b(U)-|E[U]|+\sum_{K\in\operatorname{comp}(G[T])}\left\lceil\frac{b(K)-|E[K,U]|}{2}\right\rceil\right\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If every vertex demand is at most its degree, the minimum size of a simple b-edge cover equals the stated maximum over disjoint vertex sets T and U, with K ranging over the components of the subgraph induced by T.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min\{|F|:F\subseteq E,\ \deg_F(v)\ge b(v)\ \forall v\}=\max_{\substack{T,U\subseteq V\\T\cap U=\varnothing}}\left\{b(U)-|E[U]|+\sum_{K\in\operatorname{comp}(G[T])}\left\lceil\frac{b(K)-|E[K,U]|}{2}\right\rceil\right\}.

knowledge_statements.title: Capacitated b-Edge Covers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integer edge multiplicities bounded by capacities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph, let \(b:V\to\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\), and let \(u:E\to\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\). A capacitated \(b\)-edge cover is an integer vector \(x\in\mathbb Z_{
\ge0}^{E}\) satisfying
\[
0\le x_e\le u(e)\quad(e\in E),
\qquad
\sum_{e\in\delta(v)}x_e\ge b(v)\quad(v\in V).
\]
Here \(x_e\) is the number of copies of edge \(e\) used; the simple variant is recovered by setting \(u(e)=1\) for every edge.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A capacitated b-edge cover assigns bounded nonnegative integer multiplicities to edges so that the total selected incidence at each vertex meets its demand.
assumptions_latex: \(b\) and \(u\) are nonnegative integral vertex demands and edge capacities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Feasible multiplicities satisfy \(0\le x_e\le u(e)\) and \(\sum_{e\in\delta(v)}x_e\ge b(v)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $G=(V,E)$, $b\in\mathbb Z_+^V$, and $c\in\mathbb Z_+^E$. A $c$-capacitated $b$-edge cover is a vector $x\in\mathbb Z_+^E$ such that $x(\delta(v))\ge b(v)$ for every $v\in V$ and $x\le c$ componentwise.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A capacitated b-edge cover is an integral b-edge cover whose multiplicity on each edge does not exceed its prescribed capacity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x\text{ is a }c\text{-capacitated }b\text{-edge cover}\iff x\le c\text{ and }(\forall v\in V)\;x(\delta(v))\ge b(v)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Linear Description of the Capacitated b-Edge-Cover Polytope
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complete description by capacity bounds, vertex-demand inequalities, and residual odd-set inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $G=(V,E)$, $b\in\mathbb Z_+^V$, and $c\in\mathbb Z_+^E$. The $c$-capacitated $b$-edge-cover polytope consists exactly of the vectors $x\in\mathbb R^E$ satisfying
\[
0\le x_e\le c(e)\quad(e\in E),
\]
\[
x(\delta(v))\ge b(v)\quad(v\in V),
\]
and, for every $U\subseteq V$ and $F\subseteq\delta(U)$ such that $b(U)-c(F)$ is odd,
\[
x(E[U])+x(\delta(U)\setminus F)\ge\left\lceil\frac{b(U)-c(F)}{2}\right\rceil.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The capacitated b-edge-cover polytope is exactly described by edge-capacity bounds, vertex-demand inequalities, and the stated residual odd-set inequalities for every eligible pair U and F.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P_{b,c}(G)=\left\{x\in\mathbb R^E:\begin{array}{l}0\le x_e\le c(e)\ (e\in E),\\x(\delta(v))\ge b(v)\ (v\in V),\\x(E[U])+x(\delta(U)\setminus F)\ge\left\lceil\frac{b(U)-c(F)}2\right\rceil\\\text{for all }U\subseteq V,\ F\subseteq\delta(U)\text{ with }b(U)-c(F)\text{ odd}\end{array}\right\}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Min-Max Formula for Capacitated b-Edge Covers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact minimum-size formula, subject to existence of a capacity-feasible b-edge cover.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $G=(V,E)$, $b\in\mathbb Z_+^V$, and $c\in\mathbb Z_+^E$, and suppose that a $b$-edge cover $x\le c$ exists. Then
\[
\min\{x(E):x\in\mathbb Z_+^E,\ x\le c,\ x(\delta(v))\ge b(v)\ \forall v\in V\}
=
\max_{\substack{T,U\subseteq V\\T\cap U=\varnothing}}
\left[b(U)-c(E[U])+\sum_{K\in\operatorname{comp}(G[T])}\left\lceil\frac{b(K)-c(E[K,U])}{2}\right\rceil\right].
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a capacity-feasible b-edge cover exists, its minimum size equals the stated maximum over disjoint vertex sets T and U, with one ceiling term for each component of the subgraph induced by T.
assumptions_latex: \{x\in\mathbb Z_+^E:x\le c,\ x(\delta(v))\ge b(v)\ \forall v\in V\}\ne\varnothing
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min\{x(E):x\in\mathbb Z_+^E,\ x\le c,\ x(\delta(v))\ge b(v)\ \forall v\in V\}=\max_{\substack{T,U\subseteq V\\T\cap U=\varnothing}}\left[b(U)-c(E[U])+\sum_{K\in\operatorname{comp}(G[T])}\left\lceil\frac{b(K)-c(E[K,U])}{2}\right\rceil\right]

knowledge_statements.title: Weighted b-Edge Covers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimum-cost simple (b)-edge covers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph, let \(b:V\to\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\), and let \(c:E\to\mathbb R\). A minimum-weight simple \(b\)-edge cover is a vector \(x^*\in\{0,1\}^{E}\) solving
\[
\min\left\{\sum_{e\in E}c(e)x_e:
\sum_{e\in\delta(v)}x_e\ge b(v)\text{ for every }v\in V,
\ x\in\{0,1\}^{E}\right\}.
\]
Equivalently, its support is a simple \(b\)-edge cover of minimum total edge weight.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A weighted b-edge cover meets every vertex demand while minimizing the total cost of the selected simple edges.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^*\) has minimum cost among all binary edge selections meeting every demand \(b(v)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Integral Min-Max Formula for Weighted b-Edge Covers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integral dual characterization for nonnegative integral vertex demands and edge weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a graph, \(b\in\mathbb Z_+^V\), and \(w\in\mathbb Z_+^E\). Then
\[
\min_{x\text{ a }b\text{-edge cover}} w^\top x
=
\max\left\{
\sum_{v\in V}y_vb(v)+\sum_{U\subseteq V}z_U\left\lceil\frac{b(U)}2\right\rceil:
\begin{array}{l}
y\in\mathbb Z_+^V,\ z\in\mathbb Z_+^{\mathcal P(V)},\\
\displaystyle\sum_{v\in V}y_v\chi^{\delta(v)}+
\sum_{U\subseteq V}z_U\chi^{E[U]\cup\delta(U)}\le w
\end{array}
\right\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The minimum weight of a b-edge cover equals the maximum integral combination of vertex-demand and subset-demand bounds whose total edge-incidence vector is componentwise at most the edge-weight vector.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min_{x\text{ a }b\text{-edge cover}}w^\top x=\max_{\substack{y\in\mathbb Z_+^V,\ z\in\mathbb Z_+^{\mathcal P(V)}\\ \sum_v y_v\chi^{\delta(v)}+\sum_U z_U\chi^{E[U]\cup\delta(U)}\le w}}\left(\sum_{v\in V}y_vb(v)+\sum_{U\subseteq V}z_U\left\lceil\frac{b(U)}2\right\rceil\right)

knowledge_statements.title: Capacity–Weight Interaction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Monotonicity of the capacitated minimum-cost value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For fixed \(G=(V,E)\) and demand \(b\), define
\[
z(u,c)=\min\left\{\sum_{e\in E}c(e)x_e:0\le x_e\le u(e),\ x_e\in\mathbb Z,
\ \sum_{e\in\delta(v)}x_e\ge b(v)\text{ for all }v\in V\right\}.
\]
Whenever the relevant instances are feasible, \(u'\ge u\) componentwise implies \(z(u',c)\le z(u,c)\), because capacities enlarge the feasible set. If \(c'\ge c\) componentwise, then \(z(u,c')\ge z(u,c)\), because every feasible vector is nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Increasing capacities cannot worsen the optimum, while increasing edge costs cannot improve it, provided the corresponding capacitated b-cover instances remain feasible.
assumptions_latex: \(G\), \(b\), \(u\), and \(c\) define a feasible finite capacitated \(b\)-edge-cover instance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(u'\ge u\Rightarrow z(u',c)\le z(u,c)\), and \(c'\ge c\Rightarrow z(u,c')\ge z(u,c)\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: elementary feasible-set and objective monotonicity
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Both monotonicity claims are correct for the stated feasible finite integer model, but the property has no supporting source or locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Matching–Edge-Cover Relations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cardinality correspondence in finite undirected graphs without isolated vertices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph without isolated vertices. Every maximum matching \(M\) extends to an edge cover with \(|V|-|M|\) edges, and every edge cover \(F\) contains a matching of cardinality at least \(|V|-|F|\). Consequently,
\[
\nu(G)+\rho(G)=|V|,
\]
where \(\nu(G)\) is the maximum matching cardinality and \(\rho(G)\) is the minimum edge-cover cardinality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a finite undirected graph without isolated vertices, maximum matching size and minimum edge-cover size sum to the number of vertices, with the corresponding matching and edge-cover transformations attaining the complementary bounds.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is finite, undirected, and has no isolated vertices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\nu(G)+\rho(G)=|V|\), and the stated transformations attain the complementary cardinality bounds.

knowledge_statements.title: Edge-Cover Polyhedra
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the dominant edge-cover polyhedron of a finite undirected graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph without isolated vertices, and let \(\delta(v)\) denote the edges incident with \(v\). An edge cover is a set \(C\subseteq E\) satisfying \(C\cap\delta(v)\neq\varnothing\) for every \(v\in V\). Its dominant edge-cover polyhedron is
\[P_{\mathrm{EC}}^{\uparrow}(G)=\operatorname{conv}\{\chi^C:C\subseteq E\text{ is an edge cover}\}+\mathbb{R}_{+}^{E}.\]
Thus the binary points generating the dominant encode edge covers, while addition of the nonnegative orthant makes the polyhedron upward closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The dominant edge-cover polyhedron is the convex hull of edge-cover incidence vectors plus the nonnegative orthant.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_{\mathrm{EC}}^{\uparrow}(G)=\operatorname{conv}\{\chi^C:C\text{ covers }V\}+\mathbb{R}_{+}^{E}\).

notation.meaning: set of edges incident with vertex v
incidence vector of edge set C

knowledge_statements.title: b-Edge-Cover Polyhedra
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the integer-hull dominant for vertex-demand edge covers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be finite and undirected, and let \(b:V\to\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}\). A binary \(b\)-edge cover is an edge set \(C\subseteq E\) such that \(|C\cap\delta(v)|\ge b(v)\) for every \(v\in V\). When such covers exist, their dominant polyhedron is
\[P_b^{\uparrow}(G)=\operatorname{conv}\{\chi^C:C\subseteq E,\ |C\cap\delta(v)|\ge b(v)\ \forall v\in V\}+\mathbb{R}_{+}^{E}.\]
For \(b\equiv1\), this specializes to the ordinary dominant edge-cover polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A b-edge-cover dominant is generated by binary edge sets meeting every vertex demand, together with all nonnegative coordinate increases.
assumptions_latex: At least one binary \(b\)-edge cover exists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_b^{\uparrow}(G)=\operatorname{conv}\{\chi^C:|C\cap\delta(v)|\ge b(v)\ \forall v\}+\mathbb{R}_{+}^{E}\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: direct demand generalization of the edge-cover dominant

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The binary demand generalization is mathematically coherent and definition is the appropriate content kind, but no cited source establishes this precise b-edge-cover convention or dominant polyhedron.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relates edge covers, binary feasible points, and the integer hull of the degree relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a finite undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) without isolated vertices, define
\[Q(G)=\{x\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{E}:x(\delta(v))\ge1\text{ for every }v\in V\}.\]
Then \(C\subseteq E\) is an edge cover if and only if \(\chi^C\in Q(G)\cap\{0,1\}^{E}\). Moreover,
\[P_{\mathrm{EC}}^{\uparrow}(G)=\operatorname{conv}\bigl(Q(G)\cap\mathbb{Z}^{E}\bigr).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Edge covers are exactly the binary points of the degree-covering relaxation, and their dominant equals that relaxation's integer hull.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G\text{ bipartite}\Rightarrow Q_b(G)\text{ integral}\), whereas \(Q_{\mathbf{1}}(K_3)\) has the vertex \((1/2,1/2,1/2)\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: total-unimodularity boundary and triangle obstruction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Contrasts bipartite integrality with the fractional odd-cycle obstruction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(b\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}^{V}\) and
\[Q_b(G)=\{x\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{E}:x(\delta(v))\ge b(v)\text{ for every }v\in V\}.\]
If \(G\) is bipartite, its vertex-edge incidence matrix is totally unimodular, so every vertex of \(Q_b(G)\) is integral. This fails for nonbipartite graphs: for a triangle and \(b\equiv1\), the vector assigning \(1/2\) to every edge is a fractional vertex of \(Q_b(G)\). Hence degree inequalities alone do not generally describe the edge-cover integer hull outside the bipartite regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The degree-covering relaxation is integral on bipartite graphs, but a triangle already has the fractional extreme point assigning one-half to each edge.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: TDI Description of the Edge-Cover Polytope
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polyhedral description and total dual integrality of the odd-set edge-cover system for loopless graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be loopless. The system
\[
0\le x_e\le 1\quad(e\in E),
\qquad
x(E[U]\cup\delta(U))\ge\left\lceil\frac{|U|}{2}\right\rceil
\quad(U\subseteq V,\ |U|\text{ odd})
\]
determines the edge-cover polytope and is totally dual integral.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a loopless graph, the unit bounds together with the odd-set edge-cover inequalities describe the edge-cover polytope, and this system is totally dual integral.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P_{\mathrm{EC}}(G)=\left\{x\in\mathbb R^E:0\le x_e\le1\ (e\in E),\ x(E[U]\cup\delta(U))\ge\left\lceil|U|/2\right\rceil\ \forall U\subseteq V\text{ with }|U|\text{ odd}\right\},\quad\text{and this displayed system is TDI.}

knowledge_statements.title: Interval Degree-Set Tractability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polynomial-time feasibility for factors with lower and upper degree bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given a finite undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) and integers \(0\le l(v)\le u(v)\le d_G(v)\), an interval-constrained factor is an edge set \(F\subseteq E\) satisfying
\[l(v)\le d_F(v)\le u(v)\qquad(v\in V).\]
The existence of such an \((l,u)\)-factor can be decided in time polynomial in \(|V|+|E|\) and the binary encoding length of \(l,u\), via reduction to polynomial-time degree-constrained matching or flow machinery. A feasible factor can also be produced within the same polynomial bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Factors whose permitted degree at each vertex is an integer interval can be found, or shown not to exist, in polynomial time.
assumptions_latex: \(0\le l(v)\le u(v)\le d_G(v)\) for every \(v\in V\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The \((l,u)\)-factor feasibility and construction problems belong to \(\mathrm{P}\).

allowed integer degree interval at v

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polynomial-time feasibility for parity intervals and, more generally, allowed degree sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each vertex \(v\) of a finite undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\), let
\[B(v)=\{a_v,a_v+2,\ldots,b_v\}\subseteq\{0,1,\ldots,d_G(v)\},\]
where \(a_v\le b_v\) and \(a_v\equiv b_v\pmod 2\). The parity-factor feasibility problem asks whether some \(F\subseteq E\) satisfies \(d_F(v)\in B(v)\) for every \(v\). This problem is decidable in polynomial time as a special case of the general-factor problem with allowed degree sets whose consecutive elements differ by at most two; a feasible factor is constructible in polynomial time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A factor with one prescribed parity and interval bounds at each vertex can be found or ruled out in polynomial time.
knowledge_statements.title: Parity Degree-Set Tractability
Arbitrary Degree-Set Hardness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complexity boundary for unrestricted vertex degree lists.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In the general-factor decision problem, the input consists of a finite undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) and explicitly represented sets \(B(v)\subseteq\{0,1,\ldots,d_G(v)\}\). The question is whether there exists \(F\subseteq E\) with \(d_F(v)\in B(v)\) for every \(v\in V\). With unrestricted degree sets \(B(v)\), this decision problem is NP-complete. Membership in NP follows because an edge set \(F\) is a polynomially checkable certificate; hardness shows that the interval and parity-interval structure cannot be discarded while retaining general polynomial-time solvability unless \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Allowing arbitrary permitted-degree sets makes general-factor feasibility NP-complete, unlike the structured interval and parity-interval cases.
assumptions_latex: Each \(B(v)\) is given explicitly as part of the input.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Unrestricted general-factor feasibility is \(\mathrm{NP}\)-complete.

knowledge_statements.title: 2-Factor–Hamiltonian-Cycle Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Connectivity changes polynomial 2-factor feasibility into Hamiltonian-cycle recognition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A \(2\)-factor of a finite undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) is a spanning edge set \(F\subseteq E\) satisfying \(d_F(v)=2\) for every \(v\in V\); it may contain several disjoint cycles. Existence of a \(2\)-factor is decidable in polynomial time by factor or matching algorithms. Requiring the selected \(2\)-factor to be connected makes it a single spanning cycle, exactly a Hamiltonian cycle. Consequently, connected \(2\)-factor existence is NP-complete, even though unrestricted \(2\)-factor existence is polynomial-time solvable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A 2-factor may be a cycle collection and is polynomially detectable; requiring it to be connected gives the NP-complete Hamiltonian-cycle problem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(2\text{-factor existence}\in\mathrm{P}\), while \(\text{connected 2-factor existence}\) is \(\mathrm{NP}\)-complete.

knowledge_statements.title: T-Join Feasibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complete feasibility criterion for edge-set T-joins in possibly disconnected graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph and \(T\subseteq V\). A \(T\)-join is an edge set \(J\subseteq E\) whose set of odd-degree vertices is exactly \(T\). Such a \(T\)-join exists if and only if
\[|T\cap V(K)|\equiv0\pmod2\]
for every connected component \(K\) of \(G\). In particular, when \(G\) is connected, feasibility is equivalent to \(|T|\) being even.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A T-join exists exactly when every connected component contains an even number of vertices from T.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G\text{ has a }T\text{-join}\iff |T\cap V(K)|\text{ is even for every component }K\).

notation.meaning: vertex set of connected component K

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: classical componentwise T-join feasibility criterion

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The componentwise parity criterion is correctly formulated for disconnected finite undirected graphs, and theorem fits the leaf. No source reference or theorem locator is supplied.

knowledge_statements.title: Componentwise Parity Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Describes all feasible T-joins as an affine translate of the cycle space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be finite and undirected, and suppose the componentwise parity condition for \(T\subseteq V\) holds. Fix one \(T\)-join \(J_0\). Then every \(T\)-join is of the form
\[J=J_0\mathbin{\triangle}C,\]
where \(C\subseteq E\) has even degree at every vertex, equivalently \(C\) belongs to the binary cycle space of \(G\). Conversely, every such symmetric difference is a \(T\)-join. Thus the family of \(T\)-joins is an affine coset of the cycle space over \(\mathbb{F}_2\), decomposing independently across connected components.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Once one T-join exists, all others are obtained by symmetric difference with an even subgraph, independently in each component.
assumptions_latex: \(|T\cap V(K)|\) is even for every connected component \(K\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{J:J\text{ is a }T\text{-join}\}=J_0\triangle\mathcal{C}(G)\), where \(\mathcal{C}(G)\) is the binary cycle space.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: affine-cycle-space description of parity solutions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The affine-cycle-space representation is mathematically consistent and representation is the correct role, but it lacks an inspectable citation establishing the coset description.

children.title: Disconnected-Graph Feasibility Boundaries

knowledge_statements.title: Disconnected-Graph Feasibility Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shows why global even cardinality is insufficient in disconnected graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The condition \(|T|\equiv0\pmod2\) alone does not guarantee a \(T\)-join when \(G\) is disconnected. Let \(G\) consist of two disjoint connected components \(K_1,K_2\), and choose \(t_i\in V(K_i)\) with \(T=\{t_1,t_2\}\). Then \(|T|=2\), but every edge set has an even number of odd-degree vertices within each component, whereas \(|T\cap V(K_i)|=1\). Hence no \(T\)-join exists. Componentwise evenness, rather than merely global evenness, is the sharp feasibility boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two T-vertices in different components give globally even T but no T-join; parity must be even inside every component.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|T|\text{ is even}\) but no \(T\)-join exists because \(|T\cap V(K_i)|=1\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample correctly identifies the disconnected-graph feasibility boundary and failure_boundary fits the leaf. The record nevertheless has no cited source or exact locator for the componentwise handshaking argument.

knowledge_statements.title: Minimum-Cardinality T-Joins
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shortest-path metric-closure algorithm for an unweighted feasible T-join.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Input a finite unweighted undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) and \(T\subseteq V\) satisfying componentwise evenness. For each component \(K\), compute shortest-path distances between vertices of \(T_K=T\cap V(K)\), form the complete weighted graph on \(T_K\), and find a minimum-weight perfect matching \(M_K\). Choose a shortest path in \(K\) for every matched pair and take the symmetric difference of all chosen paths over all components. The resulting edge set \(J\) is a minimum-cardinality \(T\)-join, and
\[|J|=\sum_K w(M_K).\]
Output \(J\); infeasibility is reported when some \(|T_K|\) is odd.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pair T-vertices by a minimum perfect matching in each component’s shortest-path metric, then combine the paired shortest paths by symmetric difference.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The algorithm outputs a minimum-cardinality \(T\)-join, or correctly reports infeasibility.

notation.meaning: minimum-weight perfect matching in the metric closure of T_K

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: classical reduction of minimum T-join to metric perfect matching
exact algorithm or theorem locator required

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $G=(V,E)$ be a graph and let $T\subseteq V$. Then the minimum size of a $T$-join equals the maximum total value of a packing of $T$-borders.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a graph and vertex subset T, the minimum size of a T-join equals the maximum total value of a packing of T-borders.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min\{|J|:J\text{ is a }T\text{-join}\}=\max\{\text{total value of a packing of }T\text{-borders}\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Minimum-cardinality T-join min–max theorem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimum-cardinality T-joins and bounded-multiplicity T-cut families in an undirected graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be an undirected graph and let \(T\subseteq V\) with \(|T|\) even. Then
\[
\min\{|J|:J\subseteq E\text{ is a }T\text{-join}\}
=\frac12\max\left\{|\mathcal C|:\mathcal C\text{ is a family of }T\text{-cuts and every }e\in E\text{ belongs to at most two members of }\mathcal C\right\}.
\]
Moreover, the maximum is attained by a cross-free family \(\mathcal C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an undirected graph and an even-cardinality vertex set T, the minimum size of a T-join equals half the maximum number of T-cuts in a family that covers each edge at most twice. The maximum is attained by a cross-free cut family.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min\{|J|:J\subseteq E\text{ is a }T\text{-join}\}=\tfrac12\max\{|\mathcal C|:\mathcal C\text{ is a family of }T\text{-cuts covering each edge at most twice}\},\quad\text{and an optimal }\mathcal C\text{ can be chosen cross-free}.

knowledge_statements.title: Minimum-Weight T-Joins
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite undirected graphs with edge weights and a feasible even terminal set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph, let \(T\subseteq V\), and let \(w:E\to\mathbb R\). A set \(J\subseteq E\) is a \(T\)-join when the vertices of odd degree in \((V,J)\) are exactly those in \(T\). If at least one \(T\)-join exists, the minimum-weight \(T\)-join problem is
\[\tau(G,T,w)=\min\left\{\sum_{e\in J}w_e:J\subseteq E,\ \operatorname{Odd}(V,J)=T\right\}.\]
Any feasible \(J^*\) attaining this minimum is a minimum-weight \(T\)-join.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A minimum-weight T-join has odd-degree vertex set exactly T and minimizes the sum of its edge weights among all such edge sets.
assumptions_latex: G=(V,E)\text{ is a finite undirected graph}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: w(J^*)=\tau(G,T,w)

notation.meaning: vertices having odd degree in the spanning subgraph with edge set J
sum of the weights of edges in J

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is mathematically precise, matches the minimum-weight T-join container, and uses an appropriate content kind. No cited source or inspectable locator supports it, so it remains needs_source.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: T-Cut Inequalities and the T-Join Covering LP
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines T-odd sets and T-cuts, derives their parity inequalities, and records the LP lower bound, its nonnegative-cost exactness, and its negative-cost limitation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A set S\subseteq V is T\text{-odd if }|S\cap T|\text{ is odd}; then \delta(S)\text{ is a }T\text{-cut}. For every T\text{-join }J,\ |J\cap\delta(S)|\text{ is odd, hence }\chi^J(\delta(S))\ge 1. Consequently, \min\{c^Tx:x(\delta(S))\ge1\text{ for every }T\text{-odd }S,\ x\ge0\} is a lower bound on the minimum T\text{-join cost. For }c\ge0\text{ this bound is exact; with negative costs it remains valid but may be unbounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every T-join crosses each T-cut an odd positive number of times. Thus the nonnegative LP requiring at least one unit across every T-cut is a valid lower bound. It is exact for nonnegative edge costs, while negative costs can make the relaxation unbounded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: |J\cap\delta(S)|\equiv1\pmod2\quad\text{and}\quad\chi^J(\delta(S))\ge1;\qquad c\ge0\implies\operatorname{OPT}_{LP}=\operatorname{OPT}_{T\text{-join}}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Circuit Optimality Criterion for a Minimum-Weight T-Join
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary and sufficient optimality condition for arbitrary real edge weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be a graph, \(T\subseteq V(G)\), \(c:E(G)\to\mathbb{R}\), and let \(J\) be a \(T\)-join. Then \(J\) is an optimum \(T\)-join if and only if \(c(J\cap E(C))\leq c(E(C)\setminus J)\) for every circuit \(C\) of \(G\), where \(c(F)=\sum_{e\in F}c(e)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A T-join is minimum-weight exactly when, on every circuit, its selected edges have no greater total weight than the unselected circuit edges.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: J\text{ is an optimum }T\text{-join}\iff \forall\text{ circuits }C\text{ of }G,\;c(J\cap E(C))\leq c(E(C)\setminus J)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Minimum-cost T-joins and their parity-cut representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines minimum-cost T-joins, gives their proper parity requirement, and records polynomial solvability and the two-terminal specialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(T\subseteq V\) have even cardinality. The minimum-cost \(T\)-join problem seeks a minimum-cost edge set whose vertices of odd degree are exactly the vertices in \(T\). It corresponds to the proper function \[f(S)=\begin{cases}1,&|S\cap T|\text{ is odd},\\0,&|S\cap T|\text{ is even}.
\end{cases}\] The problem is solvable in polynomial time. When \(|T|=2\), it reduces to the shortest-path problem, and the primal-dual algorithm for 0–1 proper functions reduces to a bidirectional-search variant of Dijkstra's algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an even vertex set T, a minimum-cost T-join is a least-cost edge set whose odd-degree vertices are precisely T. Its proper cut requirement detects cuts containing an odd number of T vertices. The problem is polynomial-time solvable; with two terminals it reduces to shortest path, and the stated primal-dual method becomes a bidirectional Dijkstra variant.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The minimum-cost }T\text{-join has the stated proper parity-cut representation, is polynomial-time solvable, and has the stated }|T|=2\text{ specialization.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Optimal T-Join via Shortest Paths and Perfect Matching
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constructive minimum-cost T-join algorithm using a negative-edge parity transformation and metric-closure matching.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let N=\{e\in E:c_e<0\} and T'=\{v\in V:|\delta(v)\cap N|\text{ is odd}\}. Replace (c,T) by (|c|,T\triangle T'). For every pair u,v in the transformed T, compute a minimum-cost u-v path P_{uv} of cost d(u,v). Find a minimum-weight perfect matching M in the complete graph on T with weights d(u,v), let J=\triangle_{uv\in M}E(P_{uv}), and return J\triangle N.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Toggle the required odd-degree vertices by the odd-degree boundary of the negative-cost edges, replace costs by their absolute values, compute shortest paths between the transformed terminals, and find a minimum-weight perfect matching in the resulting metric closure. The symmetric difference of the matched paths, toggled by the original negative edges, is an optimal T-join.
assumptions_latex: \text{each connected component contains an even number of vertices of }T\triangle T'
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: J\triangle N\text{ is a minimum-cost }T\text{-join for the original }(c,T).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Edmonds–Johnson minimum-weight T-join algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reduction to terminal-pair shortest paths and a minimum-weight perfect matching on the terminal metric closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be an undirected graph, let \(T\subseteq V(G)\) have even cardinality, and let \(c:E(G)\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}\). Assume every pair of terminals is joined by a finite minimum-weight path. For each distinct \(i,j\in T\), choose a minimum-weight \(i\)-\(j\) path \(P_{\{i,j\}}\). Form the complete graph \(K\) on \(T\) with \(c'(\{i,j\})=c(P_{\{i,j\}})\), and let \(S\) be a minimum-weight perfect matching of \(K\). Then \[P:=\mathop{\triangle}_{\{i,j\}\in S}E(P_{\{i,j\}})\] is a minimum-weight \(T\)-join of \(G\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compute shortest paths between every pair of terminals, find a minimum-weight perfect matching in the resulting terminal metric closure, and take the symmetric difference of its matched paths. This produces a minimum-weight T-join.
assumptions_latex: \text{Every pair }i,j\in T\text{ admits a finite minimum-weight }i\text{-}j\text{ path}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathop{\triangle}_{\{i,j\}\in S}E(P_{\{i,j\}})\text{ is a minimum-weight }T\text{-join of }G.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Reduction of signed-weight T-joins to nonnegative weights
knowledge_statements.scope_note: An objective-preserving symmetric-difference transformation for arbitrary real edge weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be an undirected graph, let \(T\subseteq V(G)\) have even cardinality, and let \(c:E(G)\to\mathbb R\) be additive on edge sets.
