knowledge_statements.title: Lower-Quota Nonexistence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A minimal many-to-one instance where lower-quota feasibility excludes every stable matching.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let residents be \(R=\{r_1,r_2\}\), hospitals be \(H=\{h_1,h_2\}\), and set \(\ell_{h_i}=u_{h_i}=1\) for \(i=1,2\). The acceptable pairs are \((r_1,h_1)\), \((r_2,h_1)\), and \((r_2,h_2)\). Resident \(r_2\) prefers \(h_1\) to \(h_2\), and hospital \(h_1\) prefers \(r_2\) to \(r_1\); all other comparisons are immaterial. Quota feasibility forces the unique matching \(M=\{(r_1,h_1),(r_2,h_2)\}\). The pair \((r_2,h_1)\) blocks \(M\), because both endpoints prefer each other to their assigned partners. Hence no matching is simultaneously stable and lower-quota feasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lower quotas force a unique feasible assignment, but that assignment is blocked; therefore a quota-feasible stable matching need not exist.
assumptions_latex: Preferences over acceptable partners are strict.
A full hospital may participate in a blocking pair by replacing a less-preferred assignee.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{M:M\text{ is stable}\}\cap\{M:M\text{ satisfies all lower and upper quotas}\}=\varnothing\).

notation.meaning: Lower and upper quotas of hospital h.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite counterexample is internally correct and counterexample is the appropriate content kind, but no inspectable citation or explicitly marked standard-field rationale is supplied.

children.title: Common-Quota Nonexistence
children.top_down_role: Stable-outcome failures caused by shared quota restrictions.

knowledge_statements.title: Common-Quota Nonexistence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite certificate of nonexistence under upper quotas shared by sets of contracts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a finite contract set and let \(\mathcal Q\subseteq 2^X\) carry common upper quotas \(q_Q\). Call \(M\subseteq X\) feasible when each agent signs at most one contract and \(|M\cap Q|\le q_Q\) for every \(Q\in\mathcal Q\). Fix the agents' strict preferences and the quota-constrained institutional choice rule \(C\). A nonexistence certificate is a function \(b\) assigning to every individually rational feasible \(M\) a contract \(b(M)\in X\setminus M\) such that its agent prefers \(b(M)\) to its assignment in \(M\) and \(b(M)\in C(M\cup\{b(M)\})\). Such a certificate exists exactly when no stable feasible matching exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonexistence is certified by exhibiting a quota-compatible blocking contract for every individually rational feasible matching.
assumptions_latex: The institutional choice rule \(C\) is fixed and explicitly evaluable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists b\text{ as specified}\iff\nexists M\text{ that is individually rational, common-quota feasible, and stable}.\)

notation.meaning: Family of contract sets sharing quotas.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Certificate is an appropriate content kind, but the equivalence assumes that every unstable feasible matching has a singleton blocking contract. Common-quota choice models may instead permit setwise blocking, so an authoritative source must specify the choice and stability definitions and the hypotheses ensuring singleton witnesses.

children.title: Quota Feasibility Failures
children.top_down_role: Instances where quota requirements admit no feasible assignment.

knowledge_statements.title: Quota Feasibility Failures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lower- and upper-quota feasibility represented as a circulation problem, with a minimum-cut certificate of failure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite bipartite acceptability graph with resident set \(R\) and hospital set \(H\), construct a network with arcs \(s\to r\) of bounds \([0,1]\), arcs \(r\to h\) of bounds \([0,1]\) for acceptable pairs, arcs \(h\to t\) of bounds \([\ell_h,u_h]\), and an arc \(t\to s\) of bounds \([0,|R|]\). Integral feasible circulations are in bijection with quota-feasible matchings. Apply the standard lower-bound transformation and introduce a super-source \(\sigma\) and super-sink \(\tau\). If \(D\) is the total capacity of the arcs leaving \(\sigma\), then a quota-feasible matching exists exactly when a maximum \(\sigma\)-to-\(\tau\) flow has value \(D\), equivalently when every arc leaving \(\sigma\) is saturated. If the maximum value is less than \(D\), a minimum \(\sigma\)-to-\(\tau\) cut of capacity less than \(D\) is a checkable certificate of infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quota feasibility reduces to a lower-bounded circulation. After the standard transformation, feasibility holds exactly when all super-source demand arcs can be saturated; otherwise a minimum cut of capacity below the total demand certifies failure.
assumptions_latex: \(0\le \ell_h\le u_h\) are integers for every \(h\in H\).
Each resident may be assigned to at most one acceptable hospital.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{A quota-feasible matching exists}\iff \operatorname{maxflow}(\sigma,\tau)=D.\)

notation.meaning: Super-source and super-sink in the transformed network.
Total capacity of the arcs leaving the super-source.

children.title: Stability–Feasibility Conflict
children.top_down_role: Regimes where feasible assignments exist but stability remains unattainable.

knowledge_statements.title: Stability–Feasibility Conflict
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates combinatorial quota feasibility from preference-based stability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a finite matching instance with preferences and quotas. Let \(\mathcal F\) denote the matchings satisfying acceptability, assignment capacities, and all lower, upper, or common quotas, and let \(\mathcal S\) denote the stable matchings under the specified blocking rule. A stability–feasibility conflict occurs precisely when \(\mathcal F\ne\varnothing\) but \(\mathcal F\cap\mathcal S=\varnothing\). Equivalently, quota constraints are jointly feasible, yet every \(M\in\mathcal F\) admits a blocking pair or blocking coalition. Thus a feasibility certificate alone cannot certify the existence of a stable quota-feasible outcome.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quotas are feasible but conflict with stability exactly when every quota-feasible matching has a blocking pair or coalition.
assumptions_latex: The feasible family \(\mathcal F\) and the applicable blocking rule are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal F\ne\varnothing\ \land\ \mathcal F\cap\mathcal S=\varnothing\iff (\forall M\in\mathcal F)(\exists B)(B\text{ blocks }M).\)

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role fits the leaf and the equivalence is definitional once stability is fixed. An inspectable source is still required to identify the applicable blocking objects and establish that instability is witnessed by a pair or coalition in the intended quota model.

children.title: Quota-Repair Regimes
children.top_down_role: Structured quota relaxations used to recover feasibility or stable outcomes.

knowledge_statements.title: Quota-Repair Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pareto representation of integral lower-quota reductions and upper-quota expansions under a quota-independent stability rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be finite and let \(\ell,u\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^{H}\) satisfy \(\ell_h\le u_h\) for every \(h\in H\). Define the admissible repair set by \(\mathcal A=\{(\alpha,\beta)\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^{H}\times\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^{H}:\alpha\le\ell\}\), where a repair replaces the quotas by \(\ell'=\ell-\alpha\) and \(u'=u+\beta\). Suppose stability is determined by fixed preferences and a blocking rule independent of the quota values, and let \(\mathcal S(\ell',u')\) be the stable matchings feasible under \((\ell',u')\). The repair region is \(\mathcal R=\{(\alpha,\beta)\in\mathcal A:\mathcal S(\ell-\alpha,u+\beta)\ne\varnothing\}\). If \((\alpha,\beta)\in\mathcal R\) and \((\widehat\alpha,\widehat\beta)\in\mathcal A\) satisfy \(\widehat\alpha\ge\alpha\) and \(\widehat\beta\ge\beta\), then \((\widehat\alpha,\widehat\beta)\in\mathcal R\). Thus \(\mathcal R\) is upward closed within \(\mathcal A\), and its Pareto-minimal elements are the undominated quota repairs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Among admissible integral repairs, further lowering lower quotas or raising upper quotas preserves existence when the stability rule itself is independent of quotas. The repair region is therefore upward closed, and its undominated points are the Pareto-minimal repairs.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is finite and the original quotas are nonnegative integers with \(\ell_h\le u_h\).
Repair vectors are integral, nonnegative, and satisfy \(\alpha\le\ell\).
Stability depends only on the matching, fixed preferences, and a blocking rule independent of quota values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\alpha,\beta)\in\mathcal R\land(\widehat\alpha,\widehat\beta)\in\mathcal A\land(\widehat\alpha,\widehat\beta)\ge(\alpha,\beta)\Rightarrow(\widehat\alpha,\widehat\beta)\in\mathcal R.\)

notation.meaning: Integral lower-quota reductions and upper-quota expansions.
Stable matchings feasible under repaired quotas.
Quota-repair region within the admissible repair set.

knowledge_statements.title: Multidimensional Stability Hardness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Three-sided matching with preferences over partner pairs and blocking triples.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider three disjoint sets \(A,B,C\) of equal size. Each agent has a strict ranking of its acceptable pairs from the other two sets. A perfect three-dimensional matching partitions \(A\cup B\cup C\) into triples. A triple \((a,b,c)\) blocks a matching when each of \(a,b,c\) strictly prefers the other two agents to the pair assigned in its current triple. The decision problem asking whether a perfect matching with no blocking triple exists is NP-complete. Membership in \(\mathrm{NP}\) follows because perfection and the absence of blocking triples can be checked in polynomial time from an explicitly represented preference profile.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With three agent classes and preferences over partner pairs, deciding whether a perfect matching without a blocking triple exists is NP-complete.
assumptions_latex: Preferences are strict and explicitly represented.
A blocking triple requires unanimous strict improvement.
The requested outcome is a perfect three-dimensional matching.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\textsc{Perfect-3D-Stable-Matching-Existence}\text{ is NP-complete}.\)

notation.meaning: A feasible triple containing one agent from each class.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Complexity bound is the correct role, but NP-completeness depends on the exact three-dimensional stability variant, admissibility structure, preference representation, and perfection requirement. A theorem-level source with these exact restrictions is necessary.
